author: Robert Jordan
introFa: کتاب «Winter's Heart» نوشته Robert Jordan یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح B2 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «Winter's Heart»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

content: 1 ALL MAGIC HAS A SMELL. For some, it smells like warm spring breezes or a cold mountain top just as the sun strikes its peak. For others, it may have a smell of home. Of warm bread and big down comforters. Niamh inhaled the scent of her own magic, nutmeg and rosemary, as it thrummed inside of her, preparing itself to heal. The young boy in front of her looked at her with trepidation, as if he expected her magic to hurt him instead of mend. Niamh could feel these changes in temperaments. Grabbing a handful of rosemary, just to ease the sting, Niamh laid a gentle hand on the boy's exposed forearm. She looked him in the eye. "This might hurt a little, Bjorn. Can you be brave for me?" Bjorn nodded, determination setting his mouth, even if she caught it wiggling slightly. Niamh let her magic unspool itself like a ribbon, softly letting it flow through her hand, through the thread stitched into her glove, and into his arm. Bjorn hissed and fussed around a bit, squirming in his chair. Niamh only smiled kindly and continued. "Almost finished." She soothed, keeping her eyes on the boy's face as she felt her magic stitching together his bones as if he’d never broken them. The scent of her magic was stronger now, filling the whole room. Her gloved hands glowed a warm yellow against the boy's skin. Just as the last of her magic mended the last bit of broken bone, she finished off her work with an extra burst of soothing energy. Just enough to quiet the other aches and pains she felt in his muscles, but not enough to put him to sleep. Niamh had only just removed her hands before Bjorn was inspecting his arm with wide eyes. Niamh stifled a laugh. She’d seen that look so many times before, but it never failed to amuse

her. Living in Eira, the country with the most connection to the ancient magics of the natural world, and still many of its people were still so enthralled by simple healings. It was endearing. “There. All fixed.” She announced cheerily, rising from her seat at the kitchen table. His mother smiled gratefully from the sink. “Thank you for your trouble. He won’t be out climbing trees again for a while.” The boy’s mother gave her son a look full to the brim with a warning. “Right, Bjorn? You’ll be thanking Miss Niamh.” Bjorn nodded quickly. Niamh gathered her coat from the hanger by the door and smiled over her shoulder. “It’s no trouble at all. Just be sure to be more careful.” She closed the front door of the humble cottage with a thud of heavy wood against the doorpost. A bit of snow fell from the low roof, adding to the tall pile nearing the windowsills. Fresh, mountain air greeted her as Niamh made her way down the switch-backs of the path. Clear skies and a sharp wind from the North made for a colder day than usual. Niamh gathered her fur collar about her neck more snuggly and headed down the path toward home. Well, home away from home, in this case. She lived at the castle, located in the heart of Ahealarth, the capital city, right in the center of Eira. She didn’t live in the castle, merely slept there. Her home away from home was her healer’s cottage, snugly in the back of the ice gardens within the castle walls. She curated every inch of that place, and every part of it was her own. Her heart thrilled with excitement for the comfort at the end of her walk. She walked faster. This particular house call, one of many in her usual week, happened to be a mere twenty minute walk from the city. Between her growling stomach and the particularly frigid temperatures that day, she was quite ready to be indoors for the rest of the evening. Her thoughts drifted to the hot mug of tea that awaited her; to the blazing fire that she was eager to ignite in her fireplace. The sun began to set behind the mountains, casting everything in a deep orange light. This was her favorite time of day, when everything felt cozy and warm, despite the deep snow on the ground and craggy mountain peaks above. Within minutes, the city appeared just over the hill. Warm browns and grays of the roofs flowed upward like lichen on the mountain side within the stone

walls, all leading to the centerpiece of all of Eira. The castle sat regally against the mountain behind it, the snow mingling with the icy structure of the outside. Golden light twinkled through the prisms of the five icy spires rising from it, creating a beacon of light for the entire city to see. It had been there for longer than anyone could remember. The first magicians of Eira had constructed it of ice, finely carved wood and stone, with the Grand Library in the center as a foundation of magic. Once her boots hit the slick stones of the streets of the city, it was a brisk walk through the wide avenue through the center of town to reach her destination. On her way, she purposefully didn't stop by any of the shops whose open doors called to her, nor any of the brightly lit taverns promising warm food and drink. Niamh was certain she would never reach her cozy haven if she saw anyone that she knew, so she did her best to keep her head down and her feet moving. PRINCE FANE LOOKED every bit the part he played. His dignified stature and handsome head of blond hair, his fine clothes. and steady gaze gave him an air of royalty. Fane’s days were filled with many of the activities anyone would expect of a prince, such as fencing, riding, archery, and reading on various topics. Reading was something he especially enjoyed, as it gave him a glimpse into the world outside the walls of his palace. A world he’d never seen for himself. Today was different. Fane stood in the royal stables, stroking his prize stallion’s nose. At the creak of leather boots behind him, he turned to see his friend and head guard standing in the open doorway. Rune’s auburn hair glowed red in the sunrise behind him, and his face was obscured by shadow. “Are you ready to leave, your Highness?” Rune asked. He carried two large saddlebags with him, already filled with whatever supplies they would need for the day’s hunt. Fane nodded, taking one of the bags from Rune. It was heavy, heavier than he would have expected. “We’re only going out for the day.” Fane commented, weighing

the bag in his hand with emphasis. “Don’t you think this is a bit much for a hunting trip?” “You’ve never been hunting,” Rune said lightly, strapping his bag to his own horse. “So how would you know?” “I suppose you’re right.” Fane laughed. Rune was the only person that dared to joke with him as if he was a friend. All the other guards kept him at an arm’s length- the price of being the prince. “And that means you have, Rune? Been hunting?” Fane continued, trying to keep the conversation going to keep himself awake. “Of course,” Rune replied, grinning. “One must sometimes hunt for their food living in Eira.” Fane sometimes forgot that his friend wasn’t native to Aridia. Rune spoke with a slight accent, and he was considerably taller than the average Aridian as well. “And you’re sure we’ll be back before sundown?” Fane added, trying to hide the tint of anxiety in his tone. Rune raised an incredulous eyebrow. “It’s your birthday- that’s the last thing you should be worrying about.” Though that hardly answered his question, Fane had nothing to say in protest. His elder brother, King Friedhelm, would give him a tongue lashing if he knew Fane was going out. Fane had hardly left the palace, save for special events and appearances, and he knew Friedhelm would have intended to keep it that way. Rune had been the one to suggest this hunting trip. Fane hadn’t told anyone, save his closest guards, and the party was up early that morning to avoid being seen. Rune had assured him that the morning hours were when all the game would be out in the forest. Fane strapped his leather vambraces to his forearms, his leather guard to one shoulder, and mounted his horse. His fine prince’s hunting leathers displayed the seal of Aridia, an identifying mark just in case he were ever lost. That thought comforted him as he and Rune led their horses out into the dim light of the morning. The pair rode quickly toward the castle courtyard’s gate, joined by four other guards all dressed and supplied for the wilderness. One among them was a man named Daener, Fane’s other closest friend. He had dark hair, unusual for an Aridian, and a large, beautifully carved hunting knife on his belt.

“Your Highness.” Daener greeted, a cordial hand to his chest. Fane nodded back. “What are we hunting for today?” Fane asked. Daener was silent only a moment longer than what was comfortable.“You’ll know it when you see it.” He replied. Rune straightened in the saddle where he was on the other side of Fane. Fane thought no more on the matter. He trusted that the other men would know what to do if it came to it. The gates opened, and the party made their way down the silent streets of the capital city. They reached the edge of town sooner than Fane thought, approaching the ever-open gates. The sunrise glowed a deep red behind the white mountains in the distance, filling the sky with swaths of rich color. As the warm winds of Aridia hit his face and rustled his hair, Fane didn’t care what kind of punishment or verbal thrashing he would get when he got home. Fane stared into the deep forest beyond. The trees in Aridia grew strong and tall, and their forests were thick with greenery and all manners of wildlife. He'd always seen these woods from his window, but had never stepped foot past their boundary. The others plunged forward with confidence into the darkness. The forest was just as exhilarating as Fane always dreamed. There was nothing here to keep him contained; no walls of stone, windows of glass or iron. He could see nothing but trees for miles ahead. He felt the damp richness of the air here, so different and full of life compared to the stuffy, hot air inside the castle’s walls. He was suddenly a new person. The path in front of them was nothing more than dirt, with edges hidden by moss and roots of trees. Fane rode at the head of the group. His guards chatted amongst themselves behind him as he busied himself with admiring the scenery. After a short while, Rune appeared beside him. Fane swallowed his sigh of relief that he didn’t have to pretend to enjoy being excluded. “The forest is much different than the palace gardens, don’t you think, your Highness?” Rune said pleasantly. Rune’s leather gloves creaked as he gripped his horse’s reins much more tightly than Fane thought necessary.

“Yes,” Fane answered. The sun was over the mountains now, casting a warm light through the golden-green leaves of the trees. Sunlight dappled the path in front of them, inviting Fane to continue forward. “I much prefer the wildness of this place.” “I’m glad to hear you say so,” Rune said. After a moment, Rune lowered his voice. “Fane, listen to me. You must stay close to me, whatever happens. And don’t get off of your horse unless you have to.” Rune had never used Fane’s shortened name before. Not in the entire time he’d been employed at the castle. “You must do whatever I tell you, and you must only trust me. You can’t trust anyone else in Aridia, not even your brother.” “But why?” Fane asked, lowering his own voice. Why would Rune be saying these things? And why now, of all times? “Just trust me,” Rune said, a warning in his voice. “I can’t tell you now, but I will.” Just as Fane was about to reply, he spotted a stag ahead on the path. Its coat was as white as the stars, its antlers ancient and twisting into each other. Its eyes glowed with an unnatural light as gold and green as the trees above them. “Is that-?” Fane began to ask. As he looked around him, it didn’t seem that any of his party saw what he did. It ran. Fane spurred his horse forward in pursuit, Rune’s warnings forgotten.

2 NIAMH CONTINUED TO the castle, into the courtyard, passing guards standing in shining silver armor, accented with blue. The colors of Eira. The courtyard was a wide open area, flanked by walls of both stone and ice, intermingling naturally by design. The wind picked up on her walk, and now blew snow down from the many gabled roofs of the castle, creating a small snow storm in the courtyard. It whistled around the spires, bringing an ominous tone to a once- cheery winter day. This only served to motivate her to step into jog, closing the wide expanse quickly. Above the tall wooden door, carved into the stone, was a snow leopard on the right and a wolf on the left. They were caught in a never-moving duel forever etched in the stone. Snow leopard for courage and tenacity. Wolf for strength and self-reliance. All four ideals that Eirans held dear to their hearts. Above the both of them, its small feet only barely touching the heads of the two battling predators, was a white mink, carved from ice and integrated into the stone. The symbol for healers. Around the three animals were ice stars set into the wall. It was designed so that when the late evening light shone onto it, it would reflect light into the entire courtyard. Niamh smiled as she walked under their banner, pushing one of the heavy double doors open and shutting it behind her. An empty lobby stretched before her, the wind howling outside giving it an air of loneliness. Bathed in a cold, blue-white light from the outside sun filtering through the snowy-glass roof, the entrance was a stunning wintery display of artistry. High above Niamh's head, arched ceilings magically formed of ice were further decorated with the patterns that would be found on snowflakes, though enlarged and spread outward from the center of the room.

The oldest parts of the castle were constructed of heavy stones, some areas were carved from the mountain itself. As one climbed upward, to the public areas, to the areas for nobility and council meetings and gatherings, more and more ice was used in construction. It glittered and fractured the light coming through, creating beautiful patterns and illuminating just where it needed to be. It was the duty of the Head Mage to maintain the ice walls and floors periodically, going back for generations. As far back as the castle had been first built, carved into the mountain like a sentinel of civilization in the wild country. The heritage of mages, stretching back hundreds of years. The ethereal elegance of gold and silver patterns under clear floors and soaring walls and ceilings of ice contrasted with the hardy stone and carved wood of the lived-in areas of the palace. Great chandeliers of the clearest glass hung in the lobby, three in a row, their candles never going out, nor dripping down to nothing. As one walked forward toward the grand staircase at the end of the long room, more ice animals watched as they passed. Mounted on pedestals built into the white stone columns, a different animal looked on at their opposite, guarding the castle and its inhabitants with a silent gaze. An antlered deer lifted its front legs as if bounding over an obstacle. Tradition. Another snow leopard crouched directly across. Courage. Diagonal from that was a snowbear, lifting one massive paw. Power. A raven across from the snowbear, seemingly restless on its icy perch. Wisdom. The parade continued, each animal representing dearly held values of Eira. At the end of the main hall was a grand staircase crafted of ice. Mist fell down the steps like a slow waterfall. A man stood at the top, studying a huge painting of the royal family. His fiery red hair and equally crimson robes gave him away before she reached him. Master Hael, her teacher under which she was apprenticed and the Head Mage of Eira, was older than he looked. Many people thought he was about one hundred or so, but he appeared young thanks to the overabundant magic flowing through his veins. Though his demeanor might have given him away, as he often showed his age by being generally irritable and cantankerous. A great, tawny bird sat on his shoulder, and it looked at her as she walked up the steps. The fire in its eyes flickered as she reached

the top, as if in greeting. Her master didn't turn around as she approached. "Niamh. That took you long enough." Today must have been one of his grumpier days. "Yes, sir. I'm sorry about that." She stepped up to stand beside him. The painting was at least as tall as the wall. Three painted faces gazed out solemnly, watching over the front door to their castle. The painting was of the royal family. The current king, Airem, hadn't started a family of his own yet, so it was of his parents and him when he was young. All three figures possessed solemn, serious golden eyes and hair black as midnight. Hael turned to the portrait towering above them with something that resembled sentimentality in his expression. "He should have been married a long time ago. Thirty years old and without a queen." He paused, his tone turned prickly again. "The new queen will be arriving soon. I expect that you'll be on your best behavior." As if I'm ever not? Niamh thought, stifling a smile. Niamh prided herself on her best behavior. It kept her out of trouble. "I may be your master, but a king or queen can dismiss you without either my knowledge or permission. I have the protection of my position, but you, as my apprentice, do not." Hael crossed his arms over one another, the red and orange of his robes mingling and hiding whatever skin might have shown. In answer to the question that Niamh didn't have the chance to ask, her master continued: "She comes from the kingdom to the east, on the sea. Corseils. She will have been traveling for some time, so she likely won't be in the best of spirits when she arrives. No one but Airem has laid eyes on her before." Master and apprentice stood at the top of the stairs staring at the painting. Hael was known for these long stretches of silence, and Niamh had learned to wait until they were finished. The only sound in the great, tall room was the soft sigh of the mist and their own breathing. Speaking up would be contrary. And Niamh strived never to be contrary. "We’re running low on several supplies, from what I've noticed." Hael said finally, cutting through the silence. "You'll be going down to the Wizard to retrieve them as soon as the wedding concludes." Niamh bristled inwardly. Wasn't she above these sorts of trips now? These little errands were better suited to one of the castle aides or someone of similar standing. That thought was soon

followed with an inner scolding. Healers aren't prideful. Outwardly, she plastered an agreeable smile on her face. She'd worked hard for her position, and she wasn't about to lose it over petty excuses. "Yes, sir." Niamh said cordially. The bird on Hael's shoulder ruffled its feathers, as if it could sense her displeasure. She shot it a look, as if to say "You're to keep your beak shut." Hael nodded thoughtfully, seemingly unaware of Niamh and the bird's discourse. "Bring me a list of the items that we need and I'll put in the order tomorrow." Niamh bowed slightly at the waist and backed up a few steps, before turning and trotting down the icy stairway. Her cottage waited for her at the edge of the castle's ice gardens, sitting like a homey oasis away from the high-browed politics of the castle. The outside was rustic and handbuilt of stone, so different from the rest of the castle. Niamh didn't know who built it, but it had seen many generations of healers and apprentices over the decades. It had a homespun element to it, which made her feel right, comfortable and familiar. Upon opening the door, the fire magic in her gloves made the hearth jump to life, crackling with a merry fire at her waved hand. She gazed at the small red flower, so meticulously stitched into her glove. A wave of nostalgia washed over her. It had been her first thread. The first flower in her glove that she'd stitched herself after much struggle to attain the thread when she'd first been training in the academy in the city. Fire was usually much later in a mage's training, but she'd been given a thread made from a phoenix's feather before she'd graduated, and she put it to good use. Niamh was never sure who had sent her the thread. Chamomile, echinacea, lavender, and other dried flowers all hung in neat bundles on twine that crisscrossed the low ceiling of the cottage. She smiled up at their dried leaves and blooms. There were plenty of rare herbs that Niamh had taken care to gather over her year at the castle, painstakingly drying and preserving them for later use. One round window at the back of the cottage let the light stream in, illuminating her workspace. The walls were nothing but shelves full of hundreds of books, rows of bottles and vials of various sizes, and collections of artifacts and magical objects. All within arm’s reach were her bottles and jars, containing more magical ingredients. Things like bottled night

sky, gathered by mages from the tops of some of the tallest mountains in Eira, useful for sleeping tinctures. One of her rarest acquisitions was a bottle of mermaid tears, straight from the mages of Corseils on the eastern coast. Hael had gone to great pains to get it for her, and it had taken months to arrive. To her knowledge, there were only a few bottles in existence in the entire world. Nothing was to be denied to the Head Mage, however, so his apprentice reaped the benefits. Her hand fell affectionately on a jar of crushed frostflowers, taken straight from her hometown, right around her front door of the house that her brother had built for the two of them. Niamh liked to think that it was infused with love and affection, just by its origin, and adding it to any medicine of hers would make it that much more effective. She pulled her stone pestle closer and set to work crushing a few flowers. FANE DIDN’T PAY ANY heed to the branches reaching for his face, one right after another, nor for the shouts of his companions behind him. There was only wind against his face and the rush of the forest flying by. The party gave chase for several minutes. Fane’s stallion galloped far ahead of the rest, so far that he could hardly hear his companions anymore. Just as suddenly as the stag had appeared, Fane found himself flung out of the forest’s cover and into a wide open glade. Golden waves of grass fluttered in the breeze. The stag stopped suddenly at the opposite edge of the field. It turned, and watched Fane with an eerie, steady gaze. Fane slowed his horse, the field and wind and sky darkening, slipping into the back of his mind as he locked eyes with the stag. Prince. Its mighty head nodded slightly, as if acknowledging him. Fane vaguely felt his prince’s braid brush against his jaw, the warm wind whisper through his hair and bringing the ancient voice to him across the field. “Who are you?” Fane asked, his voice lost in the great distance. The stag didn't answer, but slowly turned and glided into the dark forest beyond. Fane couldn't bring himself to give chase again.

The wind resumed stronger, ominously whipping through the grass. Fane couldn’t move. He was snapped out of whatever trance he’d been put in by the jerk of the reins. “Fane!” Rune’s voice shouted, right near him. Fane looked up to see Rune next to him. His horse was breathing heavily and Rune himself was sweating. His hunting leathers were splattered with something wet and dark. Blood. “What are you doing out here?” Rune demanded, spurring his horse into a gallop. Fane’s horse followed suit, being dragged by the reins. “What’s going on?” Fane could hardly breathe. Why would Rune have blood on him? As they neared the edge of the field, shouts rang out across the grass from the forest he’d just left. The clang of steel against steel, the thud of steel against flesh. Chaos erupted behind them, as Rune led their horses into the cover of the forest. They sped down the path a little further, before Rune’s horse screamed in pain. It collapsed on the path. Rune fell to the ground, narrowly rolling out of the way of his horse falling on him. Fane halted his horse frantically. Just as it skidded to a stop, Fane leapt from his saddle and to Rune’s side. Without a word, Rune scrambled to his feet. Another arrow shot out of the cover of trees and caught Fane’s horse in the neck. Fane darted to Rune’s side, before both of them crouched in the thick brush nearby, Rune jerked Fane’s hood over his head. “What’s going on?” Fane whispered, trying to peer through the leaves. Rune shushed him with a sharp hiss. Fane managed to get a glimpse of Rune’s fallen horse. An arrow, one of his guards’ arrows, protruded from one of its front legs. Why would these criminals have my guards’ arrows? Fane crouched lower, Rune followed suit. His hands clenched and unclenched over the hilt of his dagger. Not as soon as Rune hushed him, boots appeared on the path. Whoever it was left footprints of blood in the dirt, and their sword was stained already. The breath caught in Fane’s throat. Surely his guards must have been ambushed while he was in the field. And if he were back there with them, if the stag hadn’t distracted him, he would have been there too. “We know you’re here.” The man said. He lingered in front of where Rune and Fane hid for half a second before continuing

forward. “Your horses are here. So you can’t be far behind.” Fane shivered involuntarily. Rune’s blue eyes darted to meet his. Stay here. They seemed to say. Fane nodded. Another assassin passed by their hiding place. His sword, too, left droplets of blood behind him. Another moment, and he was gone. Rune grabbed Fane by his shoulders, the urgency clear in his face. “Whatever happens, don’t go back, Fane. Don’t go home. You have to keep going toward Eira.” Rune rasped. His hands dug into Fane’s shoulders, making him flinch. “You have to find the Pheonix. Whether I’m with you or not, you have to go toward the mountains. Do that, and you’ll reach Eira. The Pheonix will help you.” Fane nodded silently. He had no idea what all of this meant, but he trusted Rune. “Your Highness?” Daener’s voice called from the path. He sounded frantic, panicked. Daener was his friend, too. Perhaps he wanted to escape with them. Fane stood from the brush without thinking, even with Rune’s jerk on his sleeve. “Oh, there you are, my Prince.” Daener said, relief clear on his face. “I was worried for you.” “What’s going on?” Fane asked. “Where are the other guards?” “They’re dead, your Highness.” Daener answered. He drew his dagger from his sheath slowly. Fane heard the frantic rustle of the bushes behind him as Rune stood from his hiding place. “Just like you’re about to be.” Fane hardly had time to step back before Daener swiped for his chest. Fane stumbled back, fumbling for his own dagger. Rune intervened, disarming Daener with a swipe. Daener drew his sword and countered Rune’s dagger, engaging him in battle. Fane watched helplessly for the tense few seconds this went on. Rune must have already been nursing an injury Fane hadn’t seen, because blood was already staining his side red from under his hunting leather. “Fane!” Rune shouted, his voice strained. Don’t just stand here. Despite the inner urgency, Fane couldn’t move. The bow strapped to his horse called for him to do something. But Fane stayed where he was. “Fane!” Rune barked again. This snapped Fane into action, as he

dashed for his horse. The buckles were far too slow to be undone, his hands shaking with adrenaline. He freed his bow. Daener hissed in pain as Rune landed a blow. Fane drew an arrow from his quiver, and aimed it at Daener. Something in him hesitated. This man was his friend. Both of them were. How could he kill one of them in cold blood? Fane drew his bowstring back, it creaked, the sound loud even in the chaos. Daener struck Rune’s ribs, driving his sword deep into his side. Rune stumbled back gasping, blood staining his leather armor and white shirt underneath. Fane let the arrow fly. It drove itself into Daener’s shoulder, though it hardly deterred him. Daener darted toward him, taking Fane’s collar in his good hand, and brandishing his sword at Fane’s throat with the other. “Why would you do this?” Fane rasped. Daener’s fist pressed into his throat, making his eyes burn. Daener didn’t answer, merely inclined his head to show Fane a flash of his neck. He sported a new tattoo that Fane hadn’t seen before- the image of what looked like a jewel, broken down the middle, the jagged edges dripping blood. Fane barely had time to register this before a sword protruded from Daener’s chest. He gasped and crumpled to the ground. Rune stood behind him, panting, his sword wet with Daener’s blood. The chaos in the forest was getting closer. Men were shouting, jeering, and laughing as they crossed the field. They were about to be overwhelmed. “We need to leave.” Rune gasped, stumbling toward their horses. In the second that Rune’s back was turned, an arrow whistled from the trees, embedding itself in the bark near Fane’s head. Fane jumped, darting to where Rune stood. The two men stood back to back, Fane scanning the trees for their attacker. Another arrow flew from the leaves, catching Fane’s arm and sending a shooting pain through his body. A bowstring twanged behind him. Fane turned just in time to see the arrow flying toward his chest. All Fane saw was a flash of auburn as Rune jumped in front of him and hurled his dagger into the trees. The traitorous guard fell to the ground with a crash. Rune said nothing, breathing heavily, as he limped toward his

horse. Fane followed behind. As Rune attempted to mount, he fell backward, buckling to the ground. “Rune!” Fane gasped, coming to his side. Rune coughed, a horrible, wet sound, as blood fell from his mouth. Two arrows protruded from his chest, one of them already broken at the fletching. Fane cradled Rune’s head in one hand, desperately pressing into the wound in his friend’s side with the other. The blood was coming too fast- there was no stopping it then. “Rune, I’m sorry.” Fane grit his teeth. I should have listened. There was too much blood, it covered his hands, running like water. Rune struggled for air. He grasped Fane’s forearm tightly. “You need to leave, Fane.” He murmured, his voice weakening by the second. "Go to Eira. Find the Phoenix in the mountains." Rune continued. Fane could hardly hear him through the pounding in his head. His friend's voice was becoming weaker every painful second that ticked by. Rune slowly reached under his leather chest piece, pulling a simple pair of rings on a chain from under it. He pushed it into Fane’s shaking hand, closing his fingers over it. “Take these home for me...” He whispered. A cruel laugh sounded from the trees, only a few hundred feet from where they were. “Where are you, prince?” A man shouted. The traitor’s crashed through the brush. There were at least five of them. Too many for Fane to fight on his own. At the same moment, the Stag, the same from the field, bounded over the brush Fane and Rune had taken shelter in. It stood expectantly, its back exposed to Fane. Come with me, Prince Fane. It whispered. “Leave, Fane.” Rune rasped, “Go!” With hardly a thought, Fane dashed to the first opportunity he had. He scrambled atop the Stag’s back, grasping the fur on its neck. As he mounted, the other assassins appeared on the path, their eyes lighting with a murderous joy as they spotted him. Fane took one last look at his friend dying on the ground, before the Stag flew down the path, faster than any horse. “That’s right, run, prince!” One of his former guards shouted after him. “We’ll find you, wherever you go!” Fane could do nothing as he held on with all of his strength. Branches of trees whipped his face, stinging his eyes, filling his ears
with nothing but the rush of leaves. The Stag took him in the direction of the peaks scraping the red sky, and Fane left his life as a prince behind him in the blood-soaked forest of his old country.

3 THE DAY BEFORE THE wedding, the king threw a welcoming party to celebrate the arrival of his new queen. The new queen, still a lady, arrived earlier in the afternoon, attended by many courtiers from her home country. Niamh hadn't been present when the opulent sleigh had first pulled up to the front gates, but she'd heard from the servants there that it was like Maire was already royalty. The king must have gone to great lengths to provide such opulence. She'd thought, dressing in the only fine clothing she had. Her dress was handed down from her mother. A simple garment made of a dark blue material, and decorated with small white flowers along the neckline. Niamh hadn't thought to buy anything nicer in the time she'd been in the castle, simply because there was previously never a reason to. The first event of the evening was a grand dinner, to which all the nobility and gentry from around the kingdom had been invited. Eira was a fairly small country, and not as rich or populated as neighboring kingdoms, but the guests arrived on time and in their finest clothes. Streamers of blue and white, floating lights in soft glowing colors, and dangling ice flowers hung from the ceiling of the dining room and the ballroom beyond. Weddings could go for days in Eira. Niamh imagined those for royalty might extend even longer. Hael sat at the long table at the king’s left, and Niamh sat next to him. Across the way, the Lady Maire sat at the king’s right and Maewyn, her cousin, apparently, next to her. This put Niamh directly in front of Maewyn who, Niamh was slowly realizing, never ran out of things to say. Maire showed mild disinterest in whatever it was Maewyn was prattling on about, and slid her green eyes toward Niamh briefly.

When Maewyn had sufficiently reached the end of her list of talking points with her cousin, she turned her bright eyes toward Niamh and she could see her bringing up another mental list of questions for her. Niamh had successfully avoided her for the most part, but there was nowhere to run here in the prison of social graces. Niamh relented inwardly, motivated by the guilt of avoiding their guest. “So...” Niamh began, clearing her throat so her voice could be more clearly heard above the din of the dining hall. “What brought you to Eira with your cousin?” “I came here for the same reason that many people do,” She said, grinning, “To study magic. Isn't this where magic comes from?” Doesn't she know the answer? Niamh thought. She replied instead with a light “Oh? Yes, it is.” A deep suspicion bloomed inside of her. Maewyn looked positively mischievous, as if she was sitting on some great secret. "So when do you start at the academy, then?" Niamh asked. Maewyn didn't look to be much younger than herself, which was far too old to be just starting a magical education. "There's an academy, here?!" Maewyn's eyes widened, as if this was the first time she was hearing about it. Niamh resisted the urge to quirk an eyebrow. The suspicion grew larger. Maewyn, unfortunately, continued. ”I’ve heard so many stories of the great Phoenix Mage back in Corseils, and I wanted to meet him for myself.” Maewyn said, nodding in Hael’s direction. If Hael heard her, he didn’t show it, being completely entrenched in some serious looking conversation with the king. Maewyn shifted excitedly in her chair as Niamh flushed, suddenly being more interested in the soup in front of her than before. "I've come to train to be his apprentice!" Maewyn finally crowed, as if she could hold on to her secret no longer. "Oh." Niamh's tone was no longer light, her face growing even hotter. She was acutely aware of how childish that sounded, even as she tried to tamp down on all the injustice rising inside of her. "I guess you've got some competition now." Maewyn teased, grinning. After everyone had eaten their fill, the party continued in the ballroom. Sometime later, Niamh stood awkwardly with her

champagne glass near one of the small doorways leading to the gardens. Although she'd been living in the castle for almost a year, she was still not socially versed in parties and balls. She occasionally made small talk with whoever happened to pass by her in between dances, but kept to herself for the most part; observing the swirling dancers and elegantly dressed courtiers. Niamh peered across the space to see Maire standing alone as well. She was hard to miss in her deep crimson gown. It was tight across the top, with a dipping sweetheart neckline that exposed more cleavage than Niamh had thought possible. At her waist was a cage-like corset with swirling patterns, the skirt of the dress flaring out from it creating a mountain of flowing fabric. Silver embroidery matching the corset decorated the hem and sleeve, accentuating the silvery-white of her hair beautifully. Hael had guilted her earlier that day about her apparent lack of manners in avoiding introducing herself to her new queen. As awkward as she felt, as if she herself was ill-fitting for the higher rank that she possessed, Niamh knew that she needed to do what was expected of her. Here we go. Niamh thought to herself. She strode across the ballroom, doing her best to appear more confident than she felt. Upon her arrival, Maire acknowledged her presence with a blank stare, as Niamh dipped courteously. “I thought I might formally introduce myself, Lady.” She said, “My name is Niamh Sagesinger. I’m studying to be Head Mage under Master Hael here at the castle.” Maire made no indication that this information was at all relevant to her, so Niamh continued. “I..um.. I grew up here in Eira, in Wolfrau. How are you enjoying our fair country?” Maire turned her head to stare out at the mingling guests in their bright colors. The silence between them went on a moment longer than what was comfortable, and just as Niamh was about to give up, Maire answered in a distant voice. “It’s...charming. I suppose.” Niamh smiled kindly, “Y-Yes, I do agree-“ “If you consider crude manners and sleeping on the floor with the horses charming.” Maire’s green eyes slid to the side, noticeably gazing at Niamh’s attire in a sweeping fashion. “Did you rip that from some impoverished laundress in that little village of yours?” Maire’s voice was all at once cold and needling.

Niamh glanced down at her own modest dress, suddenly aware of the older style. Her sleeves came to a soft point at her hands, handmade ivory lace peeking from the ends of her sleeves and the rounded neckline at her collarbone. It had a shorted hem, allowing her gray laced boots to be displayed, and a black sash at the waist. The rest of the dress was a deep midnight blue, her favorite color. She admitted to herself that it wasn’t the fanciest or the most stylish, but she had indeed brought it with her from her mountain home and kept it in good condition with pride. It was perfectly fine for the small gatherings and bonfires at home, but... “Um, yes, I did, actually. I need to get a newer gown sometime, I suppose.” Niamh looked down at her boots in embarrassment. Fingering her champagne glass self-consciously, suddenly feeling as if every eye was on her. Maire continued. “Not that I would expect an uncultured village doctor such as you to have any money, or taste for that matter, to buy such finery as to befit this court.” She looked straight ahead again. “You can at least look like you put forth some effort before appearing before me and your King.” “Um...” Niamh’s eyes stung, and she backed away subconsciously. “Y-yes. I suppose you’re right.” Niamh bowed again, her brimming eyes obscured by her bangs. “I will endeavor to improve my attire for the next time.” Maire smirked, satisfied. “See that you do.” Niamh turned and walked toward the gardens, leaving behind the happy guests and graceful music and bright lights of the ballroom. Heart beating fast and hands shaking, she opened the glass doors and stepped out into the silence of the night. Her half- empty glass abandoned on the palace steps. The next morning, as the castle was abuzz with preparations, Niamh quietly slipped from her room in the castle and out to the main road to town. There was only a few more hours before the wedding. The sun was shining, casting fragile blue shadows onto the fresh snow fall. The air was crisp, and she inhaled deeply savoring its freshness. As she walked down the main road to the market, she passed several sleighs filled with her fellow countrymen from across every village and township across Eira. People rode on horseback, and walked together in groups up the hill, chatting excitedly amongst themselves. Niamh strode in the opposite direction, a basket under her arm and her most recent allowance in

her cape pockets. The castle town of Ahealarth was a cramped, bustling place. Each business ran into the next, with apartments above, a design that was meant to keep heating costs low and residents close to each other. The town sloped downward from the castle, being built from the stony mountain sides and carved into the mountain itself. A strongly built, winding staircase of wood and stone and ice weaved between the buildings, creating large walkways and tiny alleys as one moved to the outskirts. This made any trip home to the castle more difficult if one was laden with parcels, as Niamh knew from personal experience. As she neared her favorite tailor, near to her old apartment, she listened to the streams of soft music coming from the heart of the city. Directly in the center of town was a magnificent kirk with a single spire, a magical light twinkling from the top of it. The elegant sanctuary dedicated to the Father of Lights. She smiled at it thoughtfully as she entered the warm shop. The jovial face of her oldest friend in the city greeted her, as Niamh was suddenly spotted from behind the counter. “Niamh!” The other woman filled the small space with her joy, laughing as she ran out to hug her. The pair exchanged pleasantries, with much cupping of faces and warm hugs. Her friend was pregnant, putting a rounded stomach between them. Niamh pulled her blue dress from its basket. “Is there anything you can do to help me with this, Ailish?” Niamh fingered the soft blue fabric, “It’s still in good shape, and I don’t really have the money for a new dress right now.” Ailish tsked and waved her hand dismissively. “Those dress shops are always overpriced and everyone knows it.” She thought for a moment, “I think I have just the thing.” She waddled over behind the counter and pulled out a soft, sheer fabric that rippled from the bolt. "I'll work on it right now, as long as you'll stay for tea.” Niamh laughed lightly. "What else could I do?" Ailish set to work immediately, pinning and humming and ripping into Niamh's beloved dress with gusto and no shortage of precision. Niamh watched nervously, sipping her tea with furrowed brows. "Are you enjoying your new position?" Ailish asked through the pins in her mouth.

"It's hardly new." Niamh said, "I've been there for over a year now." Ailish shot her a look. "You don't have to look so constipated over there. This is my job, you know." Niamh cringed. I didn't mean to make that face out loud. "It was my mother's dress. It's just-" "It's going to be alright, Niamh." Ailish cut in, "You don't have to worry so much. I know what I'm doing." Hael told her the same thing plenty of times over. Niamh was dubious. "Even if Master Hael is the one that taught you how to use those magic threads of yours, I'm the one that showed you how to stitch them into pretty pictures." Ailish said, turning her eyes back to her work. The beginnings of a sheer overskirt were beginning to form under her expert seamstress' fingers. "You can trust me." She added. I barely trust myself. Niamh thought wryly, choosing not to respond. After a brief moment of comfortable silence, Niamh took a moment to reheat the pot of tea, slipping on her glove to amplify the simmering heat from her hand. Ailish cast an appreciative look as Niamh refilled her teacup. "What's this tea?" She asked, gazing into the pink steaming liquid. "It's raspberry leaf." Niamh answered, "If you drink enough of it, it should help your delivery when it comes time." "I'm sure my delivery will be just fine." Ailish said, laughing lightly as she ripped a strip of fabric from the neckline of the dress, barely missing the little white flowers embroidered along it. Niamh gritted her teeth. "One can never be too careful." She said. Niamh hoped Ailish caught her meaning. Ailish merely sighed. "You're going to have to loosen up one of these days, Niamh. Niamh laughed in to her cup, splattering tea onto her nose. Her previous worries forgotten for the moment. After a couple quiet hours of conversation, and a promise to return soon, Niamh was promptly shooed out without being allowed to pay some of her allowance for Ailish’s trouble.

On her way back to the castle, Niamh stopped by the shoemaker’s shop to buy simple silver shoes with the monthly allowance that Ailish refused. Her new shoes wrapped in pretty paper, and her pockets jingling with left-over allowance, she rushed excitedly back through town..

The embroidery on her silver shoes was styled to look like frost on a windowpane, wispy patterns flowing over each other. She pulled from her private stock of flowers, kept fresh by magic, to intertwine into her hair. Gazing in the mirror, she took in her ensemble a final time. Her dark auburn hair, normally tied back in a single braid to her waist, was loose and flowing save for the crown braid she secured around the back of her head. The white flowers she collected were placed carefully through her crown braid, bringing a bit of springtime, or at least what she imagined to be springtime, to her hair. The hem of the dress reached just above her ankles, displaying her shoes perfectly. She tugged at her sleeve, pleased with her appearance. Midnight blues dyed into the fabric brought out the sapphire of her eyes. Niamh gathered her skirts and left her cottage to the sparkling castle beyond the gardens. then returning to their own countries. Maire’s wedding dress was the most beautiful Niamh had ever seen, even more than her stunning dresses the night before. Her huge bouquet was made up of the rarest flowers either kingdoms’ fields could grow,

and Niamh guessed they had been imported from the flower fields and rose gardens of Aridia. Her hands disappeared in the mess of florals. The veil fell over her angelic face, creating a glow of sheer fabric to soften the rose of her cheeks. She was a vision in white, like the brightest star in the sky. Niamh couldn't read her expression as she floated toward her groom. The king reached a hand for his queen, grasping it tenderly and brought her up to stand with him. The weddings she was used to were usually accompanied by far more ale, and the people tended to be in better spirits. So weddings were usually much shorter, and the officiant had to possess the willpower to continue the ceremonial vows over shouts and teasing by the town’s residents. There were various types of bread, cheese, imported fruits and vegetables, puddings, mead, wine, stews and soups. There were roasted pheasants, wild boar, honey basted geese, and chocolate

covered frostflowers and huckleberries. It was the biggest feast most of the common people of Eira had only ever dreamed of, including Niamh. She munched on a little of everything throughout dinner, savoring each flavor that crossed her tongue. After everyone had a chance to fill their stomachs to the brim, and then even more so, the grandest of all the balls ran well into the night. Women’s dresses dripped with jewelry, expensive florals, and delicate lace. The golden designs below the surface of the ice floor in the ballroom glowed in the soft light of the chandeliers, casting a gold light on every one of the silken, rich fabrics in the room. Inevitably, Maewyn trotted over to where Niamh stood near the wall, her white and teal dress fluttering in her wake. Niamh inspected the gossamer thin designs gracing the hem of Maewyn’s dress, curling patterns of swans and ocean waves. Niamh wasn’t sure why Maewyn had taken to her so quickly, but even after only two days, she was growing begrudgingly accustomed to it. Maewyn chattered at her over the music, about everything from her favorite foods, the best ingredients to use for sleeping potions, her favorite dress shops, her favorite animal sculptures in the castle, and many other topics on her endless list of talking points. Niamh sighed inwardly. Soon, she spotted Hael standing stiffly at the other end of the ballroom on their same side. Niamh passed Maewyn off on a poor, unsuspecting noble, and strode over to stand by her master’s side. “With your permission, master.” “Hmm?” Hael glared ahead, taking a sip from his glass. He was staring straight at a fair-haired nobleman from Aridia, who was charming a group of young ladies near the grand staircase. All Aridians were fair-haired and fair-skinned. Hael had once said it was because of their Relic, and how it fed their crops. It was hard to tell them apart sometimes. “Um...I was wondering if I could run that errand down to the valley now?” She matched his gaze, watching the young ladies laugh at whatever the Aridian had said in their shared language. Hael glanced pointedly in Maewyn’s direction. “You’re looking to escape your social duties?” Niamh grimaced. He always knew. “I would get used to Maewyn being a constant presence in your life, apprentice.” Hael said, turning back to gaze out at the full

ballroom. “I think you’ll be seeing her more than you think.” What does that mean..? Niamh could only guess. The conversion with Maewyn at the dinner table the a couple nights before flickered at the edge of her mind. She gave a polite bow. “I’ll leave tomorrow morning, first light.” FANE COULDN’T THINK about what he'd just done. Not yet. The adrenaline of all of the events only a few hours previous kept him on the Stag’s back. The only thing that he could see as a marker were the occasional peaks of the mountains through the trees. The one thing familiar to him in this new world of terrifyingly open possibilities. And possibilities were dangerous. His mind was scattered, flitting from one to the next. Fane didn't have the presence of mind to see who was dead or alive back in the clearing. There was no telling who could be behind him now. They would travel for several more hours before darkness came over the forest. The forest looked completely different in the deepening evening. Less inviting, and more enclosed. The excitement and wonder that had marked his experience in the forest that morning was replaced with a feeling of small vulnerability. The light emitting from the white Stag lit the path ahead. The wind sang quietly through the treetops, filling the air with an ominous shhhhhh. A tiny shrew skittered across the short distance between the ferns on either side of the path, but judging from the distant sounds coming from all around, that was not the only animal nearby. Fane pulled the two rings that Rune had given him from under his jerkin absentmindedly. They glimmered dully at the end of the chain in the dappled starlight, only just barely illuminating faded patterning around the band. Fane squinted through the tiredness in his eyes, but he couldn't make out anything but what looked like two vague bird shapes. So small were the engravings, that he could barely concentrate on studying them any further. Fane let them fall under his shirt again. You cannot go home, Prince. It said, its ethereal voice echoing in Fane's mind. If you go back to Aridia, you will die. It said, looking back at him with glowing eyes.
The adrenaline of the day finally caught up to Fane’s tired nerves, and sleep came like a blanket, smothering him into submission.

5 FANE AWOKE WITH A POUNDING headache, and a sore body. He knew not where he was nor how long he'd been passed out. Soft bedding was beneath him and he lay under something warm. He opened his eyes expecting to see the drapery of his room, the golden Aridian morning shining through his huge windows. Instead, he only saw a humble cottage. A fire crackled in the modest fireplace across the one-room space, and a thatched roof was above. The walls couldn’t be seen under the roughly cut shelves filled with books, scrolls, vials, bottles, drying herbs and flowers, boxes, jars, and bowls of varying shapes and sizes. As clarity returned to his sleepy mind, he startled awake. A shadowy figure sat before the fireplace, rocking slowly in his chair, smoke rising above his head from what Fane only assumed was a pipe. Fane reached instinctively for his dagger that was no longer there. He cursed inwardly, not remembering where he'd lost it along the way. The figure didn’t turn around. “I wouldn’t bother, boy.” A gravelly voice came from the man in the chair. “No harm will come to you here.” Despite the reassurance, Fane didn’t relax. His palms sweat, and he glared in suspicion. “Who are you?” He asked, his throat dry and his voice thick from sleep. “I live here.” The man said simply. Fane grumbled. That doesn’t answer my question. He thought impatiently. The prince rose from the bed, albeit slowly and carefully, taking care to favor his right side. He crept to the face the man, his back to the fire. He didn’t look very threatening on first glance, his beard reaching his stomach and bushy eyebrows obscuring his deep-set eyes. Fane thought those eyes looked like they had seen the

beginning of the world itself. He did indeed have a long pipe in his hand, and he puffed on it thoughtfully. “How did I get here?” Fane asked, not bothering to hide the suspicion in his voice, against all of the gentile manners ingrained in him since youth. The old man barked a laugh. “Why does that matter? You’re here now. You’re safe.” He peered up at the prince from under his massive eyebrows. “If you must know – The Stag brought you to me.” He said, his voice softening. Fane was taken aback. The sincerity in the man’s voice, the utter assurance in which he spoke, set Fane at a strange ease. He felt his muscles relax. The old man looked at him fully then, motioning for him to sit with a wave of his hand. Fane obliged and took a seat on the footstool next to the rocking chair. Fane met his eyes steadily, waiting. “Aren’t you hungry?” The old man broke the silence, and waved a hand at the coffee table in front of the two of them. Fane noticed then the spread of food that he was sure hadn’t been there previously. Warm bread, a pot of hearty stew, fruits of every shape and kind sat on primitive plates of wood. Two huge tankards full of the sweetest steaming mead Fane ever had the pleasure of smelling also sat on the table. His stomach growled aggressively at the sight, and he partook eagerly. The old man held his own steaming tankard in his gnarled hands and smiled knowingly under his beard. "Do you know who I am?" The old man asked matter-of-factly. Fane shook his head slightly, confused and with a mouth full of bread. "You didn't tell me who you were." "I know who you are." Fane furrowed his brow. He didn't think it was all that obvious. Then again, he remembered with a nervous glance toward his hunting leathers by his bed, the royal insignia of Aridia was plainly embossed on one shoulder guard. He remained silent. Days of travel had muddied his clothes, scuffed his fine leather armor, tangled his hair, and gave him a bedraggled appearance. He barely looked like himself now. This was potentially the longest he'd ever gone without bathing. Fane tried not to think about that. “You are a prince that has never left the capital city in your

whole life, and now you find yourself lost and alone in the forest, with hardly a survival skill to speak of.” Fane stopped with his spoon halfway to his mouth. He met the old man’s eyes again. "Do you know who you are?" The man asked simply. Quietly. "I am who you have just said I am." Fane replied, mystified. His hand lowered, the bite of soup forgotten. "Mhhmm." The old man muttered, nodding, though not looking entirely convinced. "And, my next question, young Prince, is do you remember how you came to me?" Fane swallowed, "All I remember is the Stag talking to me, and it must have done something, because the next thing I knew, I was here." Fane realized how insane he must have sounded, but some part of him thought that he was in the proper company for that. "I need to go home. The king will assume that I'm dead, or kidnapped, or something else. Someone must have infiltrated my guardsmen. I need to find out who it might be so that I can warn-" The old man held up a hand. "Why would the king care what happens to you?" His tone implied that he knew the answer, but he wanted Fane to say it anyway. "Because I am the Prince of Aridia, and I cannot be away for too long, otherwise-" "Otherwise what?" The old man's voice was quiet, though he commanded the air in the room. Fane stopped. What would happen if he were gone for too long? He'd never been away, not even from the palace, for more than a few hours. He mentally ran through his list of duties, though it was not very long. In fact, he couldn't remember any instance in which the king had delegated anything to him save for some ceremonial appearance or another. Fane couldn’t answer that question before the old man was on to another. "As to your first explanation, that's not truly how you came to find yourself in my woods. The Stag led you here, of course, but how were you led to the Stag?" Fane was quickly growing restless under all of these unrelated and tiresome questions. There was really nowhere else for him to go, however. "I was hunting it." "And? What else?" "And one of my guardsmen went mad and murdered...” He stopped, resisting the urge to close his eyes against the gruesome

images that still burned themselves behind his eyelids. “...my captain and some others with us." Fane hardly believed anything out of his mouth, it was still surreal. "This guardsman must have been trying to kill you, then, yes?" The old man said, as if the point was staring Fane in his face. "I –Yes, I suppose." "So it would be dangerous for you to continue to assume your identity as the Prince." Fane had never had an assassination attempt committed against him before; he didn't know the proper behavior under such circumstances. "Yes..." Just when Fane thought that conversation was leading somewhere, the old man sat back in his chair as if he was finished speaking. After a moment, Fane thought that he had fallen asleep for how still he became. Fane cleared his throat, just in case. The old man suddenly opened his eyes again, glaring at him as if he'd just interrupted some deep thought. "It's more than your body that needs healing, young man." Fane opened his mouth to protest, before the old man continued. "I'll be getting a visitor. You can decide then if you’ll go with them or not. Until then, there are things that need doing here. You can keep yourself busy to pay me back for my hospitality." Is it really hospitality if I have to give something in return? Fane thought ruefully. Fane stayed with the strange old man in the woods for a few days. At least, he could only guess that was how long it had been. Every day became the same. Despite his oddities and occasional hours-long silences, the man was kind and taught Fane many things. They would awake before dawn, share a hearty breakfast in which Fane tried in vain to learn the old man’s name. Perhaps he had forgotten it. Or he doesn’t even have one. Fane mused to himself, chuckling through his nose. The old man put Fane to good use, having him assist with various tasks in and around the ramshackle cottage. Gardening, foraging, fixing the roof’s leaks, chopping firewood, among various other seemingly endless tasks. Fane was beginning to wonder if this was less of a kindhearted rescue and more of an indentured servitude situation. At first, the old man gruffly followed Fane around, making sure

that he was able to do the tasks he was assigned. Most of the time at the beginning, this was not the case, and he would teach Fane the basic life skills that his education lacked. In the glass palace in Aridia, princes learned things like politics, social graces, and dances. Here in the woods, they were exchanged for properly building a fire, knowing which end of an ax was up, and how to hammer nails instead of bending them beyond repair. Fane had felt a range of things as this new education went on; what started as slight indignance soon grew to frustration and a little shame, as he realized that his pampered upbringing did little to further his skills as a man in life. Deep in his heart, Fane was grateful for the opportunity to prove himself in more than just how neatly he could foxtrot. Every time he finished a task, and was rewarded with an approving nod, his heart swelled with pride. After a few days, the old man did, indeed, have a visitor at his cottage. Though judging by the old man’s reaction, Fane gathered that this was not the visitor he spoke of. Fane found that he would get these passers-by every so often, retrieving herbs and spices, or more rare magical objects. All of them were mages. Fane could tell by the way they carried themselves: graceful, lithe, knowing exactly which elements were around them for use. He thought they walked with a certain sense of power, sometimes arrogance. He thought of the high mages in his own court, native Aridians that had trained in the mountains of Eira. Only rumors circulated down into the valleys and forests of the high up academies and training grounds of the fabled magic users of the Northern land. No one had been permitted to travel to the more remote places, or to be privy to the secrets kept in the stone halls of the magicians unless one ventured to train in those high places. Mages were a mysterious and terrifying brood, indeed.

6 THE JOURNEY TO THE cottage in the woods where Hael acquired most of his rarer magical items was a shorter trip than most around Eira. While other roads required a well-packed saddlebag and sleeping arrangements in preparation for snow storms or snowed-in villages, the road down into the valleys was wide and clear much of the time. This made an easy and pleasant trip whenever Niamh wanted to take a jaunt through the nature around her. She'd taken the trip several times over the course of her training. It was this same well-maintained and wide pathway that the visiting dignitaries and nobility had traveled only a few days before to attend the royal wedding. If their opulent, bulky carriages could do it, then so could her sure-footed horse. It was a safe road too, as most bandits preferred to go after the remote villages rich with farms and resources. They were less likely to attack such an open and well-traveled area such as this. The surrounding mountains and the mines within them were where most of Eira’s riches lay, anyway. For generations, the people of Eira had traded these precious minerals to bigger, more advanced societies of Aridia and Corseils in exchange for basic necessities such as fabric, fresh produce and flowers, among other precious everyday items. It was a balanced tradition that had given Eira a purpose for decades. Niamh felt safe nestled in these mountains around her. Their gentle white slopes and jagged gray peaks only served to remind her how fortified and secure her small country was. A safety blanket against the world. As the scenery changed from craggy peaks and deep valleys with treacherous rivers at the bottom, to rolling hills and deciduous trees, the air became warmer, more humid. Narrow, switching-back paths became a wide and well-maintained road. The snow became

shallower, wetter, and some areas had none at all. Her destination sat directly on the border between Eira and Aridia, and so the land around it respected the normal four seasons the rest of the world enjoyed. The hard needles of evergreens gave way to the soft crunch of oak and birch trees as Niamh came closer to the border. The heavy coat she wore was promptly exchanged for a lighter cape, and her horse snorted as they entered the dense forest ahead. The light changed from the cold winter sun to a lovely green-gold, filtering through the canopy above. They were almost there. Niamh neared the location where the dwelling sat, and she constantly had to check herself to remind herself where it was. Knowing the Wizard of the Wood, he might change the location just slightly out of spite or paranoia, but it was never more than a mile or two. It was surrounded by thick trees, barely seen through the branches. Even thicker than the trees was the magical barrier around the perimeter; no one was allowed in that was not invited. Which is why she was surprised to see the old man had company. As she rounded the corner, the owner of an unfamiliar voice came into view. He was a tall young man with blond hair falling in front of his features. He was bending over throwing some recently cut wood onto a huge pile accumulating near the entry to the hut. The old man she was seeking reclined in a makeshift chair to the side, shouting orders and critiquing the younger man on his work. His raspy, high pitched voice carried across the yard. The young man’s facial expression, when she finally did glimpse his face, made her stifle a giggle as he was obviously holding back his aggravation. When the old man caught sight of her, he chortled in his throat and stood. “Now here’s a respectful young person." Niamh grinned, greeting him with a wave. The young man sighed, as if whatever he was about to say had to have been repeated several times over the day. He grumbled something under his breath. The old man either chose not to listen or didn’t hear his comment, dismissing it with a grunt, and scurried back into the cottage to retrieve Niamh’s package that she'd come for. For a few moments, this allowed her a good chance to study the man she was left alone with. Now that he was standing and moving on to his next task, Niamh saw that he carried himself with a regal bearing. A ramrod

straight back, measured steps, and purposeful movements all told her he was not raised in the forest. He had medium length hair for a man, it reached only a little above his shoulders, but the color was a beautiful blond. Like spun gold shimmering in the dappled light of the trees. On the right side of his face, a small section of his hair was braided and fell to his shoulder. His jaw was clenched in frustration at the moment, but she could see it had an elegant line. This line was repeated in the shape of his nose, which was pointed and straight in a strong profile. He was wearing a simple white shirt that looked like it had seen better days. It was torn in a few places, and stained with dirt and grass. His black breeches were in better shape, looking like they were woven of fine, thick material, tucked into tall, black boots. They were not in the Eiran style, however. They were too thin- looking for that. Finally, he turned to face her. His silver gray eyes glancing into her blue ones for a moment. “I see he has you working hard.” She offered, smiling good naturedly. He grimaced. After a moment of awkward silence, the only sound between them the rustle of leaves in the breeze, Niamh shifted. “I'm Niamh.” She offered, attempting to cut the tension. He nodded. “Please excuse my manners.” Fane reached for her hand, which she offered after a moment’s hesitation. He was most definitely not raised in the forest. "I'm-" He hesitated, as if not knowing how to continue. "-Fane. I'm Fane." He said. Niamh nodded, skimming over the awkwardness of that introduction. “I make monthly stops here for rare herbs for my work since he-” She gestured toward the cottage “is the only one within several hundred miles that produces them.“ Niamh cocked her head slightly, “I’ve never seen you before. How did you come to be in the service of the old man of the woods?” Fane chuckled, there was a nervous edge to the sound. “Ah. Well, he helped me. And in return, he asked me to do some chores for him. I didn’t realize that they would be so numerous and laborious.” He hesitated, studying her face. She guessed he was gauging if he should tell her the whole story or not. Finally, after a moment, he relented. “I actually came here by accident. I lost my way in the woods, and if it were not for him, I would have died.” “Where are you trying to go?” She asked

“North.” He answered simply. Niamh wasn’t sure if she should continue pressing him, considering how cryptic he seemed to be. Maybe he’s running from something? Just as she was about to open her mouth to ask more, the old man toddled out of his hideaway. He promptly handed Niamh her package, wrapped in brown paper. “I found a special surprise that I added to your order this time.” He winked, “Use it wisely.” As he turned to Fane, the old man’s face took on a crooked, sly smile. “Did you finish repainting my roof? “ He asked. “Yes, as well as stacking your wood, cleaning off the side of your house, sweeping and dusting all the interiors twice, and stacking the stones along your pathway. “ Fane replied with a hint of resentment. “Well done.” The old man clapped his hands together once in finality. He looked at Niamh, then back at Fane. He appeared to be thoughtful for a moment. “Now if only there was something else I could think for you to do...” As the apprehension in Fane’s expression grew more and more prominent, Niamh interrupted the silence. “ I...I could use an escort back through the forest.” She offered. Fane looked at her with as much surprise as she felt hearing that come out of her mouth. “If he wants to accompany me.” She added, with a cautious look from under her bangs at him. He hesitated for only a moment, and she caught his eyes flickering between herself and the old man. “Of course. It would be my honor.” Fane finally said, something like a mask covering the authenticity in his voice present only a moment before. Satisfied, the old man shoved a pack of items toward Fane, as if this had been his plan all along. “Good! Excellent. Thank you for the help, Fane, but you are no longer needed. “ Niamh stifled her giggle as the old man gave Fane an enthusiastic clap on the back, making the younger man stumble. The two of them departed the house. Barely looking behind him, Fane took a place next to her as she sat atop Alvyss, her horse. His blond head was level with Alvyss’s neck, and he had to look up at her as he'd offered his hand in assisting her mount. After a few moments of awkward silence between them, she cleared her throat. "Would you mind telling me where we're going?" Fane asked,

breaking the silence. Finally, a conversation. “We’re heading to Ahealath, the capital city of Eira.” “Ah, so that’s where we are.” His gray eyes darted around, taking in every pine tree, sheer cliff face, and white slope. A hare jumped across the path. “Were you trying to go to the king’s wedding?” Niamh asked. Perhaps he’d just lost his way. His accent wasn’t quite Eiran, but it didn’t sound like any other accents Niamh had ever heard either. “Wedding?” Fane still looked a bit distracted, taking in the scenery with an awed expression. “Yes, you’re not from Eira, right?” Otherwise he would have known. “I-” Fane turned wide eyes to hers again. Why is he so nervous? Niamh wondered inwardly. “I- no, I’m not. I’m from...Close by.” “Oh, you mean in the woodlands?” Then why would he have been lost in the woods? “Yes, the woodlands here. Right between Aridia and Eira.” Fane nodded resolutely. That must be why his accent is so strange. Niamh would have never said this out loud, especially not to the young man’s face, but she couldn’t place his accent at all. It was also strange that a man from the woods would be so properly mannered. And finely dressed. But, then again, Niamh hadn’t ever left Eira. So how could she know what traditions might have been different in other parts of the world? “Well, I’m sorry you’ll be missing the wedding, but I’m sure you’ll get to taste some of the special treats they made for it.” Niamh forced brightness into her voice to drown out the suspicion that bubbled up there. “So it might be like you haven’t missed it at all. There will be plenty of Aridian people there, so maybe you’ll see someone you know.” His strong grip on the horse’s bridle tightened along with his rigid spine. Niamh immediately felt as if she’d said something wrong. “Yes. Perhaps.” Fane answered after a moment. Another long period of silence stretched between them. It seemed to last for hours. “Thank you for allowing me to accompany you.” Fane said. His

voice seemed more relaxed than it had been before. “Who knows what else that old man would have had me do for him if you hadn’t come along.” Niamh obliged him with a short laugh. This seemed to break the tension between them for the moment. Fane seemed to be of good-humor, and followed each one of her questions with one of his own. Most of Fane’s answers were cautious, but polite and steady, as if he thought intentionally about what he was to say. He did appear to casually side-step any specific questions about where he came from or his past, giving her vague answers or redirecting her back to her own answers. Niamh had seen King Airem play the exact same political game, and so she knew when to let it go. Once Niamh had determined she would not be getting much from him by way of his origin, she gave up and moved on to other topics. FANE HAD NEVER SEEN a glacier, but he could imagine the sensation every time the young woman looked his way. The heart of glacial ice sat in her eyes; clear and blue and depthless. The rest of her was rather unremarkable. Fane noted she wore no color on her cheeks, eyes, or lips like many of the women he’d encountered in his court. She was, Fane realized, refreshingly normal. Not that he'd interacted with many “normal” people, between the tittering, blatantly cheeky maids that followed him around his own home. Or the vain, gossiping women of his court, including the multiple of their number that emerged from Friedhelm’s quarters every morning. From his readings into Eira’s culture, he remembered that both the men and women of the northern country wore their hair long. This was the case for the Eiran in front of him, as her rich auburn hair was tied back in one long braid that reached past her waist. She was shorter than he by a head, but she'd swung herself up onto the giant draft horse between them with the ease of someone that had done it their entire life. It was a wonder to him that someone of her stature could even reach the stirrup, much less mount the hulking creature. They rode in silence for the better part of the rest of the ride,

Niamh apparently having reached her conversation limit. The prince distracted himself by watching the wildlife, and allowed himself to fall into his own thoughts. He enjoyed the feeling of the wind ruffling his hair again after his time in the enclosed, stiflingly deep forest. He wondered who would be searching for him by now. Friedhelm, like their father before him, had never been a warm or affectionate type, but he would surely care that the prince of the realm had never returned home. There would be search parties, or perhaps the king’s personal guard dispersed into the town, questioning residents and scouring the woods. And if what Niamh had said was true, and there were visiting Aridians in the capital, Fane could only hope that word of his disappearance hadn’t reached this far yet. If Niamh was so easily able to place where he might have been from, then how much more easily could someone of his own countrymen discover him? Fane grimaced at the thought. As soon as the Eiran had appeared in the clearing at the cabin, Fane knew he would need to improve his accent if he was ever going to blend in in this new place. She sounded like Rune had, and Fane tried to draw on his recent memory to bring Rune’s accent to his own speech. The hard r’s at the end of words, and the lilt upward at the end of sentences, would be the hardest to master.

7 A HULKING WOODEN GATE appeared before them, towering to the ramparts many feet above as they rode toward it. The blue and white of Eira's banners flapped merrily in the breeze. Now, this was familiar to Fane. Fane had rarely wandered from the beautiful white walls confining him to his home in the castle of Aridia. From what he saw from his window, however, Traehjem, Aridia's capital city, was bigger, more sprawling and expansive, compared to the little mountain kingdom's capital. What Ahealarth lacked in size, it certainly made up for in height. The buildings, mostly constructed of wood and stone, stacked high. Each level was either a family home or reputable business - tailors, schools, taverns, dressmakers, bakeries, and the like. Each equally as charming and welcoming as the last. Though Eira’s capital city streets were narrower, older, and a great deal more rickety, the hustle and bustle was a familiar sight. As the two of them entered the city square, vendors could be heard shouting from all directions. Patrons scurried between each other, all carrying baskets and wrapped parcels tucked under thick, coated arms. Fane inhaled to take in the spices permeating the cold air: nutmeg, clove, freshly baked breads and pastries, warm smelling sugared squash and savory meats, cinnamon, apples, and all other manner of homely smells intermingled around him. It made his mouth water. They continued toward the shining castle on the hill, passing through the marketplace, up past shops, fine houses, not so fine houses, and many, many people. Fane guessed that the city had to be built smaller to allow for the roads to be more easily cleared of the snow, and to keep people warm in their dwellings. Niamh skirted around the edges, her horse parting the way for them as they made their way through town. Neither of them spoke

for the duration of the ride, mostly because Fane was still taking in his surroundings, and Niamh looked to be concentrating on maneuvering her horse through the crowd without interference. For a moment, he’d forgotten that there were supposedly Aridian visitors in town. As soon as he remembered that fact, his admiration of the capital was far less pleasant. He began scanning the tops of heads for the trademark Aridian blond, but found none. This survey continued all the way up the slope of the wide cobblestone street to the front gate of the castle. Niamh led her horse through the castle gates, walking into a snowy courtyard lined with soldiers. Fane was not unused to this sight, and he was set at ease being among the things familiar to him again. Battlements, castle gates, courtyards. These were the things of his childhood. He relaxed only slightly. The Aridian nobles may have been inside the castle too, but at least there were no more crowds for them to hide in. Fane was unsure if he would be recognized at all, as he rarely appeared outside of his own palace walls, but he couldn’t afford to take chances now. Niamh handed off the horse to a stable hand, as a bright voice appeared in the courtyard. “Niamh!” A young woman about the same age as his companion shouted from a stone arch a ways away from the pair.
