Niamh turned to face her, a flicker of a grimace in her eyes, and the girl sauntered up to them. She cast an appreciative eye toward Fane, looking him up and down like so many of the women of his court. “Well, hello there.” She turned a raised eyebrow to Niamh, “Where did you pick him up?” The young woman in question bristled a bit, but didn't answer. “What do you want, Maewyn?” Maewyn sighed, seemingly thwarted in her attempts to get a rise out of Niamh. “Hael is looking for you. He said you would be back later and he needs his supplies. And also,” A mischievous smile crept over her face, smirking at Niamh knowingly. “He’s letting me take part in the trials for apprenticeship.” “Oh?” Niamh asked, sounding completely uninterested. “I’m supposed to be starting them tomorrow. Maybe you’ll have me as a new partner soon?” She poked at Niamh playfully. The young woman brushed her hand away. “Many people take those tests, it’s not always to become an

apprentice.” Niamh answered, barely containing the ire lacing her voice. Fane raised his eyebrows. Just as he was about to open his mouth to ask what tests she might have been referring to, Niamh turned from Maewyn to face the saddle. Maewyn, completely unruffled, turned away, blowing a kiss to Fane as she sauntered off. “Well, I guess we will be making a short stop to see my master.” Niamh said, sighing. She gathered up her saddlebags from her horse as he was led off to the stables, and motioned for Fane to follow. They cut through the same open air arches that Maewyn had emerged from, and came upon a stunning garden made entirely of ice and frost. Bears and elk sculptures loomed over them as Niamh weaved through a labyrinth of sculptures and delicately trimmed evergreens. There were fountains that flowed with water, despite the cold, and frostflowers dotted the landscape. Fane was used to the overflowing greenery of Aridia’s famous gardens. These felt lifeless to his eyes, but he was sure that they were magnificent to a native of Eira. Several minutes later, after a brief stop at a cozy looking cottage nestled in the corner of the ice gardens, they stood outside another house. This was further up the hillside, away from the castle, and looking down on everything in the valley below. It was a relatively easy trail up to it, and they reached it without difficulty. The house was more exeptional than most of the cottages he'd seen so far, being built of fine wood and strong stone. Carvings of Eira’s folklore and rare flora decorated the areas around the doors and windows. Niamh knocked once before the door opened for her, seemingly on its own. She stepped inside with confidence, carrying a small box of the supplies she'd retrieved from the old man in the woods. “Master Hael?” She called, her small voice barely reaching to the top of the foyer. A cleared throat from the room to their right led them into a warm office, filled to the brim with books of every size and shape. A man that looked a little older than his brother, in casual dress sitting in a plush armchair in the middle, a steaming cup of liquid at his elbow on the side table. In his lap was an old looking book, its pages frayed from age. At a distracted wave from the red-haired man, she set the box on his side table. “I...may have found something else at the Wizard’s cottage.”

Niamh began hesitatingly. The man looked up at him. His brown eyes were, to Fane, far older than he looked. “Indeed. You did.” He grumbled. Niamh gestured between the two men. “This is Fane. I met him at the cottage in the woods, and the Wizard sends with him his highest...recommendation.” Fane couldn’t help but notice the hidden smile in her voice at the last word. Niamh continued, “He was living there for some time when I allowed him to accompany me back here.” She smiled at Fane, attempting to break the tension in the air. “Fane, this is Master Hael, the Head Mage of Eira.” Fane tensed. If the mages in Fane’s parents’ court terrified him for the power they had, he couldn’t fathom how much power lay behind those ancient-looking eyes. Fane bowed politely, calling on every princely instinct he had in the wake of the stirring in his gut. “It is an honor, sir.” He straightened. “I have heard stories of your great power even in my home country.” And truly, he had. The stories of the great Phoenix Mage of Eira spread worldwide. The mages of his parents’ court, even as distant as he was from their personal lives, spoke of him with awe and reverence. Hael, unfazed by any of the praise that was heaped upon him, put the book down and uncrossed his legs. “Where do you come from?” He asked, not at all politely. Fane nodded his head in a counter greeting, and put his best effort into mimicking Hael’s accent back to him. “I’m a stranger to this land. I...” He looked to Niamh, revealing a detail he hadn’t mentioned on the way back to the castle. “..can’t go back to where I’m from. I was told I would die if I returned.” He grimaced at her surprise. The man nodded, thinking and rubbing his fiery red, short cropped beard. If he’d noticed Fane’s strange quasi-accent, he made no sign of it. “I hope you’re not running from the law.” He said, warning in his voice. “No, of course not.” Fane bristled only slightly. He’d never, in his life, been accused of any criminality. And he intended to keep it that way. Hael looked as if he was considering him for a long moment, still rubbing his beard. Fane waited, gripping his hands to his side to distract himself. “Normally,” Hael said, rising and walking toward the huge fireplace. His back was to them. “The proper way to go about this

might be to appear before the king, and ask permission to stay here in Eira. But the king was only married yesterday, and there’s no point in him holding court for one vagabond that’s wandered into his kingdom.” Hael turned toward them again, the fire illuminating him from behind. Fane swallowed. “So it’s best if I deal with you.” Fane didn’t like the sound of that. “You’ll be allowed to stay here, but only on the condition that you contribute something to our country.” “I would be grateful.” Fane replied, almost automatically. It’s strange they would just give a stranger a job. Though Fane was in no position to question it. It’s not as if he had a choice in the matter anyway. He imagined himself investigating the theaters in this new place, if only to find somewhere comfortable and familiar to him. As his mind tumbled down the list of possibilities on how he could contribute, as Hael said. Hael threw on official looking crimson and sunset robes, covering over the casual shirt and pants that he was already wearing, and not looking entirely happy about it. “If you’re going to be staying here, you had best find something suitable to wear.” Hael said grumpily. “Niamh, why don’t you take a trip to the market with our guest to find clothes for him after I take him for his work.” “Work?” Fane interjected in surprise. Niamh stifled a giggle next to him as Hael nearly rolled his eyes. “We can’t have you wandering around the castle and potentially get lost like some vagrant off the road. Although that’s exactly what you are.” Fane visually bristled at that, but the mage continued. “And since getting lost is apparently a special skill of yours, we’ll endeavor to fix that.” Hael handed Fane a small handful of coins. “These are on loan. I expect you’ll pay me back as soon as you’re able.” He turned to Niamh. “Meet him at the front gates in two hours, apprentice. Until then, I want you to be preparing for Maewyn’s upcoming trials.” Niamh bowed her head politely. “Yes, sir.” “Wait.” Fane looked between the two of them. “If he’s your master, then that means...” He hesitated, “You’re a mage too?” Niamh gave him a strange, incredulous smile. “Yes, of course. I’ve been training here in the city for at least ten years now.” Her eyes flicked once between Hael and himself. “But Master Hael only

took me on as an apprentice last year.” Fane was too shocked to reply. Niamh didn’t seem to know what to do with his apparent surprise. “Um...Most mages come here to learn. From all around the world.” It was as if she’d just told Fane there were wolves around every corner. “Yes, yes, now that that’s been established, you’re to follow me.” Hael said briskly. Fane felt a strange wind at his back, pushing him out the door with the master mage. He couldn’t tell if he was imagining it or not, but Fane was sure there would be much of that feeling for the foreseeable future. He snuck a glance behind him at Niamh’s amused expression, wishing he could have stayed with her. She, at least, seemed the least dangerous of his options.

8 FANE WAS LED THROUGH the one place that was the most familiar to him since he left the morning of his hunt. The castle was magnificent. Rustic and rich in history. The heart of a kingdom that was even more so. The life of royalty, the grand structures and lush carpets and tapestries felt like home to him. So different from the wild lands and humble cottage of the old man in the woods. Though, the castle of Eira was smaller in scale than that of Aridia, not as delicate and decorated in less expensive materials. Where Aridia's palace had gold, silver, crystal, and glass, Eira had wood and stone. Fane had grown up reading of places like this, and he’d taken the time to memorize the layouts of each of the great castles in the countries surrounding Aridia. And he’d had plenty of time. The impromptu tour as Hael led him through the castle was merely putting sight to words and diagrams he’d poured over for hours in his youth. Fane was not about to reveal that information to his present company, and instead called upon every diplomatic skill he ever learned to easily slip into the role of student. The role of landless, homeless stranger intent on inhaling every detail of the grand palace around him, as if he'd never seen such elegance in his life. Fane stared at these grand places from the doorways of each, taking in the small details of each location before being swept off to another. Fane thought back to his studies and the books he had read his entire life; of Eira's histories, battles won and lost, folklore, fairytales, and culture all flowing before his eyes in tapestries, golden patterns and painted over ceilings or along hallways. Mere words on a page now spread before him; a reality. No turn was a surprise to him, no door concealing any secret that he hadn't read about. As they neared the top floors of the

castle, after briefly passing the Great Hall and throne room, Hael led him to looming doors of carved wood and gilded figures. Truth be told, this was what Fane was anticipating the most out of everything he’d glimpsed on the way. The Grand Library of Eira. The most respected, the most famous, the most sought after places for magic users in the world. Rivaled only by the libraries of the academy of magic deep in the heart of the mountains of Eira. Even more than the throne room or the Great Hall, this Library was situated in the place of highest honor. Its doors decorated to reflect its rich history and the reverence that was bestowed upon it. Some said that the castle was built around it, that it had been the heart of learning and wisdom for all the world before Eira as a country even existed. Hael pushed the gilded doors open with what looked to be some effort, revealing the grandest library Fane had ever set his eyes upon. Even more than the libraries of his own palace, this one outstripped them all. What lay before him was a room bigger than the Great Hall and the throne room combined, bigger than all of the libraries in his own palace put together. Swirling spiral staircases led to the five levels, all stuffed to the brim with books and scrolls and all manner of materials. Countless shelves of warm mahogany wood, pristine white marble floors, gold accented the decor in select places. Hallways led to other parts of the Library, itself a fortress all on its own. At once, Fane felt that one could spend days, even weeks inside and never be finished reading through all of its treasures or exploring every room. He completely forgot about Hael's presence as he strode past him, gazing upward at the high ceilings painted with the colors of the heavens. Just as he stepped forward, he felt something warm and fluffy push against his legs. He looked down to see a large cat-like creature, with giant paws and disproportionately long legs. He jumped back in surprise, but it just bridged the gap between them and weaved between his legs again. Something like a purr rose from its throat, rumbling and deep. "Don't mind him, he's deciding whether or not you would make a good meal." An ancient voice drifted to him from behind the giant desk to his left. The old woman that popped her head from behind it was so thin and frail that he wondered how the wind hadn't

carried her off the second she stepped outside. If she ever stepped outside. Her hair was as white as the moon, her skin thin and speckled with age. Thin glasses sat on her nose, and her robes were cream colored lined with ashy gray fur. She frowned seeing Hael standing in the doorway. "Hael, are you still pretending to be a young and spry thing?" She tutted, "That hair and beard should have been gray a long time ago." Hael scoffed, "With as old as we are, I am allowed a little vanity." The ancient woman shook her head, "Who is 'we', apprentice? I seem to remember when you were no more than a wide-eyed teenager who couldn't grow a beard to save his life." Hael fingered his fiery beard with a touch of self-consciousness in his face. He quickly wiped it away when he caught Fane staring at him. Now mages could mask their true appearances? What couldn’t they do? Fane could hardly trust his own senses. This only served to fill him with even more dread. Hael cleared his throat. "This young vagrant here was found wandering the wilderness." He motioned to Fane. Fane wished he would stop calling him that. The lynx, that's what Fane finally remembered what the animal was called, continued to wrap itself around the prince's legs purring at him and nuzzling the tops of his boots. The old woman fixed her eye on him, peering at him over the rim of her glasses. "Do you like books, boy? Do you seek to learn and gain wisdom?" Fane felt a flicker of unease, as if the eyes of some ancient creature were staring into his soul from the foundation of the world. "I-uh...” He was at a loss for words. "Yes, I do. Books are some of my greatest passions." "Hmm...” Was the only reply from the old woman. She glanced at the lynx now chewing absentmindedly on Fane's boot laces, and appeared to make a decision. Her countenance changed in an instant. "I have needed a helper here in the Library, if that sounds agreeable to you." Now that sounds familiar. Fane thought, thinking back to the last time an ancient being had asked for his "help". More like indentured servitude. Hael grinned slyly, the only pleasant expression that Fane had

seen from him in the short while he had known him, and rubbed his chin thoughtfully again. “The only other thing I thought you might do is a position in the stables. It’s quite cold out there this time of year...” That sounded like Fane’s worst nightmare. “I’ll take the Library, thank you.” He said, holding back a cringe. Hael nodded, as if he expected this answer. “Then that’s settled.” The master mage turned, grinning, and strode from the library, not giving Fane another glance. The huge doors closed with a boom. Fane was left alone in the Library with the ancient lady, who looked him up and down with an appraising eye. Two more lynx had joined their companion, creating a swirling trap of fur and purring to keep him in place. Finally, she spoke. "I've had many names over the years. But you may call me the Keeper. For I keep knowledge, insight, and wisdom." The air thrummed with power, and Fane knew he was not in the presence of an ordinary mage. "No evil will be done in this Library, and only Truth resides here." She looked fixedly at him, holding his eyes to hers. "So don't just stand there." She heaved a stack of books into his open arms. He nearly fell over with the weight of them. The three lynx sat in a line in front of him, calmly staring him down. "My Lore Cats will help you. Follow them." She dismissed him with a wave of her hand, going back to her own book behind the desk. NIAMH HAD SPENT THE better part of the last two hours putting together different recipes for Maewyn to replicate. She’d considered making them impossible to solve, but she’d refrained knowing that Hael would have caught her sabotage. An hour later, as promised, Fane walked up to Niamh waiting at the front gates. She'd just been chatting with one of the guards standing at the entrance to the guardhouse when he emerged from the palace doors. He looked bedraggled, and ran a stressed hand through his hair as he approached. She smiled at him as he stopped in front of her, his dirty breeches covered in a layer of cat hair. “You must have just spent some time in the Library.” She said,

laughing. “And I will be for the foreseeable future.” He replied, smirking humorlessly. “It seems that the Lore Cats took a liking to me and their mistress requires my help.” “Oh yes. “ Niamh laughed harder at the memory coming to her mind, “I seem to remember that she had me under her employ at one point too. It’s practically a rite of passage.” She touched his forearm softly, leading him to the main gate toward town. Maewyn came bounding up behind them, making her presence known with a bright laugh and a call of “Wait!” that carried across the courtyard. Her short boots slid as she skidded behind the pair, nearly running into Fane. Niamh suspected this was on purpose, judging from the way she was eyeing the man earlier that morning. “I want to come too!” She announced, wedging herself between them with a bright smile. “I can’t let you have all the fun with our new guest, Niamh!” Her voice was gratingly excited, almost shrill, as she batted eyelashes at Fane. He smiled politely, bowing his head in acknowledgement. That was all the encouragement that Maewyn needed, and she eagerly wrapped an arm through Fane’s. Niamh didn’t detect a hint of resistance in Fane’s face as he offered his arm almost naturally. As if he'd been doing it his whole life. “We’re only going shopping for a few clothes for him, Maewyn. It won’t be anything special.” Niamh commented, resisting the urge to roll her eyes at her blatant flirting. The younger mage puffed her cheeks indignantly. “Clothes shopping is always fun, Niamh. You obviously don’t appreciate it as much as I do. You need me along!” She turned her simpering eyes to Fane, who still looked as proper as ever. “I can already tell you that I will be a much greater help than she will.” Niamh scoffed lightly at that. “Just leave it to me.” She trotted self-satisfyingly next to Fane, and Niamh had to pick up her pace to keep up with them. The three of them walked out of the castle’s front gates and down the long path to the city.

9 MAEWYN BOUNCED BETWEEN the stalls ahead of them, clearly in her element, as her arms filled with layer upon layer of soft, warm clothing and even softer and warmer pastries. Niamh walked calmly near his right side, occasionally pausing to speak softly to a vendor along the way. Fane looked at her with new eyes, trying to notice any small details about her countenance or the way that she moved to indicate to him that she was a mage that he missed earlier. He found himself walking just a few more feet away from her, even if by accident. She came away with her own small basketful of far more practical items than her counterpart. Her other basket was begrudgingly utilized for Maewyn’s surplus purchases. He reached into his pocket to finger the coins Hael had given him. The thought suddenly occurred to him that he'd never physically spent his own money, or handed coins to anyone in his entire life. He tried to pay attention to the girls’ interactions, to see how it might be done. Try as he might, he could never hear Niamh’s voice above the din, though hearing Maewyn was not so difficult. “Would you go down to one hundred?” “It’s already two hundred! Why would going down make any difference? I’m already giving you a deal.” The poor young man running the stall that Maweyn had stopped at was clearly disconcerted by the pretty young woman in front of him. Though his words were confident, the terror in his eyes was one Fane had seen in plenty of stable boys over the years as soon as a female showed themselves in the stables. Maewyn leaned over the counter conspiratorially. “Because then I would have that much more to spend on other things from your stall, of course.” She nodded to a scarf hung near the soft boots she was trying to haggle for. “If you throw in that scarf with the boots

for two hundred, you’ll have that much less to sell by the end of the day.” The boy wavered, looking very much as if he was about to take this “deal”. As soon as he was about to open his mouth to accept, an older woman that looked like his mother stepped from behind him from somewhere else in the booth. “No. Two hundred for the boots and that’s the final price.” Maewyn grimaced, clearly aware her charms would be of no use against this new foe, and handed over the correct amount with a pout. As soon as she walked away with her new boots, however, the encounter seemed completely forgotten as she piled her new purchase on top of the ever-growing pile in Niamh’s other basket. “You should probably get some boots of your own.” Niamh suddenly said near him. “Those don’t have any treads. They won’t be of much use on ice.” She added. Fane looked down. It was true- his boots were made for walking the smooth marble of palace steps, and were thin enough to be worn in the warm weather of his home country. He also noted, with some embarrassment, that the fine leather was marred already by scratches and gouges. Probably from his flight through the forest, and his subsequent hard labor afterward. They’d only been out for less than an hour, and Fane was already feeling the cold air snaking into his thin clothing. Though he wore a long-sleeved shirt, he couldn’t stand to be outside much longer without a coat. As the group continued their slow trek through the human jungle, Fane nearly forgot the reason they had come. Not that he even knew where to start with his staggering lack of all he needed. As if reading his mind, Maewyn suddenly squeaked and dashed forward to an uncommonly opulent-looking stall hung with clothing. She proudly displayed a fine leather jerkin, elegantly tailored and embroidered with golden images of deer intertwining around the other. He edged closer, Niamh close behind him, as they inspected the fine masterwork together. “You would look so handsome in this!” Maewyn said with a wink. A look he'd seen so often in his life, it had no effect on him anymore. Niamh exhaled in annoyance next to him. “You should definitely buy this one! It’s so suited to you.” Maewyn added. Niamh pawed at the garment to grab the price tag. Her eyes widened. “Maewyn, this is one thousand mynt! That’s far too much

to spend on one thing. We have to find something more frugal.” The more he listened to people talking around him, and the more often he witnessed the exchange of money, the more his education on Eira’s culture came flooding back to him. He was quick to associate that word- mynt- with the money that changed hands in front of him. “Here.” Niamh said, moving to a handsome coat hanging nearby. “This is a much better use of money. Fane, what do you think of this?” Niamh held it out for his inspection. It was a practical coat - Made of light brown woolen material, brown fur at the collar, and no extra decoration save for small leaves embroidered into the cuffs in a dark brown thread. It looked to be a bit oversized, but Fane didn’t mind at that point. “It’s the same price as the jerkin, but I think this will suit you much more.” Niamh added. “I think you’re right.” Fane said, handing the money to the merchant. Niamh took the coat off of the stall and handed it over to him. As soon as Fane put it on, his core warmed almost immediately. It was far thicker than it looked. Fane was pleased with his first purchase. Niamh wandered ahead, despite Maewyn’s protests and subsequent distraction by an orange dress at the same stall. Niamh walked to the next stall, followed closely by a curious Maewyn, and Fane did his best to follow. He passed by a small covered stall selling flaky-looking pastries. His mouth watered, and he was sorely tempted to use one of his mynt on it. When he looked up again from his pastry-induced stupor, he found that Niamh and Maewyn had moved several stalls down. He set off after them, still thinking of that pastry. Now that he wasn’t shivering, Fane could wander through the market as his leisure. He inhaled the pleasant savory spices wafting through the cold air, mingling and creating a pleasant warmth in his head. Fane smiled for the first time in a few days, savoring the bright colors and equally bright voices around him. He was so focused on looking around for blond heads, that he completely lost track of the auburn and white ones that he was supposed to be following. Fane looked around once more, and realized he was alone in the crowd. He drifted through the churning people, slowly taking in the atmosphere and keeping a watchful eye out for his newfound

companions. There was no way to tell how much time had passed, but surely they couldn’t have wandered too far away. Just as soon as he’d lulled himself into a sense of security, he saw another fair haired head bobbing only a few patrons ahead. The woman turned, and he saw at once that it was someone he knew. The daughter of a duchess of one of the outlying territories surrounding Trajhem. He’d only met her a few times, and she was about his age. Fane couldn’t even remember her name, but he always remembered faces. He paid no attention to the others surrounding him as he ducked inside one of the nearby bakeries. Fane felt the shop owner’s eyes on him as he nervously pretended to admire the breads inside the display case, all the while keeping his eye outside. As soon as the Aridian girl had passed, Fane scurried out to the street again. He realized with a start that he was in the worst possible place to be running into people he knew. If Fane were to have any hope of remaining undiscovered, he would need to get somewhere else. Anywhere else, really. He slipped into one of the thin alleys along the street, disappearing into the shade and emerging on the other side. Fane continued walking, hoping he would find the right direction back to the castle soon enough. Less and less people filled the streets as the light dimmed. The buildings gradually grew older, shorter, and more room between each one as he walked. The cobblestone streets sloped downward, away from the center of the city. Soon, the roar of rushing water reverberated off the walls. Mists rose and flowed over the cobblestones, creating a thin layer of ice that covered every surface. It was a challenge just to remain upright in his boots of soft leather. He thought back to the sturdy treads on Niamh's boots. She was right. Now he wished he’d listened sooner. Lights of glass and flame flickered to life in the deepening gloom. The sounds of merry voices faded away, leaving only the rushing water and the faint sounds of tavern noises and the occasional brawl drifting into the street. Fane stopped, taking a look around. The castle, its shining towers of ice, was nowhere in sight. With no small amount of panic growing in his throat as icy as the air around him, Fane tucked his parcels under his arm lamely. A prince never carried his own groceries, much less found himself in the slums of his own city. Then again, this wasn't his city. Fane realized, with much chagrin, that he was unarmed.

However, just as he'd done in the forest, he kept moving, willing his feet to carry him through the labyrinth of city streets. Fane made his way to the edge of the street, looking over the wooden railing to see the origin of the sounds of water. Three great rivers crisscrossed underneath tall, multi-leveled docks that built on each other. This section of the city seemed to be built on stilts, to make up for the slope of the mountain underneath. Ships of varying sizes sat moored against the current of the rivers, and Fane could see loads being moved from their decks to the great warehouses below. Fane found himself forgetting his earlier panic in the midst of his fascination with Eiran trade. A shout rose behind him. He turned in time to see a man in black, masked with only his eyes revealed, sprinting toward him. The man was thumbing a weapon into his hand as he ran. Fane stepped to the side, letting him speed past him. He soon saw that he wasn't running toward him at all, but instead running away from someone else. Right on his heels, another man gave chase. Hooded and cloaked in a deep moss green, he carried two axes on his back by way of a sturdy leather sheath. Fane stood still. His instincts told him to ignore them, to keep walking toward the safety of the castle that he couldn’t see. To forget all about it. He ignored all of these thoughts and ran after them. The ice-misty air was somehow worse as he ran, it pushed itself deep into his lungs and creeped under his shirt, chilling him to the bone. Though he almost lost the man in the cloak several times, he always found him again by some tug of instinct that drove him. Finally, the man in black was overtaken by his pursuer and they crashed to the ground. Fane stood back, watching them pummel each other, rolling around on the slick cobblestones. Neither of them noticed his presence. The cloaked pursuer grasped the man's collar, his large fists nearly the size of his face. He gained the upper hand and sat atop him, pinning his arms to his sides and growling ferally. Fane could barely hear anything over the roar of the rivers below, but the words "sickness" and "fade" came from the man in black, followed by the wet sound of a punch being landed. Fane winced despite himself. Rarely ever was he exposed to such raw violence. The nobility of his court preferred to settle matters

with early-morning fencing matches, or silent assassinations in the dead of night. As the cloaked man arose, hauling the unconscious criminal with him, he finally caught sight of Fane standing there staring at him dumbly. A hiss. "What do you want?" Fane was taken aback, though he shouldn't have been the least surprised at the tone he took. "Why are you taking that man in? What did he do?" The man in green was silent for a moment, his eyes glowering from under his hood. "That's none of your concern." Fane pushed forward, "Are you hunting him? Are there more of him?" He honestly didn't know why he was bothering to ask, considering the demeanor of this vigilante. Another pause. "Yes. There are more." His voice was flat, and he brushed past Fane, dragging the man behind him. Fane followed. "And you're hunting them alone?" Giving an exasperated huff, the man hiked the criminal to his shoulders. "Yes. Now go away." Fane stopped, watching him walk away, seemingly unaffected by the hulking weight on his back. Fane resumed walking after him, hoping that maybe he would be led to some more reputable parts of town. He followed, silently as possible, from a distance away. When he noticed that the taller man stopped again, he stopped in turn. "I told you to leave." Fane stared at him blankly. "I'm trying. But I am also new to this place and I can't seem to find my way back to the castle." "The castle, huh? No wonder you're so weak and thin looking." The prince bristled, feeling self-conscious of the parcels tucked under his arm. "I could tell that you were some preening nobleman from a mile away." The deep voice rumbled with some amusement. Fane chose not to respond, knowing full well when to press and when to withdraw. A skill he learned from years of determining his brother's changing moods. The taller man remained standing, not looking his way. Until finally, "Continue up this walkway until you get to the kirk in the center of town. From there, you can find your way back." And with that, the man was gone, running down the darkest alley to his left. Fane took his advice and continued forward, until

he reached where he had indicated. Sure enough, the white and blue spires of ice peaked above him, stretching to the stars. It took him several more minutes of jogging through empty city streets, but he at last came upon the castle gates again.

10 NIAMH HAD BEEN SO SWEPT up in the crowds and trying to keep Maewyn from buying everything at the market, that she realized after several minutes Fane was nowhere to be seen. She'd shrugged it off at the time, but several hours had gone by and he was still missing. She and Maewyn had already made their way home with packages bursting from their arms, and Niamh felt the pinprick of concern at the back of her mind. Ahealarth isn't that big, she comforted herself, and the castle is clearly visible from most areas of town. He’ll find his way back. Niamh nodded definitively. It wasn't worth worrying about yet. Maewyn had run to her room to put away all of her spoils some time before, so Niamh took advantage of the quiet to clean some of her own things. With the last of her underdresses hung neatly in a row drying by the fireplace, Niamh ventured out of her room with what was left over from the mynt that her master had given her. She didn't have to search long before she found him. His red hair glowed in the late afternoon light streaming in from the ice dome above the entrance hall. He turned to watch her walk down the main stairway toward him. "Here's the money that you gave me, master." Niamh dropped the few coins that were left into his waiting hand. "Though I don't know where Fane went." "He'll turn up, I'm sure." Hael said, not without some measure of irony in his tone. Just as she was about to leave him alone again, the new queen joined them in the hall. The Queen Maire, with Maewyn in tow, strolled up to them. Their matching green eyes couldn't have had more different expressions; Maewyn's bright, curious. Maire's blank and unimpressed with anything around her. Now that the wedding was

over, Maewyn was wearing more practical everyday clothing, though still revealing her lithe figure. Maire remained ever fashionable, her long gray dress sweeping around her in layers of gossamer. Both master and apprentice bowed. "I've heard so many great things about the unmatched power of the famous Phoenix Mage." Maire's silky voice drifted from her blood-red lips, her Corseilian accent smooth. "But..." She cast her eyes to Niamh, looking over her nose. "Nothing about his diminutive apprentice." Niamh straightened, "Oh, that could be because I only just became his apprentice a year ago and-" "How can you be sure that she's so deserving of the title, master Hael?" The queen continued, talking over Niamh as if she hadn't said anything. Niamh withdrew, giving Hael a pleading look. "I can guarantee that she is deserving, your majesty. Her power is great, and her skills as a healer even greater." Hael replied, not looking at Niamh. The corner of the queen's mouth lifted slightly in a smirk. "We shall see about that, won't we?" It was then that Maewyn piped up, "How about a duel, Niamh?" Her bright eyes sparkled with excitement. “I think it would be much more fun than the ingredients test that you made. No offense intended.” Niamh highly doubted that. She hesitated, "I don't often duel-" "You're saying you're not powerful enough, then?" Maire interjected, gazing at her fingernails absentmindedly. Niamh's eyes flitted to Hael briefly, looking to her master for some form of support. He offered none. Instead, nodding slightly and petting his red beard. “This would be a better substitute for the entrance trial.” He mused. “It would be over much more quickly.” Maewyn offered a hand, "Come on. It will be fun." She offered, smiling sweetly. You and I have a very different idea of fun. She thought, but finally conceded, taking Maewyn's gloved hand in her own. She noticed, however, that there was no embroidery of magical threads sewn into it. "Alright. I accept." She caught a glimpse of Hael's smirk, a silent challenge between the Head Magician and the queen. A short time later, the two women took their places across from one another. The reflective walls of the space Hael had made for

such a purpose cast the light of the floating lanterns in the air, creating a swirling pattern of color across the floor. Niamh finished braiding her hair into a crown around her head, and laced her boots tighter. Their overcoats hung neatly by the entrance, and any extra outerwear was discarded. They both kept their gloves. Maewyn looked confident, unruffled. She paced slowly, fixing Niamh with focus in her green eyes. Niamh held her gaze, refusing to show any sign of intimidation. Maewyn had flown through the initial stages of Hael’s entrance trials. What had taken Niamh two or three weeks had only taken Maewyn two or three days. Niamh hadn't seen Maewyn use magic at all in that time for herself, and from the looks of her bare gloves, she had no idea how Maewyn was even able to wield it at all. “Mages.” Hael began, his voice filling the space and reverberating off the walls. “Take your positions.” Niamh slid her feet into a defensive stance, setting herself as tall as she could. Maewyn bent at the waist, her hands becoming clawed. A pause. “Begin.” Before Niamh could react, Maewyn used those clawed hands to send a stream of fire toward her, bringing the scent of peaches and ocean breezes with it. The effect was quite disconcerting. Niamh jumped out of the way, throwing up a shield of water in the process. The fire dissolved into a thick steam. How is she able to use fire magic? Niamh thought indignantly. There were no red threads anywhere on Maewyn’s clothing. Channeling her raw magic through the blue threads in her gloves, Niamh kept the wall of water up for the next attack. Maewyn’s fire was blue and hotter than ever. Where on earth was Maewyn getting these types of magic? Niamh hadn’t even learned how to make blue fire yet. It crackled and sizzled over the surface of the shield, but she remained upright. Niamh allowed the water she held to crash down again, surrounding Maewyn in a tight stream, holding her arms in place. The room was filled with the scent of rosemary and nutmeg. Maewyn’s responding glare didn't sway her as she dug in tighter. The water split apart with a crack as Maewyn sent a bolt of magic shocking up Niamh’s arms. She cried out, and backed up toward the wall, pooling her magic in her gloves for another

defensive maneuver. Maewyn’s white hair flowed outward as she gathered her power, bringing more fire to her fingertips. Wherever she was hiding those threads, Niamh guessed that she only had fire. Though, to make it as hot as it was, she must have possessed a huge well of magic. The only way to test this was to keep pushing her opponent. Before Maewyn could attack again, Niamh channeled her magic through her rarely-used air thread, wrapping Maewyn’s hands in a suffocating ball of swirling wind. The fire died, inciting another dirty look from its owner. Hael stood near the door, his hand on his chin and a shield of his magic surrounding him. It neither shivered nor waivered at the impact of every ripple of magic that came against it. Maewyn, frustration growing on her face, tried again, her magic flying from her arms like birds of heat and flame. Niamh responded with her own wall of fire, absorbing them on impact. It continued like that for several minutes, Niamh wordlessly responding to each of Maewyn’s attacks with a shield or defense or incapacitation. When Maewyn attacked with fire Niamh met her with water. Niamh countering every attack that came her way eventually led to Maewyn’s cries of annoyance and frustration. They stood apart, Maewyn panting and beginning to sweat, while Niamh stood as serenely as possible. She would not give her the satisfaction. Maewyn glowered at her, Niamh watching as thoughts went through her mind one by one. She took a moment to collect herself, straightening. Niamh waited. Neither of them spoke a word, both women growing still. Without warning, Maewyn rallied her magic and threw more daggers of fire toward Niamh. Niamh threw up a shield of water, again, but not until seeing that Maewyn immediately followed up with a mixture of fire, white hot and blazing. Niamh panicked inwardly, dropping her water and shifting to a wall of fire, but Maewyn’s magic was too much for Niamh’s to contain. The resulting inferno sent her slamming into the wall behind. Hael waved his hand out of the corner of her eye, and all the fire dissipated. Alright. That’s it! Niamh stood, her patience at an end, stalking toward Maewyn with a look in her eyes the younger mage hadn't seen before. Maewyn was briefly alarmed as Niamh touched her first two fingers to her opponent’s forehead.

Any defense Maewyn had stirring in her hands fell to the ground and her body became rigid, her eyes staring straight ahead. A moment later, both women were standing before a wide expanse of water. The ocean. Columns of white marble rose next to them, and Maewyn stood alone in a sea green dress of flowing fabric to her knees. Sandals on her feet, and a delicate hairpiece of pearl in her hair. Maewyn stared ahead at the ocean in front of her, her eyes brimming with homesickness. Niamh felt a twinge of guilt at resorting to illusion magic. She knew it was lying, a convoluted and magical lie. It was the same thread she often used for healing- the one that dealt with internalized magic in another’s body. Niamh was not fond of delving deeply into people’s memories, trapping them in them until she deemed it necessary, and this was the first time she used it offensively. “In illusion, a good magician uses his opponent’s memories against them.” Hael had said, plopping a sizable tome in front of her. “A better magician can manipulate those memories to do his bidding. And...” He leaned across the table, fixing his eyes to hers. “The best magicians can invent illusions from nothing. Making his opponents see and feel things they may never have before.” Niamh was not the best. Not yet. So the illusion before both of their eyes was just one of Maewyn’s memories. Her home country of Corseils, Niamh guessed, from the open air architecture around them. A ship, far out on the water, sailed from view. The breeze became cold and the sky darkened. Maewyn’s white hair billowed in the increasing wind. A storm. Maewyn gazed out on the water, though Niamh couldn’t decipher her expression. Was it longing? Pain? Niamh had barely a moment to decide before Maewyn’s expression changed again. Realization melted across her face, and she turned her eyes to stare directly into Niamh’s. She’s a good magician. Niamh thought with a begrudging sense of pride. Maewyn smirked. “You nearly got me there.” Her two fingers came up to Niamh’s forehead before Niamh could counter and the world changed. “Another advanced skill that I could teach you:” Hael had added, “If you are without a corresponding thread for what you need, a skilled mage can channel their magic through the thread of another’s just by

touching them. Though, that takes much practice and no shortage of audacity.” At Niamh’s widened eyes, he continued. “It’s not a ‘clean’ move by any means, but it can help you win if you’re desperate enough.” Now, instead of a shimmering white palace, it was a humble cottage in the mountains. A tall, auburn haired young man stood, shuffling maps and papers on a desk as she stood in the doorway. Nythaniel. The day he left. “This is private.” Niamh said through gritted teeth. Maewyn merely shrugged, moving to stand in front of the illusion of her brother. “My, he’s handsome.” She smiled mockingly at her. “I guess he gained all the good looks of the family.” Niamh glared at her. She dared not look at Nythaniel’s face as he turned, his lips mouthing her name in the memory. Niamh instead gazed purposefully at the fire raging in the fireplace, allowing it to rekindle the determination that was slipping away in her heart. Once she'd gained enough sense to move her arms again, Niamh snapped her fingers. The cottage melted away into the deck of a grand vessel, the flag of Corseil’s snapping in the breeze above them. Maire, then only a Lady, stood with her cousin at the rail. Her white hair flowing from a long tail at the back of her head. Maewyn placing a comforting hand over Maire’s slim, white fist. Glimmering tears streamed down both of their faces. Maewyn glared at her this time, “Don’t touch that.” She growled. “The trick to an illusion in any sort of battle is to make your opponent forget that he is fighting; forget his own rage and incapacitate him before he realizes what’s happening.” Hael had said, flipping Niamh’s tome to a certain page. “If you can’t make him give up by that method, the next way is to scare them into submission.” Maewyn’s anger rippled off of her in force. She stalked across the deck, her boots clicking on the imaginary wood. The scene shivered, Niamh searching for a different memory to cast as an illusion. The deck became a wet city street, the foul stench of trash and rot rising from the corners. People in fine white clothes drifted by silently. There was no sound other than carriage wheels clattering against the cobblestone streets. Two girls huddled together in the shadow of a marble column. One of them no older than five and the other around eleven or twelve. They shivered in the rain pouring from their matching white hair. Their bare feet were dirty, their faces thin and weary.

“Don’t. Touch. That.” Maewyn snarled near her, tears already welling in her eyes. I went too far. Niamh thought, letting her hands go slack quickly, shattering the illusion around them. “Maewyn, I’m sorr-“ Niamh’s mouth opened, but was quickly shut again as a new illusion sprung up around her. Fire. The neigh of panicked horses. A young woman’s screams and the sound of weapons being drawn. Cruel laughter floating over the flames. She stood in a pantry, the door to it open slightly to the sight of a cottage ablaze. Fear struck her heart, though she didn’t remember why. She felt the heat on her face, and instinctively she stepped from the doorway into the fiery room. A couple lay on the floor, the flames overtaking their dead bodies. The scent of burning flesh filled the air, mixed with smoke and ash. She turned. Three more men lay on the floor, screaming in agony. She looked down. Her hands were covered in flame. It climbed up her sleeves, licking her chin as it reached her chest. It’s only an illusion. She thought, frantically to herself. Panic rose in her chest, and she dove to her knees, taking her head in her hands. It’s only an illusion. She closed her eyes, squeezing them shut against the tears that threatened to spill out. “How do you know how to scare them?” Niamh had asked her master, her eyes wide with innocence. Hael grimaced. “To win, you must be ruthless. If you can dig deep enough, you can find a person’s worst memories and make them relive it just enough to get them to heel.” A scream filled the air, though Niamh didn't know whose it was. Hael’s deep voice cut through the screaming in her head. “Enough.” He yelled, cutting through the scene with a handful of magic. The flames, bodies, and fear faded away, leaving only Niamh gazing at her own terrified face in the reflection on the floor. Her eyes wide, tears spilling over the edges, her head in her hands. All the pleasant magical scents wafting around the room faded away, leaving only the cold, bitter air. Maewyn was teary-eyed and panting, standing across the room from her defeated opponent. Maire stood cooly by the door. Niamh dared not look at her face. The queen had been right, and she knew it. Maire turned to leave without a word, but not before her and

Hael shared a glance. “Maewyn of Corseils.” Hael rumbled, “You have hereby passed the entrance trial. Welcome to your training.” His eyes flashed with anger, and Maewyn bowed. “Be in my office first thing in the morning.” She bowed deeper, moving to retrieve her overcoat and casting a glance full of regret toward Niamh who remained on the floor. She fled the hall, leaving master and healer alone in silence.

11 AFTER CONVINCING THE guards at the gate that he did, in fact, now live at the castle and he was not up to trouble despite the early hour, Fane finally made it home to his assigned room. Hael had apparently spoken ahead of him and found a bed for his use, but Fane would have wandered the servants' halls forever if someone hadn’t left his door open for him. His room was private, at least, if not much else. Barely bigger than a closet, there was nothing but a bed and a nightstand with a washing sink above it for furnishings. Fane wondered what Hael had to say to get him a place like this, and if he’d mentioned that Fane did have a job in the castle. He wasn’t about to look like some freeloader and invite the ire of the servants there. The few clothes he now had were stashed under the bed in a neat box. He flopped onto the hard and squeaky bed, his aching body finding relief even in that poor excuse for comfort. A dust cloud poofed up as his body hit the sad mattress. He groaned. What he wouldn’t give to be in his luxurious warm bed at home, his silken sheets and weighty comforters around him. His thoughts drifted to the ivy hanging in front of his window, looking out onto the castle grounds and gardens beyond. His favorite view in the mornings. He remembered often seeing Friedhelm the younger strolling with their father, Friedhelm the elder, in the many lonely mornings of his childhood. It was never friendly; never a bonding moment between a father and his eldest son. Although he could never hear what was being said on those walks, it always seemed as if it was an obligation and a dreaded chore for his brother. Fane’s eyes drooped closer and closer to sleep. He himself would never have to bear the weight of the largest and most prosperous kingdom in the world. No, he was able to enjoy forever the privilege that princes enjoyed: Freedom. Time. A life free of the

crown and duty to rule. He could love his home without keeping the peace, and that suited him just fine. But this, Eira, was his home now. At least for the time being. Niamh didn't move from the floor for several minutes. She breathed, allowing her magic to settle into a calm wave inside of her, crashing against the boundaries she set for it. Back and forth. Breathing in and out. Slowing. Steadying. Hael waited patiently, familiar with his apprentice’s rhythms. He himself had gotten her to this point before too, during some of their more intense training sessions. He taught her how to bring her magic back to heel, how to force it back into submission inside of her when it was flaring and trembling to be released. Finally, she rose to her feet slowly, sighing deeply as she did. Hael’s face was simmering with anger, far more than his usual exasperated expression. She felt a pang of shame. “If you’ve collected yourself, let’s talk in my study.” He growled. Oh, he was angry. It must have been because she’d just humiliated him and herself in front of the new queen. Embarrassment washed over her as she gathered her overcoat and discarded staff by the door and followed him up the winding stairs. Once they emerged into Hael’s quiet study, Niamh delicately lowered herself into a soft armchair. The lightning that Maewyn had thrown against her had affected her body more than she initially realized, her limbs shaking from stiffness. Careful not to get too comfortable, lest she not be able to get up again, Niamh kept herself on the edge of the cushion. A cold, empty teapot sat on Hael’s desk. As he bent to retrieve two mugs from one of the large drawers, steam rose from the spout. He lifted it to pour the pungent healing tea into the mugs. Niamh allowed the scent of oranges, sweet spices, and honey to wash over her senses. The magic imbued into it was already working through her body by the time she took the first sip. With the hot cup nestled in her tired hands, she waited. The tick of a clock coming from somewhere in the dim of the room. Hael waited, scowling at the stained glass window above his desk. Finally he spoke, his voice low and measured in the stifling air of the small space. “Do you know at what point you lost?” He asked. Her chest tightened. “At the end, when I lost control. That opened the door for Maewyn to strike a killing move.”

“No” His tone was clipped. “You could have easily won that duel, Niamh, if you really wanted to.” His eyes flashed with fire. “But that’s just it. You didn’t want to.” Her heart fluttered with indignance. Her master stood to face the glass window, his hands clasped behind his flaming robes of crimson. “Maewyn may have great power, maybe even more than you do.” Niamh opened her mouth to protest. “But,” He continued, holding up a silencing finger. “You make up for something that she lacks. And that is control.” He turned to face her again, seeing her swallow her pride. “Control, Niamh. You gained and held on to that control throughout the entirety of the duel.” Heat simmered behind his steady gaze, holding her in her seat. “The thing that Maewyn has that you don’t; the one thing that practically handed her that victory is her commitment. Her drive. Her confidence. Her need to win. And next time, your hesitation may just cost you your life or the life of a patient.” He sighed and pinched the bridge of his nose with a thumb and forefinger. “I understand that you struggle with offensive magic; you always have. But...” His hands came down on the desk softly as he leaned forward to fix her eyes on his. “If Maewyn had been a real threat; if I hadn't been overseeing... It doesn’t matter how much power you have, how much control... The second you hesitated would have gotten you killed.” Niamh couldn’t keep the burning thoughts contained in her mouth any longer. “But I thought that a good healer is supposed to have empathy?” “A good healer makes decisions.” His voice hardened. “A good healer does not waver in doing what needs to be done.” The burning in her eyes grew to brimming tears. “That means defending the weak. That means healing, or protecting, without reservations. The moment that you hold back could mean the difference between life and death.” She nodded silently. Silence fell between them again. The correction hung in the air. As if sensing her thoughts, he spoke again. “I know this is all new for you, Niamh.” Hael’s tone softened, and he finally took a swig of his own tea. “Maewyn has skills and a depth of power that are

beyond any other candidate at the academies. But I believe that you can still surpass her if you really try.” Niamh stood and nodded. He wouldn’t replace me with her. She reminded herself. Niamh had earned her spot at the castle. She’d worked and studied, given up her whole life in the academy, just to be chosen. Hael wouldn’t do that to her. The healing power of the tea she drank soothed her aching limbs and her frayed nerves. She bowed respectfully, and brought a gracious hand from her chest to extend out to him. The formal end to any lesson between mages. Though she didn't like being corrected, she accepted his authority and trusted his advice. “Thank you for watching out for me, Master.” She felt a fire-warmed breeze ruffle her hair a bit as she stood. Her master hid the smile tugging at the corner of his mouth as he took a sip from his mug and waved a hand dismissively. “I should hope that someday you two will get along.” He said as she turned. Another nod and she was leaving the dimness of the study behind, shutting the door behind her with a click. Niamh sulked back to her cottage in the gardens, its warm light welcoming her to its cozy interior. Though her bedroom was in the castle, and she felt comfortable there, the work cottage was her real home. Her heart was comforted by the thought of a hot mug of spiced tea and sitting near her fireplace with one of her tomes in her lap. What a nice ending to a horrible day. As she approached, weaving through the ice animals dotting the gardens' landscape, the thatched roof and sturdy stone walls came into view. And something else. Sitting outside her cottage, its front door wide open, was a small cart full of belongings. It overflowed with foreign looking tools and clothes, scrolls wrapped around golden centers, books of bound fabric instead of wood and leather, and multiple containers of varying sizes of herbs and spices. And none of it hers. Her steps quickened to stand in the doorway to the small building. What she saw made her catch her breath in disgust. All of her carefully arranged drying herbs were now mixed in with others that hung lower, obscuring her view of the back of the cottage. The bookshelves were overflowing. Her books, her precious private collection was shoved to one side, and other books now filled the shelves in the Corseilian language. Niamh stared,

shoving down the irritation rising in her stomach. The large desk that took up much of the back corner of the cottage was now divided as well, her supplies and extra papers and mixtures placed carefully on one side, all of her potion shelves and jars and bottles stacked too-full on the few shelves above her new half of a desk. And in the middle of it all, Maewyn stood with an armful of her personal belongings. "Oh! You're back!" She said cheerfully, setting Niamh's things gently on her armchair. As if nothing had happened between them. As if they hadn’t just exposed their worst memories to each other. Her ocean eyes were only slightly apologetic, and Niamh knew it was not for anything that had happened during their duel, but more for touching her things. "I was cleaning up to make room for my supplies." Niamh gritted her teeth silently, casting a protective glance at her pictures and the box she kept on the mantle. Fortunately, Maewyn hadn't reached them yet, and they were still in the same place. "Is that so?" Niamh ground out. Oh, this was insult to injury. I did not need this today. Niamh grabbed her most personal items from the mantle, and tucked them into her cape pockets. Niamh stalked over to the armchair and scooped up what Maewyn had moved, stacking it carefully in her arms and stormed from the cottage without another word to her rival. She trudged all the way back up to her bedroom in the castle, passing servants and nobility without a word of greeting. She felt their confused looks as she passed them. Felt them and didn’t care. She plopped the pile on her bed unceremoniously "No." She said aloud, clamping down hard on the anger that she was allowing to rage through her head. She took a deep breath. Anger is not befitting a healer. Another deep breath. In and out, again and again until her anger dissolved into tears that slipped from her eyes briefly. This is nothing but my bruised ego. She thought, wiping her eyes. It's not Maewyn's fault. It's mine for failing to win. “No.” She said aloud again, breathing. Control. You maintain control. You are a healer. Gracious. Kind. Gentle. The deepening evening light streaming in through the windows calmed her frazzled nerves. The solid stone of the walls of her modest room

were a welcome steadying sight, giving her a visual stability as she continued breathing. In and out. Like a wave. Gracious. She walked to her pile, carefully picking up each item and placing it in a new home. Kind. Her precious box and picture frame, containing one of the only portraits she had of her family together. She placed them both in her nightstand drawer, shutting it softly. Gentle. Standing in front of the cold light from the windows, she took one more calming breath. Niamh stayed in her room for a couple more hours afterward. Before long, her stomach was growling and her mind was looking for an occupation. She left her room and headed for the Library, hoping that Maewyn wouldn’t have the same idea.

12 FANE, AT LAST, AFTER what seemed like the better part of the day, emerged from the depths of the Library with a nearly empty cart. Three Lore Cats were under his feet, making his trek slow going back to the Keeper. He thought he’d stop by the last room on his way out. What horrible things will she have for me this time? He was never sure of anything in the Library. It hadn’t taken him long at all to learn that he could not trust his eyes, or his feet for that matter, when he was entrenched in the halls of the magical place. He was glad for the cover, though. A place to hide in plain sight with the crop of Aridian nobles running around the city. He thought back to the close run-in with the daughter of the duchess. There was no guarantee that anyone would recognize him, but considering his circumstances, he could hardly take any chances. He plucked the last handful of books from his cart, and started up one of the many rolling ladders attached to the shelves. Just when he reached the top, a Lore Cat darted from the shadows and swiped the ladder with a massive paw. He sighed. This had become the Cats’ favorite game. In an effort to keep himself balanced he would grab the top of the ladder and drop whatever was in his hands. The first time, he’d fallen and taken all of the books down with him. He was sure this amused those cursed Cats greatly. Muttering a curse, he clamored down the ladder. This sent the Lore Cat plunging for the darkness again. He was sure it was laughing as it went. Another moment and Fane realized that laugh had come from someone else. He turned, flustered, and dropped the book that he'd just bent to retrieve. The tips of his ears became hot. "Niamh." The mage he'd lost in the market was nearly bent over laughing. “Thank you. I needed a good laugh.” She said between gasps for air. Niamh cleared her throat sheepishly. "It looks like you found

your way back here after all?" The offending Lore Cat that had been plaguing him all day peeked a curious and malevolent eye around the corner of the bookshelf at him. He averted his glare to offer an embarrassed glance at Niamh. "Eventually, yes." He thought back to the dirty streets and even grimier inhabitants of the docks, a place that Niamh likely never stepped foot in. She cocked her head, her braid falling from her shoulder. "Eventually? It shouldn't have taken you more than fifteen minutes to reach the castle again from the markets." He grimaced, placing the book in his hand back on the cart. The Lore Cat watching him looked a bit chagrined. "It didn't look that way from all the seedy taverns I stumbled in to." The Lore Cat with Niamh emerged from the shadows and unceremoniously leaped onto Fane’s back, its claws digging into his vest. A look of confusion that turned into alarm passed over Niamh's face. "You were down by the docks, weren't you? Fane, that is not a place that you just 'stumble' in to." He felt the heat of color staining his cheeks again. "I'm not the best with direction, apparently." He grunted as the Lore Cat hiked itself higher on his back, bending him over with its weight. Despite Niamh's tone, he saw the corners of her mouth turn up. "Well..." Her hands reached for the book that he had discarded on the cart. "I'm glad you made it back safely, at least." Fane was torn. How could someone with such a terrifying power be so kind? She took a step forward toward him while he took a step back. If she noticed, Niamh didn’t show it as she gracefully slipped up the ladder and placed the book in its correct place, as if she'd done it a thousand times. The Lore Cat left her alone, he thought with a grudging glance at the offensive creature at the corner. Once she was back on the ground, Niamh delicately peeled the Cat from his shoulders and set it on the floorboards again. “What were you here for?” Fane asked, and cringed inwardly at how rude it probably sounded. Niamh held up the book in her hands, “Oh, just some... Fairytales. Nothing really.” “Oh,” Fane raised his eyebrows, “I like fairytales too.” Niamh looked up at him from under long lashes. “Yes? Which

ones?” “I haven’t read any since I was a child, but I can’t say I know enough to say.” Fane replied. The conversation came to a screeching halt. Averting her eyes, Niamh fiddled with the end of her braid. The awkwardness hung there like a heavy blanket. Just as he was about to open his mouth to say something, anything, a Lore Cat chose that moment to race around the corner. The scratching of claws on the wood was enough to break the silence as the Cat rammed into the cart, sending it flying down the aisle with a loud rattle. Fane's embarrassment only worsened as Niamh walked away, her long braid swaying as she disappeared through the door again without another word to him. In the silence that followed, he tipped his head back to stare at the high ceiling. Why didn’t I say anything? Pinching his nose between a thumb and forefinger, he glared at the Lore Cat now grooming itself peacefully. "I hope you're happy with yourself." It only offered a self-satisfied meow in response. Shortly after, as he was passing the front desk, the Keeper popped her head from behind the desk with a peeved expression. This was her constant state of being, Fane was learning. “You took forever to shelve that cart. I thought a strong young man such as yourself would be at least a little more efficient.” She tutted at him. “And I should know what forever is, boy. Do you see how old I am? I might have finally died of old age by the time you returned.” Fane huffed in annoyance, though said nothing. He didn’t even dare to think in her presence, lest she could somehow read his thoughts. Fane shoved the empty cart to stand with the rest. He couldn’t even have confidence that the carts were finally empty, as he didn't trust her to leave them un-enchanted with some kind of spell that made them fill again each time he pulled a book. The old mage shook her head at him, wagging a finger. “What other useful skills will you need that you don’t have?” Fane bristled. “I have plenty of skills. I am well-trained in the art of diplomacy, theater, politics, culture, musi-“ She cut him off with an upraised hand. His mouth closed without his input. “How are those going to help you if an enemy is knocking down the front gates, hm?” Fane had no answer for her. Though it unsettled him that her words held more meaning than she probably realized.

The Keeper seemed to be satisfied at his stunned silence and turned back to her book, not sparing him another thought. The sun was already dipping below the mountains by the time Fane made it back down to his room. His back and knees ached from climbing up and down ladders and dodging Cats left and right for hours on end. He managed to avoid anyone walking the halls, servants and nobility alike. Unlike in his own palace, when his every move seemed to be watched and analyzed. He removed his vest, boots, and belt, lounging on his creaky bed in only a shirt and trousers. The Keeper's words sat inside of his head, even as he lay staring at the ceiling of his cramped room. Irritation rose in him by the minute. All he wanted in that moment was to be home, not worrying about the whistling winds seeping in his window, or the terrifying implication that he may be stuck here forever. The winds outside seemed to mock him. Something deep inside of him was tired of waiting on the sidelines, waiting for things to happen to him and for him, tired of being looked over even as he was the prince of a realm. And indeed...He was always being looked through, unseen beyond his title. That something inside snapped, and he sat up. With a begrudged huff, he rose from bed and strapped on his leather vambraces from his otherwise discarded hunting armor. And his new, treaded boots. Though he'd nearly forgotten about it, he hauled his bow and quiver from where he stored it under his bed. Moonlight, clear and bright, shone through the small window in his room, illuminating the metal on the tips of his arrows. They glinted beckoningly. Fane, thinking more clearly than he had in several days, took the tip of one of those arrows and carefully scratched out the small insignias on both of the vambraces. The stag of Aridia, finely carved into the leather, was quickly scraped over and marred beyond recognition. One less thing to expose his identity. He didn't know exactly what he was doing as he opened his door silently, and stepped out into the waiting silence of the hallway. Then into the silence of the streets. Soon, to the familiar rushing sound of the rivers below crashing through the alleys. He better be around here tonight or I got all the way out here for

nothing. Fane thought, grumpily. He pulled his cloak tighter around him and found a corner to wait on. He didn't have to wait long, fortunately, as the sound of feet pounding stone echoed to him from somewhere close. He smirked with anticipation. Sure enough, the tall man was there again with the same axes on his back, tussling with another man in black. This one was bulkier, bigger and definitely giving the vigilante a run for his money in terms of size and strength. For a brief moment, the vigilante in the cloak was restrained by the bigger man's choke hold. Fane chose this moment to step from the shadows, bringing as much dramatic gravitas as he could muster. "Do you want help with that?" He asked simply, leaning against the wooden corner of the nearby building. He felt himself slipping into a character- that of someone he thought the man in green might respect. The cloaked man strained, bringing his elbows to smash in his attacker's ribs. "No. I'm fine." He whipped around and punched the man in black, which sent him stumbling. The man in green got a quick look at Fane, and rolled his eyes. “Oh, you again.” Fane smiled easily in response, stepping into his cocky persona that he used whenever he wanted to irritate his older brother. This criminal was particularly resilient, and he rebounded quickly, running back at the man in green again. The vigilante grunted as he was lifted from his feet. "What can you tell me about these criminals?" Fane asked again, inspecting his fingernails. He found they were far dirtier than they had ever been in his life. He would need a bath at some point. This time, the criminal himself answered him, as he brought the cloaked man slamming to the ground. "We are the Fade. And you and your friend here would do well not to hinder us." The man in green got the air knocked from his lungs, but that didn't stop him from landing a hard hitting kick to the man's chin as he stood over him. "He's most certainly not my friend." Fane answered, smirking at the two as they fought, even as he cringed inwardly. The man in green saw this, and glared at him from where he was rising to his feet.

"I don't need your help or your snarky comments. Go. Away." Those last words were punctuated by accompanying punches landed on the man in black's face. He stumbled. Another kick to the nose sent him reeling, finally bringing him down hard in a pile of barrels nearby. Fane ignored his comment. "The Fade? It sounds like there are more than just a handful of criminals with a name like that. Perhaps an entire crime syndicate?" Fane made no move to help the man in green as he succeeded in rendering the other man unconscious. He grunted as he dragged him by one gigantic boot from where he lay. "You're sure you can take them all down by yourself?" Fane pushed, masking his expression to hide his alarm that the man in green was now stalking toward him. He shot a finger to Fane’s face, to which Fane replied with the cock of his head and a patronizing grin, though inside, he flinched. "If you're implying that I either need or want your help, you are mistaken." He snarled, that finger nearly touching Fane’s nose. "You would be of no use to me, anyway. Even with that bow, you're a weakling and you can't hide it." The prince remained calm outwardly, with great effort, refusing satisfaction to the man that was clearly losing his grip on his temper. What little grip he had to begin with, Fane guessed. "I wouldn't be a weakling if I had someone to train with." Fane said, looking pointedly at the man's finger and then into his eyes. They glowered with a simmering rage. The vigilante didn't answer, instead trudging back to lift the criminal with a heave. "Those hands don't look like they have worked a day in your life." The vigilante was neither strong enough nor big enough to haul off the criminal like he'd done the night before. He gazed down at him in frustrated defeat. Turning his back to Fane, he left the man in black where he lay sprawled on the street. "So no. Not a chance." He finished, rumbling and nearly growling in anger. Fane allowed the silence to hang between them, drawing it out just long enough to make his point. A skill he’d learned in his books on playwriting. Raise the tension, save the punchline. He thought, letting his thoughts fill the empty space. 13 THE NEXT MORNING, NIAMH was well-recovered from her wounded pride, and ventured out to her work cottage. As she inhaled the fresh morning air upon entering the gardens, the thatched roof beckoned her with its familiarity. She pushed her way through the door, feeling the wood where her hands had created their own groove. Though she hadn’t forgotten yesterday’s events, they stung less after a night’s sleep. Seeing Maewyn in the midst of all that was familiar was an unwelcome reminder of their new-found competition. As Niamh entered, she grumbled under her breath to see the younger mage standing in Niamh’s favorite spot; in the middle of the long table, right under the round window at the back of the cottage. The healer hung her cape on the hook by the door with more force than she intended. Maewyn turned to face her over her shoulder, her bright eyes greeting her enthusiastically. “Oh! Hello, Niamh.” Uncertainty flashed across her face for a brief moment. As Niamh stepped closer, she saw that Maewyn was in the middle of making a potion of some sort, her hand halfway between pouring an ingredient into her grindstone. It’s not Maewyn’s fault, Niamh reminded herself, taking her other favorite spot further down the table. “Hello, Maewyn.” A pause. If she was going to be working with her, there was no use in making it harder than it had to be. Might as well be social. Relief flickered in Maewyn’s eyes. “Oh, so you’re not upset?” Yes. “No, not at all.” She lied. “You did best me in our duel.” Niamh

didn’t turn her way as she set to work reorganizing all that Maewyn had haphazardly thrown on to her shelves. Disordered boxes of dried herbs and bottles of oils were soon reorganized, as she slid them into place by alphabetical order and then by height, and then by quantity. Just as Niamh was beginning to drown herself in this pleasant task, Maewyn’s voice cut through her thoughts again, quieter this time. “I’m sorry I used your thread without asking.” “Oh. Well...” She did turn to face her then. Seeing Maewyn’s face, so anxious for forgiveness, tugged at her heart, though she ignored it. “I started it.” The silence hung in the air between them, the crackle of the fire the only sound. As Maewyn was about to reply, Niamh turned to her work again to discourage any more engagement. Though the tension in the air was dissipated, making the task that much more meditative. After a few minutes, Maewyn was humming in thought. The healer glanced around her hand obscuring the other mage’s work, and saw that a recipe lay before her. “What are you making?” She asked mildly, trying to fill the space with more pleasant topics. “Oh. Nothing, really. Just a medicine.” Her specialty. She had to see it now. “What kind?” Maewyn didn't respond, and instead shooed the piece of paper her way. Niamh gazed at it. A simple recipe with simple ingredients, though the description was vague. A Tincture for Bad Dreams and Restless Nights. With practical elements such as lavender and chamomile ground together to make a fine powder, with a drop of night sky added for good measure. Simple and effective, used for the most mundane bouts of insomnia. “This looks easy. Did you find the bottle of night sky that I keep in here?” Niamh asked, handing the paper back. “I hope that’s alright.” Under normal circumstances, it wasn’t generally acceptable to go rummaging through a mage’s private collection of ingredients and herbs. However, considering that Maewyn was clearly making this for someone else, and they did share a workspace.... As Niamh was about to offer some advice on making the tincture more effective, the door to the cottage opened. For a split second, she expected Hael’s fiery red hair to appear, followed immediately

by a scowl and perhaps a scolding for something or another. The two women turned to see not their master, but the Queen Maire step through their door. “Maire!” Maewyn’s smile widened, and she jumped forward to greet her cousin. Niamh held back, offering a polite bow at the waist. The queen neither smiled nor offered any sort of indication that Maewyn’s presence was any more welcome than a puppy jumping around her legs. She regarded her with a measured indifference, allowing Maewyn to exhaust herself with her enthusiasm. “I finished the medicine you wanted.” Maewyn inhaled sharply, casting a quick glance at Niamh as if she'd forgotten she was there. Niamh pretended not to hear, watching the queen’s reaction with a polite smile. The queen palmed the bottle of liquid, slipping it into the fold of her voluminous skirts into some hidden pocket. “Thank you.” Maire replied. Her poison-green eyes regarded the small space around them. Her regal bearing, her very presence, was like an overwhelming luxury seeming to completely occupy the humble one-room cottage. The silk of her skirts brushed against worn legs of chairs and a small chest that lay behind one of them. She didn't say anything else, not one word wasted on court mages such as her. Niamh imagined that she probably would have made more conversation with her cousin if she had not been standing there. As if sensing the awkwardness of the room, Maewyn giggled uncomfortably and motioned for the threesome toward the door. “Would you like to walk back with us, Maire?” She asked brightly. The queen merely nodded, allowing Maewyn to walk through the door first. The younger mage turned back quickly, as if forgetting some important detail. “Erm...Let me clear this snow for you. I don’t want your pretty dress getting ruined.” She said. She obviously walked over here just fine. Niamh thought, glancing at the long layers of dry fabric flowing behind the queen. Maire nodded, and Maewyn was shooting out the door, making Niamh think of her puppy analogy again. For the first time since the ball before the wedding, Niamh was alone with the queen. Maewyn’s crunching footsteps faded further down the path, followed by the whoosh of her fire magic melting the snow.

Maire towered over the young healer by nearly a head, her white hair gleamed coldly even with the warm light of the fire flickering against it. Where her high, aristocratic forehead was once bare, she now wore the white metal of a complicated circlet.
