Interconnecting patterns swirled across it and around her head, coming to an elegant point at the back, creating the crown shape as it rose from her intricately braided hair. Her emerald green dress, though simply decorated, was well-made and fitted to her lithe body, swirling around her legs like a silken waterfall. Over her shoulders and the low-cut pointed neckline was a shawl of thick white fur, speckled with black. “It seems that my dearest cousin is now your peer.” Maire’s silken voice with that melodious accent floated over her head. Gliding to Maewyn’s work station, her white hands brushed each of Maewyn’s bottles with a delicate touch. Her thin, painterly fingers grasped one of them and peered at the label with disinterest. “Yes.” Niamh answered simply, not sure of what else to say in response. Whenever Niamh had witnessed the queen interacting with members of the court, with Hael, or even with her own husband, her demeanor was nothing but frigid smiles and measured words. Winter lay over her face more heavily than it did over the whole of Eira, and Niamh felt its chill shiver up her spine every time the queen looked at her with those piercing eyes. Niamh felt small under that gaze. “She-Maewyn-is a powerful magic user.” Niamh added self- consciously, trying desperately to fill the heavy silence. The fire sputtered as a cold gust of wind shot down the chimney and into the small room. A smile spread across the queen’s blood-red lips, though it did not set Niamh at ease in the slightest. “She may be, yes.” The queen turned to her. “But you climbed into Hael’s lap first.” Her voice slithered across the warm wood of the cottage, turning it cold. She fixed Niamh with a predator’s stare. “Perfect marks from your time at the academy? Apparently, when it comes to knowledge, you possess unmatched perfection in nearly every magical subject.” A shudder went up Niamh’s spine. How does she know that? “And apparently, a perfect string of healings too. At least on record.” The queen set the bottle back down on the counter and moved toward the door in a smooth, serpentine movement. Dread

rose in Niamh’s throat. “We would hate for that record to be marred, now wouldn’t we?” “What do you mean?” Niamh asked, trying to keep the shake from her voice. Maire seemed to hear her nervousness underneath, even as she tried to hide it, her eyes glimmering as a snake eyeing a bird. She tutted, turning her gaze away and staring out at Maewyn frantically creating a path through the snow. “It’s a wonder that Hael is even considering you for Head Mage at all, considering how very little experience you have and how...vulnerable...you might be to making mistakes.” Niamh swallowed. “A Head Mage, or even a diminutive apprentice, who makes mistakes, is of no use to the security of a nation.” Maire added. Her eyes met Niamh’s for the first time. “Hael may be your master, but all of his recommendations come under the king’s approval.” The queen remarked as she glided the remaining space to the door. Maewyn had finished her task and was waving at her two companions to join her in the yard. “You would do well to remember who holds your fate in their hands.” With that, the door closed. Niamh shuddered, despite the warmth of the fire. It genuinely had never occurred to her that the position she dreamed of, everything she had worked toward for years, could not only be denied but that it could be purposely withheld. Spitefully withheld. That scared her more than anything the queen had actually said. Niamh stayed in her cottage long after Maire left, but it felt a little less safe. A little less like her own.

14 BY THE THIRD NIGHT, Fane no longer needed to lay in his uncomfortable bed to decide his course. As soon as he heard the click of the last of the servants closing their doors, he arose and dressed quickly. He was growing tired of his old riding leathers. The scratched face of the emblem of Aridia stared back at him as he donned the shoulder guard. Many more of these excursions and he would have to find something less...obvious to wear. Fane took another arrow in hand and marred it even further. The last few nights he'd a cloak to cover it, but he couldn’t be nursing the cloak for the rest of his time in the unfamiliar country. It was that same thick cloak that he donned over his leathers, adjusting it so that only his other, unmarked shoulder could easily be seen. With silent footsteps, he made his way back out to the chilly night air by way of the kitchen's back doors. Approaching the back gate as casually as possible, in case the guard at the watch was particularly coherent that night, Fane walked toward the wooden door. As he'd hoped, the usual guard was there, slumped over in his chair and snoring softly. Fane smirked. Every trip down to the docks had become easier than the nights previous. The layout of the capital city was slowly becoming more familiar to him. The moon shone down on the city in full, illuminating his path and creating shadows for him to hide in. The moon; Hunter's Friend and Guide. That's what his brother had told him all those years ago. He could still hear the crackle of the charred wood of the dying fire mingling with his brother's younger voice. he'd been only a boy, no older than five years old. Which would have made Friedhelm about fifteen. They were on better terms back then. Friedhelm would fill his evenings with tales of heroes and great battles, of mythology and folklore. Fane smiled at the memory. That

was before the shadow fell over his brother's face. Before their parents’ death and the weight of the greatest kingdom in the world fell onto his shoulders. At the age of eighteen, when Friedhelm cut his prince's braid from his hair, signifying his claim to the throne, Fane had begun to grow his own to replace him as next in line. That same braid slapped his jaw while he ran. Even on the run, he couldn't bring himself to cut it just yet. He tried to recall if that particular Aridian tradition was common knowledge among the people of Eira. He would worry about that later. All the thoughts swirling in his head like leaves on a wind were shoved down in favor of the task at hand. As he approached one of the vigilante's favored spots, he found that he was earlier than usual. No one was in sight. He climbed onto an empty stairwell under the cover of the shadows the moon provided, wrapped himself in his cloak, and waited patiently. ROHYR WHITESTAR WAS alone, as he always was. He liked it that way. Despite his young age at twenty-nine, his body ached and his back had screamed at him when he'd woken up that morning, or early afternoon, rather. Rubbing the small of his back where he'd landed when the member of the Fade had thrown him to the stones the night before, Rohyr grimaced. He’d caught wind of the crime lords of the city banning together under one master, and one name, for some dark purpose he had yet to guess. The Fade had become the bane of his existence since then. He had no idea how deep their influence spread, nor how many were involved under their name. Every time he thought he was close to the answers, they slipped from his grasp. As it stood, he was one of the only ones, at least that he knew of, that were actively trying to deal with the problem and stamp it out before it could get any bigger. The guards of the city couldn't be trusted, not yet, lest they be involved. He'd slept in later than usual that day. He figured he deserved a reward for his success the night before in hunting and interrogating some criminals. His adventures, if he could really call them that,

were detrimental to his body, but that was an on-the-job hazard for him. And then there was the other annoyance that kept appearing. That blond whelp that kept popping up at the most inconvenient times was not a part of the Fade, if his utter lack of knowledge and direction was any indication. Thinking of that cocked smile of his sent Rohyr's blood boiling. As if he would accept anyone's help, much less some skinny nobleman from who-knew-where lost on the street. With a huff of annoyance, Rohyr rose with some difficulty from the cushioned booth that he lounged in. The sun had set, which meant the hunt was just beginning. A step into the icy air of the docks, and he was already feeling the rush in his head, though his prey was nowhere in sight. Rohyr gazed up at the stars, his constant guide and the only light that he had most nights. The horn of the great constellation Equus Alatus, a shining bright star on the tip of it, seemed to point Northward. He stalked in that direction. Alatus had never led him astray, and he trusted that it would be no different that night. He felt the suppressed magic in his veins hum with excitement. Rohyr reluctantly sent a tendril of magic ahead unseen into the night, searching for the darkness he was seeking. Normally, he avoided using magic. But tonight, he was too tired to hunt the old fashioned way. Besides, he had a feeling his magic wouldn’t let him be unless he let it out. There were consequences for disuse of one's magic. Just as he needed to keep up practice in swordplay, to keep his muscles disciplined, so did mages need to use their magic every day to keep it active and adept. Rohyr sent a tendril of tracking magic into the night ahead of him. He thumbed the twin axes free from his thigh straps, and spread his power over the blades. They sang to him in the darkness as they glowed a faint green. At last, his magic bumped against a flicker of dark power. He smiled. Turning the corner, he saw that a thin and athletic looking man in black leaned against the wall. Rohyr sidled up to him, doing his best to look casual. "Evening." He said mildly. No use scaring him off too soon. Though it was not his forte, he always tried to start as cordially as

possible. It never lasted long. The Fade member gave him a suspicious look up and down. "The stars will fall..." The criminal said, pointedly. "And all will darken." Rohyr replied. Apparently, this was the wrong thing to say because the Fade member, without another word, either for fear or uncooperation (Rohyr always hoped it was fear), took off at a sprint down the street. Grumbling, Rohyr ran after him. This one must have been new, because Rohyr easily overtook the criminal, catching his shirtsleeve. Their momentum sent them crashing to the ground, disturbing a nest of snowrats that scattered from behind nearby empty barrels. Sitting on top of the caught man, Rohyr began with his usual set of questions. "How many are you?" He growled in the man's ear as he thrashed beneath him. The man strained, attempting an unsuccessful weak-handed punch to Rohyr's jaw. Rohyr dropped one of his axes, as he took the criminal's collar in his other hand. It clattered to the stone as he lifted the man's face to his own. "Who leads you?" "A shadow." His mouth twisted and he spat in Rohyr's face. "Its roots go deep.” "That doesn't answer my question, you scum." With a heave, the criminal freed himself from Rohyr's weighty grasp and shot forward, grabbing the discarded ax as he did. With a shout of frustration, he realized that his pursuer had trapped him in a dead end. The man whirled, raising Rohyr's own weapon to strike. An arrow whizzed passed Rohyr's ear, singing through the air as it sunk itself into the man's hand. With a cry, he dropped the ax and doubled over, cradling his injury. Rohyr took this opportunity to hit the man over the head with the butt of his other ax. Rohyr glanced around him with a grumble, tensing in preparation to tangle with another foe. The archer that shot the saving arrow stepped from the shadows, that cocky grin spread across his pretty-boy features. Rohyr cursed.

"YOU AGAIN." THE CURSES rumbling from the man in green reached Fane's ears even over the howl of the wind. Fane grinned, lowering his bow to his side. Step into character. "Me again." "How many times do I have to tell you to leave me alone?" Fane really didn't know what possessed him to follow this strange man into the slums every night. Something about his mission called to that part of him that had always wanted for adventure, for a purpose. He honestly didn't know what to say to the intimidating force standing before him. Fane noticed the man's slight bend, the way he favored one of his knees. "You wouldn't have won that fight without my help." Fane kept the swagger in his voice on purpose. The man's silence answered him. "Seeing as how you have wounded yourself, I think you need help on your quest to hunt down whoever this Fade is." Fane pushed. The man remained silent, looking between his bow and the man on the cobblestones. He turned away from the prince. "I have not wounded myself. And the Fade is not a who, it's a what." "If you train me, if you help me to become as skilled as you are, I could be a valuable help to you." Fane waited, letting his words sink into the night air. A proposition of offered help would be one that the other man would be foolish not to at least consider. The woodsman paused, his back turned to Fane. The prince had seen enough of human behavior in the guarded smiles and political negotiations of the castle to know that the man was considering his offer. He pressed ahead. “I am already a skilled archer and fencer, but everyone I have ever worked with hasn’t bothered to push me to the limit. I want to become stronger. To be able to protect the ones I love and help you in your quest.” Another pause, and a deep chuckle from the man. “I knew you were a preening nobleman.” The man turned to him then, throwing his dark hood back. He towered over Fane, his hair a dark rusty color and tied in a sloppy knot. It took all of Fane’s willpower to keep his face a cocky, unreadable mask. The man smirked. “Fine. I’ll help you. Your training begins now.” For reasons unbeknownst to himself, Fane felt a rush of relief. A rush that would have remained if the man across from him didn’t

look so devious as he agreed to his offer. “Wait. Now?” Fane looked around, taking in the dark, misty alleyway and the criminal laying between them. Fortunately, the downed man was still breathing. “Aren’t you going to take him in somewhere?” “Yes. Come with me, and hopefully we’ll find another member before the dawn breaks.” The man hoisted the unconscious criminal onto his back and started back down the alley. Fane gathered up his bow and quiver and followed after him, his cloak swishing the ground as the street tilted downward. “Wait,” Fane slung his bow over his shoulder again, running a hand through his hair. “I don’t even know your name. What can I call you?” Without faltering, the mountain ahead of him glanced back with deep brown eyes and rumbled, “You can call me Whitestar.” Whitestar didn’t make further conversation, but started walking in the direction of a tower near the front of the city that Fane assumed was some kind of guards’ tower. They walked in silence. The sounds of water lapping against the docks, the raucous sounds coming from taverns all turned to silent and sleepy suburban neighborhoods. All the residents were either asleep or reading by soft candlelight in windows on the street. The two men, one rough-looking and the other only slightly cleaner, looked extremely out of place in such a peaceful part of the city. They approached the guards tower and stepped inside, Whitestar walking as confidently as if he owned the place. "What do we do with him?" Fane whispered when they stepped inside. "If you'll be patient for two seconds, you'll see." Whitestar sneered back. Fane was patient, and as they turned the corner, they came upon a simple wooden desk, illuminated by a few candles. A guard, looking about the same age as Fane, sat amidst piles of papers stacked high all around him. He barely looked up as the two of them approached. "How many nights is this, Whitestar?" He muttered, "You trying to put us out of business or something?" Whitestar merely huffed and threw his coin purse on top of the paper the guard was writing on. "If you stuffy guardsmen would just do your damn job, Foley, I wouldn't have to be here every night."

Fane watched this exchange, taking in the information for later. The guard, Foley, sighed as if he'd heard the same accusation a million times before and had grown tired of defending it. Whitestar handed the still-unconscious criminal off to another guard that appeared from the dark doorway behind the desk without a word. "Unfortunately for you, the rate has gone down." Foley turned away from them and filled the small sack with coins, then dropped it with a heavy clink into Whitestar's waiting hand. "We don’t want them here, Whitestar.” "Why has the rate gone down?" Fane blurted, determined to prove there was a reason he'd come along. Whitestar grumbled next to him, displeased with the delay. Foley turned back to his writing. "Because the prison is getting full. No thanks to him." Fane cringed as Foley's heavy-handed writing broke the nib on his pen. The guard cursed under his breath. Whitestar was already walking back to the door. “There’s only so much we can do, Whitestar.” Foley said with a huff. “That’s why I’m getting to the bottom of it.” Whitestar said over his shoulder, slamming the door shut behind him. Fane gave the poor, overworked guard a quick nod of the head before he followed his new companion out the door.

15 AS THEY HAD BEFORE, Niamh and Maewyn stood across from one another in the training area. Niamh with her staff in hand. Hael stood between them, stroking his cropped beard thoughtfully. “That first duel was Maewyn’s test to enter into consideration to become my apprentice.” He said. “This duel will serve as further demonstration of Maewyn’s abilities.” He glanced between the two girls with a warning in his eyes. “This is merely a training exercise to help you become accustomed to the other’s combat style.” Even Hael saying out loud just made it sound like a stiff, ridiculous ritual. A formality. Niamh knew, even if Hael never actually confirmed it, that this was some sort of punishment. To test how far he could stretch her patience. He’s already allowed Maewyn to take my workspace, isn’t that punishment enough? “So, that being said, don’t kill each other.” Hael finished. Niamh couldn’t tell if he was joking or not. Duels of this nature were rarely deadly, and common practice at the academies. But Maewyn was not from the academies. Maewyn shifted with anticipation. Niamh groaned inwardly. She recalled Hael’s face every time he'd tried to drill her on offensive magic or battle strategy. Disappointment. No matter which way he explained it, how many trials he put her through, Niamh was just plain unskilled in fighting magic. Eventually, her master gave up and built her skills stronger in other areas. Maewyn clearly did not share her reservations. Remembering Hael’s lecture, Niamh set her feet apart. Control. He had said, Control is my greatest strength. The challenge would be maintaining it. “Oh, and no illusion magic this time.” Hael said, with a pointed glance at Niamh. She stiffened, gripping the warm twisted wood of her staff. “To win, “ He continued, moving toward the edge of the practice

room, “you must remain upright, on your feet. The last one standing wins, as they say.” I only need to outlast her. Niamh thought, watching Maewyn’s face as her excited grin spread across it. However long that takes. “Mages.” Hael stepped back, covering them with his usual magical dome of shielding magic, “Begin.” As in their first duel, Maewyn attacked first. Sea-green fire whipped toward Niamh in a sharp stream. Niamh’s reply was a twirl of her staff, turning the raw magic blue and dispersing as a wave around her before falling to the ground. They continued like this for several rounds; Maewyn’s attacks were neutralized, Niamh refused to fight back, and Hael was visibly growing bored. Or frustrated. Niamh could never tell which. She didn’t care what Hael thought of her refusal, though, because if it only mildly irritated her master, it enraged her opponent. Niamh sent a self-satisfied smile her way. Petty, but effective. Wear her down so she can collapse on her own. Maewyn certainly possessed more power, a deeper magical well, than Niamh did. But she had control. And she would allow Hael to see that she would not lose it again. Control means stamina. Stamina means I can go longer than she can. Indeed, Niamh had nearly a full well left over, even after thirty minutes of their exchange, only using it to block or redirect. Nothing that required a deeper pull. It helped that her staff held reserves of her power for later. She filled it every morning. Staffs didn’t require a full night’s sleep to recover magic wells. Just from the reckless way that Maewyn poured herself into everything she did, Niamh guessed she was not accustomed to managing her power levels. It was only a matter of time now. As if she'd given up trying to hit Niamh directly, Maewyn stood back against the wall of the dome for a moment. She spread her arms wide like a bird of prey, igniting the training room’s floor with bright flames. Before the fire reached all the way to Niamh’s boots, Niamh lifted her staff. Bringing it down hard on the marble floor, she called forth a torrent of water. It covered the flames, sloshing against the boundary of the dome. Water rose to the girls’ ankles, wetting their boots.

This did nothing to deter Maewyn, who winked at her with a mischievous glimmer in her eye. In the time between seconds, a white hot light grew in Maewyn’s palm, pulsing bigger and brighter before Niamh could register what it was. Hael saw it first, his eyes widening. Niamh turned her own to her master, his face struck with a rare expression of alarm. Niamh could do nothing as Maewyn raised an arching hand, shooting her handful of lightning into the water. A crackling, steaming vein of light shot for Niamh who didn’t even have time to cry out as her blood turned to fire, her body stiffened of its own accord, and the world fell into darkness. The last thing she heard was the sound of Hael’s sharp voice barking Maewyn’s name, and then nothing. THE NIGHT HAD PROVEN to be unsuccessful, by Whitestar’s standards at least. After Fane accompanied him to the authorities to turn in the criminal, the two of them set out again to what Fane guessed were Whitestar’s usual haunts. Whitestar had explained with a grumble that the king’s guard was extremely invested in bringing down the Fade, whatever they were, and they used to provide a much bigger bounty. But, since the problem had only grown, and no one could figure out where it was coming from, the guards had largely given up for the moment. They had other things to attend to, apparently, Whitestar added with some resentment. “Their numbers only seem to be growing. I don’t know what they want, and I have no idea where these men keep coming from.” Whitestar said as they walked to a dark street corner. “It’s never women, either. Only men.” “What do they do? What makes them criminals?” Fane asked in a whisper. The early morning hours were bringing a chill more formidable than the evening had. His breath misted into the air. “What seems like petty crimes.” Whitestar replied, “But they never seem to take any money. Or property. And yet, the victims always disappear.” Whitestar didn’t look at him as he said this, but Fane caught the furrow of his brow. He couldn’t tell if it was anger or sadness. “No one knows where they go, and yet the Fade only gets bigger. I have

my theories, but none of them will give me answers without some... persuasion.” He added. Fane had an idea what Whitestar’s version of “persuasion” might be. “How’s that working out for you?” Fane asked, maintaining the snarky persona from earlier. Whitestar didn’t answer, merely scanned the street with his eyes for anyone standing about. Fane accepted as much of this new information as he could, even as his head was overflowing with questions. Questions he was determined to answer in the coming days. However long it took. Once Whitestar had apparently decided that stalking the streets of Ahealarth was a fruitless task for the night, he led Fane to a clearing just outside of the city’s walls. Though Fane knew he should be afraid, considering that Whitestar could drag him out in the middle of nowhere and murder him and no one would miss his presence, Fane found that he trusted the woodsman walking ahead. A short time later, the pair of them stood across from each other in a clearing. Snow fell softly around them, and the stars winked through the clouds as they passed. Whitestar stood across from Fane, stalking back and forth like a wild cat eyeing its prey. Fane did his best to keep his expression neutral, fierce, even if Whitestar hadn't allowed him more weapons than what he already had on him. A bow, and a dagger. And that was it. The bow would be useless in close combat, so it was discarded on a nearby tree. “I want to see what you can do first.” Whitestar said, thumbing one of his small axes to his hand. “Impress me.” Taking a defensive crouch, Fane held his long dagger in front of him as he had been taught. Fencing, archery, and basic combat was part of any prince's training, he supposed, and it had certainly been part of his. Though, those days always felt different. His opponents tended to be long-suffering tutors or guards under his own employ; none of them actually had a weathered bloodlust in their eyes and a personal vendetta against him. Deep down, he knew his teacher wouldn't kill him, but he didn't trust the tall woodsman not to come close. he'd seen what he'd done to those members of the Fade, and he wasn't about to be pummeled beyond recognition if he could help it. Despite everything, he still held a shred of princely vanity that valued his straight nose and undented cheekbones. He intended to keep them that way. The tall woodsman’s blade glowed green. Fane swallowed. So he had magic too, of some kind, at least. This was not about to go well.

"Ready?" Whitestar's deep voice rumbled across the clearing. Fane didn't answer but instead deepened his crouch. Whitestar took his silence as confirmation and shot toward him like the mountain cat. An ax swung for his head, he stumbled back, parrying with the knife. With one hand occupied, Whitestar swung his other ax for Fane's side. He drew it so quickly Fane hardly noticed. It was all he could do to jump out of the way as it grazed his tunic. Maybe he does actually want to kill me. Fane thought with a sense of dread. The woodsman merely smiled darkly and continued his pursuit, swinging his axes one over the other. Only when Fane thought he had the advantage, catching Whitestar's hand with the hilt of his knife, did the woodsman show him his full proverbial hand of cards. With a deft movement, he flipped Fane squarely onto his back and crossed the blades of his axes over his throat. Defeated, Fane laid back. "Where did you learn to fight? The marbled halls of a palace?" Whitestar chuckled slightly, amusing himself at his own cleverness, Fane assumed. Yes, actually. Out loud, he only gave the man a flat look and arose with a grunt. Without a pause for breath, the woodsman began another offense, twisting this way and that, easily disarming Fane. He fell to the snow again and again, each time more frustrating.

16 HER VISION BLURRED and head spinning, Niamh awoke a few minutes later. Hael’s roughened hand lay over her forehead and she smelled his healing magic, a masculine scent of burning embers mixed with the freshness of a winter’s morning. Maewyn’s face floated into view, standing over Niamh, and her face looked positively distraught. Either from severely harming her peer or from the verbal lashing she most definitely received from Hael. Niamh guessed that it was the latter. “I told you not to kill each other.” A masculine voice said sharply. Everything hurt and the world seemed far away, though it was slowly coming back in to focus as the pain was subsiding. “I didn’t mean to. I just-“ Maewyn sounded on the verge of tears. Good. She should be. Hael’s only sign of concern was the slight furrowing of his eyebrows and she could see him watching her carefully through blurred vision. Though it hurt her pride, Niamh couldn’t stifle her groan. She heard bits and pieces of Hael’s ongoing lecture and Maewyn replying in a tear-strained voice. After several minutes, sensation returned to Niamh’s limbs. Her master’s healing magic still settled over her like a fog. Once Hael was quite convinced that she would live to see another day, he removed his hand and helped her sit up. She couldn’t contain her face as she indulged a glare at Maewyn. “Are you okay, Niamh?” Her eyes wide with worry. “I’m fine.” Was Niamh’s flat reply. No thanks to you. Maewyn won again. Somehow it was more humiliating than the last time. Where did she get lightning magic?! She rose shakily from the floor with gritted teeth, swallowing another groan of pain. The water

that had sloshed around the room, that had been her undoing, was completely gone. As if it had never existed. Niamh also noticed that her once pristine blue dress was now blackened and shredded at the edges. Maewyn glanced between her and Hael nervously, an unspoken question in her eyes. Hael raised his eyebrows at Niamh, as if giving her permission to leave if she needed. A welcome relief. “We’re done for the day.” He announced, not bothering to hide his annoyance. Niamh stumbled from the room and didn’t look back. SEVERAL NIGHTS AFTER Fane had found the man he now knew as Whitestar, he fell into a consistent routine. Fane would arise from his dusty old bed in the servants’ halls downstairs after a few hours of sleep. Around eleven in the morning, he would wander upstairs to perform his daily toil in the depths of the Library. Truthfully, the task itself was hardly a drudgery at all. Fane enjoyed the quiet company of knowledge around him. And he was free to read as often as he pleased while he shelved. It was those pesky Cats that still tortured him and haunted his every step. The Keeper, however, had slowly begun warming up to him. Though she never said so, he could see it in the way that she would offer him a cup of tea after particularly long days. He could not say the same for his dark and brooding companion, however. Fane would wait until dark, when all the servants had gone to their rooms, and then he would slip from the back gate of the castle to the wilderness surrounding the castle town. Whitestar favored a certain clearing in the evergreens, where he would meet Fane every night. Fane began to wonder if the ever irritable woodsman lived in that clearing. After barely a greeting, Whitestar would begin their nightly training, run him through drills, and force him to jog up mountainsides. The woodsman would purposely lose Fane, or so he suspected, to the depths of the forest just to be waiting for him with a smug smirk when he finally stumbled back into the clearing hours later. Whitestar seemed to delight in Fane’s misery, so the prince refused to display any. He swallowed every frustrated sigh, every

pained grunt, almost every retort. Whitestar thought him a weak, pathetic “preening nobleman”, so Fane would prove to him that he wasn’t. After their most recent bout, both men were already dripping with sweat from the few hours they had been at their nightly drills. The moon was high in the inky black of the night sky, and Fane guessed it was nearing midnight. Soon, it would be the Fade’s hour to emerge in the city streets. Somehow, he looked forward to chasing down the criminals and facing death every night rather than nearly die of exhaustion from Whitestar’s sadistic sets of drills. “Left!” Whitestar shouted, swinging his ax toward Fane with far more enthusiasm for comfort. Fane feigned out of the way, catching the ax under the blade with his long dagger. Whitestar bore his full weight down on the smaller weapon, making Fane’s grip shook with effort. The prince spun away, bringing his opposite dagger to Whitestar’s neck. The woodsman grabbed his other hand, twisting the blade from it in a quick movement and shoving the smaller man to the ground. Fane ground his teeth from where he was sprawled in the snow. Again. “Even if you’re skilled, and you have every weapon you could ever want, there are these things called gravity and momentum that will make life hard for you.” Whitestar said, a smug smile on his face as he sheathed his axes again. Fane’s only response was an irritated grunt as he stood. This style of fighting was not what Fane had learned. He knew how to disarm an opponent with a fencing sword, the rules of civility that prevented him from taking the opponent out as he recovered. This style, if Whitestar could even call it that, was ferocious and wild. Unhinged, even. Fane was only slightly disgusted at the brutality of it all. Fane rarely got the upper hand against his larger and stronger opponent. The very few times he did filled his heart with pride as he'd never felt in his life. Much to Fane's disappointment, Whitestar never showed any surprise to his occasional shows of strength or skill. As if he expected it, somehow. He's probably trying to keep me from getting too confident. Fane thought with a small amount of ire. That seemed like something he would do, as he slowly got to know him over their brutal training sessions.

He wiped the snow from his person, grabbing his daggers from where they had fallen a few feet away. One of Whitestar's axes- he used only one to disarm Fane just then- lay in the snow against a tree near the edge of the clearing. Moonlight glimmered across a weathered and rough carving- two sparrows surrounded by an intertwining circle of leaves and bluebells. Seems rather feminine for someone like him. Fane thought with passing interest. Though, an unnamable familiarity flickered at the corner of his memory. He'd seen that pattern before. Whitestar seemed to notice the moon’s position a moment later. Striding toward the town without another word, he slung his jacket around his broad shoulders again and retrieved the axe Fane had been studying. Usually, Fane did his best to gather together whatever new information he’d gained from the nights previous as they walked. Whitestar always went with the same set of questions, and those questions were usually futile. The criminals, just as Whitestar said, were always men, and always dressed in the same black clothing. Thinking back to his experience in theater, actors wore black only if they were intended to fade into the background. Fane suspected there was something larger going on, if his loose association was correct. He held on to his theory, however, as Whitestar was quick to bat him down if Fane tried to contribute anything but man power. At least in the first few days of this routine. “Shouldn’t we try to disguise ourselves a bit more?” Fane asked one night as Whitestar heaved a recently unconscious criminal over his shoulder. “More of this, and they will start to take notice of us, won’t they?” “I am disguised as much as I want to be.” Whitestar replied with a grunt. He looked at Fane carefully, his eyes staring pointedly at the crown of Fane’s head. “Your hair is a dead give-away. I don't even need a disguise with how distracting it is.” Fane refrained from rolling his eyes. He knew the woodsman spoke the truth, however. No hood could hide his hair completely, and very few others in Eira had blond hair as bright as his. Just as the two of them rounded a corner to head to the guards’ tower, another member of the Fade ran in front of them. His face was obscured save for his eyes, but they widened as they met Fane’s. Occupied as Whitestar was with the man already on his

back, Fane pursued without a thought. The man ahead must have been young, for he was fast. Faster than Fane expected. The two of them careened around another corner, and the younger man slipped as he went, falling to the icy cobblestones. Fane did what he’d seen Whitestar do a few times, and sat on his chest before the Fade member could rise. Fane ripped the mask from his face. It was the boy from the dress shop. The one that Maewyn was flirting with even as she haggled with him. With barely a whisker on his chin, the boy was at least ten years younger than himself. “What...?” The question Fane was supposed to ask died on his lips. What was he doing here? “Let me go.” The boy pleaded, barely above a whisper. “How did you-?” Fane still held the mask in his hand, dumbfounded. The boy squirmed under his knees. “I had no choice, please let me go!” “What do you mean?” Fane demanded. “What did you do?” “They told me to do it. Or she would die!” The boy replied, still squirming. His eyes were moist. “Who?” Fane asked, “Who would die?” The sound of Whitestar’s heavy steps approached. “What do you mean?” Fane asked, desperation creeping into his voice. “Who are they?” “I-” The boy’s eyes clouded over, losing whatever human emotion they held just a moment earlier. “We are the Fade.” He said. Before Fane could counter, the boy drew on some hidden strength and reached around Fane’s legs to grasp his incriminating blond hair. Fane’s forehead was smashed into the street, as stars clouded his vision. The boy took this moment of weakness to squirm out of Fane’s capture and sprint into the misty darkness. It was then that Whitestar came around the corner, labored with the weight on his back. Fane held his head, the blood already seeping through his fingers. If Whitestar was concerned, he didn’t show it as he clicked his tongue in disapproval. “You let him get away. What’s the use of following me if you aren’t going to be useful?” Fane was still too dizzy to answer. The world spun around him. “Once you’ve gotten a hold of yourself, you can follow me to the guards’ tower. But you won’t be getting your cut tonight.” Whitestar added with no shortage of resentment. Fane didn’t care.
It was several minutes before he could stand again, and he took that opportunity to stumble home. There were too many questions swirling in his mind, and nothing could solve them but time and sleep.

17 AFTER A FEW DAYS, NIAMH was recovered and able to attend to everyday life again. She’d taken a couple more to relax and avoid Maewyn as much as possible. Hael had, thankfully, allowed her to languish around her room generally undisturbed. They both knew the extra time was just to nurse her wounded pride, but he allowed it nonetheless. Soon enough, Niamh received a message to meet in the Library for that day’s lesson. Despite her extra responsibilities that she’d earned over the year, she was still his apprentice. Hael took to reminding her of that in the form of infrequent lectures on various topics she'd learned over her years at the academy and beyond. The doors to the Library swung open with a groan, revealing her master standing at the circulation desk with a large leather tome in hand. The Keeper chatted with him quietly, the sound lost in the wide open space. A step inside revealed Maewyn standing to Hael’s other side. Niamh grimaced. Maewyn caught her eye and waved her over to them with an apologetic smile. “Ah, Niamh, there you are.” Hael turned his attention to her, motioning for the two apprentices to follow him. “Come along. We have much to review today.” Niamh waved at the Keeper as they passed, who acknowledged her with a twinkling eye as the young apprentice followed her master in to the depths of the Library. The endless creaking hallways spread out in front of the group. Magic tapestries decorated the walls, moving their stories along with the magic woven into the threads. They passed over the open air bridge that was always warm and never laden over with snow. They passed darkened lobbies, finally coming to the bottom room of the astronomy tower. The room that Hael led them to was a large space. A cool glow

filtered in from the high domed ceiling painted with the constellations, shelves lined the walls filled to the brim with books written in ink mixed with moonlight and the dust of fallen stars. Niamh and Maewyn took their places at one of the small desks, while Hael stood in front of them. As it always was with these lessons, Hael wasted no time with greetings or introductions. He fixed Maewyn with a stern look. “Maewyn, do you know why your lightning didn’t hurt you while it knocked your opponent unconscious?” Maewyn looked to Niamh under furrowed white eyebrows. Niamh glared ahead, doing her best to keep her face an unbothered mask of politeness. “Um...because? I don’t know, actually.” Maewyn admitted, grimacing. Niamh rolled her eyes inwardly. Did she learn nothing at any sort of magical school where she comes from? Hael seemed unbothered, waving his hand to summon a certain book from a top shelf. “It’s because a mage’s magic does not affect the caster’s person. This is an advantage when using dangerous, volatile types of magic, but a certain disadvantage if a mage is injured, for they can’t heal themselves.” Niamh saw Maewyn glance at her nervously. Hael continued. “Magic is a gift, and thus cannot be selfishly hoarded and must be given.” “This is why it is the responsibility of the Head Mage, the Grand Healer, and their apprentices under them to have a grasp of every type of magic available to them. They will be left neither undefended nor unhealed.” “Wait, but why have separate positions at all?” Maewyn blurted, ignoring any sort of manners usually observed between master and apprentice during lessons. Niamh ground her teeth at the interruption, but Hael merely smiled tightly. “Because all mages, though they can be skilled in all types of magic, are only truly talented in one. It’s what calls to them, what their hearts and hands understand best." His tone softened slightly. "The expression of their souls, if you will.” "And, of course," Hael's face noticeably fell, "So that not all the responsibility falls on one person's shoulders." Maewyn didn't seem to notice his sudden change in mood. "So why don't we have a Grand Healer right now?" Niamh shot her a look. Maewyn clearly didn't know how loaded

that question was. Hael ignored her, though Niamh saw the memories that not even she knew about flash in his eyes before he turned to the board again. Maewyn was undeterred. "So is there a way to make your magic work on you?" Maewyn asked. Niamh's eyebrow twitched slightly. "That's not something that you need to learn right now." Hael didn't even turn back toward them, and wrote several convoluted looking formulas on the blackboard behind him. "So there is a way?" Maewyn was practically tipping over her chair for how far forward she was sitting in it. Niamh had also wondered about the method for some time, and Hael would never tell her. Despite her mild protests that a healer, of all types of mages, should know. She'd given up a long time ago trying to get that information. Good luck getting it out of him. She thought smugly. Hael did turn to them, then. His face was a mixture of exasperation and dire seriousness. "Yes, Maewyn, there is a way. But you would die. So unless you have a death wish, I am not going to teach you how to go about it. That's the last I'm going to say on that subject." "Ugghh, finnneee." Maewyn's childishness was grating down every last nerve that Niamh had left, like scraping the insides from a vanilla bean. She kept silent, hoping that one of them would notice and take their cue to get back to more intellectually stimulating conversation. "Where does magic even come from?" Maewyn asked again, cutting off the breath Hael had just taken to continue. He frowned at the interruption, but answered with far more patience than he ever had for Niamh. The injustice of it all. "Magic comes from the Heart of Winter, originally. Eira's Relic. It is the source of the Lights of the North." Niamh sighed inwardly. It was like sitting in class with a first year magic student. She'd learned this even before then. Most Eiran children grew up on these stories. Maewyn, however, was completely enraptured. "Anyone born under the Lights receives the gift of magic. Even in other countries, where the Lights are not always visible, the same holds true. In the past, entire generations of mages have been born on those rare occasions when the Lights do reach the southern parts

of the world." "Where is the Heart of Winter? Have you seen it?" The younger mage's eyes sparkled with interest. "I've never seen it personally. Only a handful of mages in Eira's history ever have. It sits on the top of the tallest mountain, and the route to reach it has been lost to history. No one in recent memory has tried to find it and returned alive." A shiver danced up Niamh's spine. "How do you know that it exists?" "Scholars and skeptics have been asking that question for decades." "So how do you know?" Maewyn pressed far more than Niamh had ever considered possible. "All three of us in this room have magic, do we not?" Maewyn nodded. Niamh nodded with her. "And would the Father of Lights, the One that created all four Relics, lie?" Maewyn shook her head slowly, with hesitation. Niamh caught the uneasy furrow in her white eyebrows. "Then it exists." And that was the end of that. Hael opened his mouth again, to start on his actual lesson- "Is there a way to lose your magic?" The chair scraped on the wooden floor, accentuating Maewyn's gratingly cheerful voice in the cavernous room. Niamh couldn't take it anymore. "Maewyn, you are a mage, right?" Try as she might, she could barely keep the impatience from her voice. "So why haven't you learned all of this already?" This is something she should know if she's been using magic all this time. Maewyn looked at her as if she had two heads. "Because no one taught me." "No one taught you...what?" "Magic." Unheard of. "What do you mean no one taught you magic? How are you able to use it? Where did you get the threads?" "I taught myself." Maewyn replied, lifting her blouse from the bottom. “And I found them!” She exposed a thin belt made of what looked to be soft brown suede. Delicate waves of red and white were embroidered across it.

Niamh looked to her Master to see if he was hearing what she was. He nodded affirmatively. How can she just teach herself?! How did she just “find” thread? "How did you do that?" Niamh demanded, more forcefully than she intended. Maewyn inhaled as if she was about to launch into some epic story, but Hael interrupted. "This conversation will have to wait until after the lesson is over." Maewyn deflated and Niamh sat back in her chair. Niamh saw Hael intake a breath and she expected to hear the sound of his voice for some time after. Instead, the sound that permeated the chamber was the roar of what sounded like a waterfall intermingled with a male voice yelling in surprise. All heads turned toward the door to the side of the room that led to the room adjacent, to see Fane standing in its arch. He was soaking wet and quickly creating a puddle around him on the wood floor. "I suppose that we are all aware there is a sea dragon living in the Library?" He said to no one in particular. "Everyone but me, of course?" Maewyn burst out laughing, making Fane blush even deeper. Hael glared at him, an open book poised in his hand ready to be lectured from. "Yes. There is a sea dragon living here." He snapped the book shut. "And you managed to annoy it." "Not by choice." Fane grumbled. He sprayed stray water droplets onto the shelves next to him as he vigorously waved his hands to free them of moisture. Maewyn was still laughing. Niamh looked on as the scene unfolded, stifling a giggle herself. "If you would be so kind as to leave, master Fane, we can continue our lesson." Hael's patience was dancing on a knife's edge, Niamh could hear it in his tone, which meant that he was in no mood for conversation. Especially not with a soaking wet Library's assistant. Fane, seemingly understanding there was no place for him there,bowed awkwardly from the room. This seemed to satisfy Hael, and he opened his tome again with an air of satisfaction. Maewyn slumped dramatically back into her chair, her salvation fled and any hope of escaping a lecture gone. Niamh couldn’t help but revel in the satisfaction.

18 FANE PUSHED THE CART of books to the end of the aisle, taking a glance between the shelves and what he had on his cart to replace among the endless lines of tomes. The Library was utterly silent in the room that it led him to, save for the ticking of a clock unseen within and the occasional patter of a Lore Cat looking to torture him. As the days had passed, the Keeper treated him with no less harshness than the first day he stepped into her domain. This was a trait, that harsh stubbornness, that Fane found many of Eira’s citizens to possess, to the point of national pride, and she the sternest of all of them. Though he'd slowly realized that many of her jabs were well-meaning (usually), and he would catch her smiling to herself when she thought he wasn’t looking. He shook his head. She has a strange way of showing endearment, apparently. After his embarrassing run-in with the resident sea dragon the day previous, Fane was wary of every room he entered. He hadn't meant to annoy the creature, and he wasn't even aware that he had until he was hit in the face with a stream of saltwater spit from its mouth. It had waited for him, he guessed with some chagrin. Rolling the cart to a stop, he shelved an entire handful of books in the obvious open place for them. An entire series on defending against dark magic. The idea of magic as a whole was still unnerving to him, as his only experience with such things was from a few interactions with the court mages over his life. The three of them that his father had kept employed from his grandfather's time were vaguely dangerous, setting him at a strange discomfort any time they walked into a room. By the time he’d become a young man, they disappeared without a trace. When Fane was a boy, the mages barely regarded him on a normal day. But once, when he was deathly ill with the

sickness that had spread over the country in his boyhood, one of the rough-handed healers had made him well, but not without awful bedside manner and brusque commands. He shifted with unease at the memory. Though magic, if he were being honest, scared and mystified him, dark magic was another thing entirely. He was not involved in such matters, but even he had heard the whispers around dark corners and the quiet, nervous conversations held in abandoned rooms. It was a subject that was so awful, no one would dare talk about it in polite company. Hael, as the Head Mage, was not much better in terms of general demeanor. Though even he could tell that the Phoenix Mage truly cared for his king, his country, and his young students. He shivered at the thought of someone such as him with the amount of power that he possessed. It must have taken great strength, great restraint, to keep all of that raw energy contained. Not only contained, but controlled and honed for the good of the kingdom that he protected. Heaven help them if he ever decided to seek his own position. Hael could incinerate all of us with a wave of his hand, and all of Eira’s soldiers would be powerless to stop him from taking the whole kingdom if he wanted to. The thought made him shudder. Thinking of Hael made him remember Maewyn, who, he noticed with a certain relief, was not about to pounce on him from the shadows like the Lore Cats that now wound around his legs. Maewyn, too, possessed a great and terrible power. She was even less controlled than Hael was. That unpredictability made her terrifying. He pushed that thought from his mind too, noting with a growing anxiety that he'd gone and made acquaintance with all three of the most frighteningly powerful magic users in the one country in the world that produced magical power beyond comparison. If he were to ever end up on any one of their bad sides, they could wink his life out in an instant before he had a chance to realize what had happened. Some deep part of him feared all of them. All except one. Finally, his mind’s eye settled on Niamh. The one mage he'd met that wasn’t intent on displaying her depth of power for the world to see. A smile pulled at the corners of his mouth thinking of her eyes. The way she would blush at the slightest provocation, the red of

rose petals creeping across her nose and up to the tips of her ears. Some part of him wished she wasn’t so guarded; wished that she would show him more of her true feelings. Though he was guilty of playing a part, too. That of a perfectly polished prince. Fane turned the corner, coming upon a small sitting area furnished with red velvet chairs and a large, plush rug covering the floorboards. A lamp glowed warmly on the table in the middle, and his thoughts were interrupted by the sight of someone in the deep chairs. In a simple shirt and leather breeches that were no indication of the height and power of his station, sat the king of Eira, reading through a large leather-bound book silently. The king of Eira. Airem Wulfkalt. He didn’t need a crown on his head to tell Fane who he was. He commanded the room with his presence, cutting a striking figure against the solid wood shelves. Airem and his father had visited Aridia when Fane was still young, years before. King Airem, then prince, was only a few years younger than Friedhelm. The two princes had shared tense glances but little else. Fifteen years older than when he’d last seen him, and now a strong and unmoving monarch, Fane felt utterly inferior in his presence. His black hair flowed over his broad shoulders like liquid midnight, contrasting with his steely golden eyes. The eyes of generations of Eiran kings and queens, like a rich sunset over the mountain peaks. “Oh.” The sound came unbidden, and the king looked up. Fane wasn’t really startled; he was royalty himself, of course, and he'd spent plenty of time around them to know that they weren’t always sitting on their carved thrones in ivory towers, as many commoners seemed to think. But he hadn’t thought Airem to be very interested in reading. Between his towering stature and overwhelmingly rugged presence, Fane thought him to be better suited slaughtering mercenaries on horseback, or wrestling bears in the wilds of the forest. He paused, unsure of how to proceed. The awkward silence filled the space between them, members of two different royal Houses gazing at each other in the dim light. Remembering his status as an unknown wanderer granted a place to stay in a foreign castle, Fane bowed low, hoping the king wouldn’t recognize him. The one person that I’ve met before and he’s the one person I run in to?

Fane berated himself inwardly, still bowed. Airem’s face was a somber, unreadable mask. Those golden eyes watching him like a mountain cat spying a deer from a rocky perch. He nodded in response, and turned back to his book. Without looking up, Airem thumbed a page over. “There’s no one here to witness your façade. So you needn’t bother, Prince Fane.” Fane’s stomach dropped through the floor. Straining to keep his heart inside his chest, Fane straightened. It took every effort to keep a neutral expression on his face. No use in hiding now. “Did someone tell you?” How could he have been so stupid to think that he could have stayed here unknown to everyone. One of the guards could have caught on and spilled his secret. Maybe one of the Aridian nobility did see him at one point, unbeknownst to him. There was no knowing who could have been watching him the time he’d been there. The corners of the king’s mouth lifted in amusement. He turned those golden eyes to Fane again. “I knew from the moment you stepped in to this room.” Fane held back a strangled noise. If the king had known just by looking at him, then who else could have- “If you’re going to go into hiding, at least that’s what I assume you’re doing here, you should ensure you’re not wearing any indication of your position.” Fane stilled. Of course. His hand flew subconsciously to the damning evidence hanging by his ear. His prince’s braid. King Airem. He should have known, of all the people in this kingdom, that Airem would be the one to figure it out sooner or later. He'd met Fane’s father and brother, after all. Airem met Friedhelm when he wore the prince’s ceremonial braid before him. If anyone in Eira would be as familiar with Aridian royal customs, it would have been him. “As if that wasn’t enough, your golden hair and the silver eyes of the Stagrunner family gave you away.” Airem crossed a muscled leg over the other. “And I started receiving reports that Prince Fane had disappeared a few weeks ago, suspiciously after my Head Mage informed me he allowed a guest to stay here in the kingdom from some unknown origin.” The king barked a laugh. “You might as well have had it scrawled across your forehead that you were the missing Prince.”

Fane didn’t have the words to respond. Anything he could have said would have sounded moronic in the face of all the evidence against him. “I am curious to know why you feel the need to run from your own kingdom, however.” Airem continued. He closed the book in his lap with a thump. Though Fane was only five years the king’s junior, the gap felt astronomically wider at that moment. Airem patiently waited for an answer. “I was attacked by my own guard.” Fane said finally, swallowing hard. “I don’t know why, nor who may have hired them, but the one that I trusted most who was there with me when he...” Words failed him as the memory of Rune laying in his own blood, the arrow protruding from his chest, returned to him for the first time since he came to Eira. A memory that he dared not recall, not even in his dreams. He pushed the rising panic back into his throat. Airem nodded, understanding what he could not say. “He warned me that I couldn’t return, nor trust anyone in my own kingdom. Until I know what is happening, who is responsible or what can be done, I cannot return against his warning.” Saying all of it out loud made it both more urgent and less real; a strange and frightening juxtaposition. Airem thought for a moment, rubbing his clean-shaven chin with slender fingers. "And what prompted you to come here?" "Rune, my head guard- my friend, said that I needed to find the 'Phoenix in the mountains'. I don't know what that means, but this was the only direction that I could go that..had mountains. I just-" Fane paused, "I just didn't know where else to go." When he set out for the hunt all those weeks ago, he didn't expect he would become the prey. He paused, the realization hitting him. Prey. That’s exactly what he was. Not a prince that had been accidentally lost or separated, but a royal that had almost been assassinated. Intentionally. Deep in his heart, he knew Daener had not acted on his own. He’d been hired by someone. There would be nothing he could gain from slaughtering an heirless prince, without a public audience no less. His mind worked through every political coup he studied through his life. Daener was the poor son of a captain, and Fane’s brother still lived. This was no attempt on his position or throne. Only on his life itself.

Airem nodded again, seemingly unbothered by Fane's awkward answers. "Perhaps you might speak with my Head Mage, Hael, and see if he might have more information to give you." "And what of your brother?" Airem continued, not waiting for Fane's response. "Friedhelm. Shouldn't he be king by now?" "What about him?" "You're the Prince. Surely your own kin would be able to protect you, if you were really in danger as you say." "I don't know. Rune said I shouldn't trust anyone. And," Fane debated revealing this particular insight, but Airem's eyes had a way of bringing the truth out of him before he could think, "And my brother and I haven't been on the best of terms for...a while." "Ah. That's not hard to believe." Airem said in a sudden admission of honesty. Fane merely nodded. "Anyway," Airem said, rising from the chair. He tucked the book he’d been reading under his arm. "I would recommend letting Hael in on your secret. He should be at home right about now." The end of this conversation was in sight, and he wasn't sure he had covered everything that he wanted to talk about. Airem didn't strike him as someone that indulged mindless chatter, however, so he nodded respectfully as the king approached the door. "And as for my part, you're welcome to stay here in the castle for as long as you need to uncover this mystery. I hope that all comes to light in good time." With that, Airem left Fane standing alone in the warm glow of the tableside lamp.

19 FANE WALKED TOWARD the small paddock a short distance from Hael’s house. He’d left the Library at once after meeting Airem, and got directions from one of the guards near the back gates. The paddock looked as if it had held horses at one time, but was now furnished as an outdoor training area. As he approached, he saw that Maewyn and Niamh were with Hael, standing some distance apart from each other inside the wooden fence. Niamh wore a dress that was slightly burnt at the hem. He wondered about it, but soon theorized that she and Maewyn must have dueled before. Niamh had an intense look in her eyes. She didn’t seem to notice his approach, but Fane could tell from where he was that she was itching to prove herself. He recognized that look from how often it appeared in himself. Hael’s deep voice called between his two students, lecturing them on terms that Fane didn’t understand. The Head Mage looked between them, he was the picture of stern annoyance. Fane had never seen any other expression on his face. Fane took a place at the fence, leaning on his forearms as he waited. He’d come to speak to the master magician about his disguise, but that would clearly have to wait until after the lesson. As frightened as he was by magic, he'd never seen any sort of magical duel before, and the prospect was intensely intriguing. After a moment, Hael joined him at the fence, regarding his presence with a tight nod. The two girls stayed in the field, taking their defensive positions. Fane thought, with some sense of familiarity, that they weren’t unlike the positions one would use in sword fighting or similar pursuits. With no outward motion of his hands, a shimmering field of light covered the paddock, filling the air with the smell of burning embers, and was suddenly even fresher than before. Fane stepped back in surprise.

“Mages.” Hael began. The two apprentices tensed. “Begin.” Maewyn lunged for Niamh. The same thrill of adrenaline shot through Fane as when he would train with his guards at home, or more recently when he and Whitestar trained, seeing them lose themselves in the drive to win. Niamh twirled out of the way, Maewyn’s fire flying past her. The fight had only begun and the air was filled with all sorts of different scents. Fane guessed, suddenly, that the smell must have been magic. Ignoring the twist of apprehension in his gut that magic inspired in him, he inhaled deeply through his nose. Along with the savory, warm scent of rosemary, there was something else. Something fresh- like the breeze coming from the sea. And- he sniffed again- peaches? The hot air that flowed from Maewyn’s fire flowed to the barrier, confirming that same scent. Niamh brought her staff to a defensive position, held out in front of her. Much like Fane would use a stave as a weapon. She spun the twisted wood once at the same moment water appeared from the ground to twist around Maewyn’s boots and climb up her legs. It was a move that could only technically be considered “defense”, as it kept Maewyn from pushing forward or backward. This allowed Niamh to control the distance at which she stood. Fane nodded to himself, considering the benefits of that move. If he had magic himself, it would make his training sessions with Whitestar that much easier. As their fight went on, Maewyn was visibly growing more frustrated. Niamh dodged and spun out of the way of every attack that Maewyn tried, preventing her from landing any blows. After a moment, Maewyn even tried to evaporate the water around her legs with fire, only to have Niamh immediately replace it with more. This brought a cry of annoyance from the younger mage, and she soon gave up on that tactic. Hael stood near Fane, his face unreadable and unmoving. If he was at all concerned for his students’ wellbeing, he did nothing to show it. Though Fane could have sworn a flicker of a smile appeared at the corner of his mouth when he saw what Niamh had done in securing control for herself. As the duel went on, Fane noticed the distance between the two mages growing smaller and smaller. With each failed attack of

Maewyn’s, Niamh would inch forward a step. Then another. Maewyn seemingly too caught up in trying to land any sort of blow to her opponent to notice. Once Niamh had arrived within a few feet, mere spitting distance to Maewyn, she stopped. Fane held his breath. What was Niamh thinking? Bringing her gloved hands outward, as a sparrow would spread its wings just before flight, Niamh smiled as water rose from the snow-covered ground. The snow melted into it, creating a shallow lake that splashed against the barriers of the magical shield separating them. Maewyn’s eyes gained a cat-like glimmer, her hand moving to claw a bright light in her hand, growing in power. Fane’s heart caught in his throat as he realized it was lightning. Maewyn was about to use lightning on her opponent in a paddock full of water? “She’s going to kill her.” Fane said, turning to Hael in alarm. “So that’s her play.” Hael muttered, a rare grin creeping over his features. Fane turned widened eyes to the master. “Aren’t you going to stop them?” Hael was entirely unconcerned. Gleeful, even, at least as gleeful as a grumpy old man was capable of. He motioned to the field. “Watch.” Before Maewyn could use the lightning that crackled in her palm, Niamh waved her lifted hands over the water. Fog arose, swirling thick and violent like white ash. The dome was enveloped in a hazy cloud, all visibility cut off from the outside. All the watchers could see was the occasional flash of blue lighting, followed by cries of “That’s not fair, Niamh!” and “Where are you?!”. Fane imagined Niamh, wherever she was in the fogged-over battlefield, was allowing herself an overdue smile of satisfaction. At least Fane knew that he would be indulging in one right about then, if he were her. They continued for several more minutes, Maewyn’s shouts and attacks growing more and more desperate. Prince and Head Mage waited in silence. THIS WASN’T fair. Niamh had been bested by her so many times before this, and though Maewyn was truly sorry for how she'd

ended their last duel, she didn’t expect Niamh to actually do something about it. Her lightning barely lit more than a few feet in front of her, and did nothing to evaporate the magically enhanced fog Niamh had summoned. Every shot was to no avail, and nothing brought her closer to revealing her opponent’s hiding place. A strange dread grew in her throat. Niamh wouldn’t actually hurt her, would she? She didn’t seem the type to stab someone in the back, not like Maire. You have to win. Maire’s voice drifted through Maewyn’s mind. She would win. She always did. I can’t fight what I can’t see. Maewyn thought, her own voice coming in more clearly. You have to be better. Maire’s voice again. Her cousin had told her that the day Hael had accepted her request to undergo the trials to become his apprentice. Across so many years, Maire would whisper that to herself too, in the dead of night when she thought Maewyn was asleep. You can’t lose. Maewyn wouldn’t. Her hands tingled with power as she attacked again and again. The fog was thick and cold, running over her skin and clothes, obscuring them from view. Maewyn attacked blindly, with every element she could think of. Her well of power was nearing the dregs, after such a long fight. How could there have been a way for Niamh to know that? Niamh couldn’t know. Could she? Regardless, there was no way Niamh could hide forever. You have to win. You have to be better. Frustration poured out of her and she was breathing heavily as her magic worked its way to exhaustion. Where is she? Maewyn stilled, doing her best to listen as Hael had been drilling in to her head since she’d arrived. No sound drifted to her other than the waft of the air. Her magic vaguely sensed Niamh’s, but her mind was too busy jumping like a circle of rabbits to focus on the source. Maewyn began to rally the last of her magic to her palm. She stretched her arm in front of her, tracing the direction where the steady presence of Niamh’s magic was coming from. All her opponent had to do was make the mistake of coming closer, coming toward her outstretched hand, and this duel would be over.

Maewyn waited. A soft hand closed over her outstretched wrist from behind. “Yield, Maeywn.” Niamh’s voice breathed near her ear. As Maewyn tried to pivot, to spin on her rival, Niamh’s other hand pressed over her eyes. Maewyn’s head tingled, her hands falling limp, before the world disappeared into a dreamless darkness. ALL WENT SILENT IN the paddock. “It’s over.” Hael announced suddenly, making Fane jump for the break in tension. The prince had no idea how Hael could have known that. But then again, he was the Head Mage. Hael dropped the shield with a wave of his hand. The fog dissipated, flowing around them and over the snow. Niamh sat on her knees in the middle of the field, Maewyn’s head in her lap. Sleeping. “Smart girl.” Hael muttered, stalking over to the two of them. Niamh smiled at Fane from where she knelt, and he couldn’t help but smile back at how she looked so pleased with herself. The master magician knelt to scoop his student from Niamh’s lap. Hael rose from a crouch, taking Maewyn in his arms as he stood. Niamh stood as well and primly brushed the mud and snow from her skirt. They walked toward Fane who still stood at the fence, watching as Niamh caught his eye again. “I’m sorry you had to see that.” She muttered shyly, her cheeks flushing. Fane nearly sputtered. “Sorry? Don’t be sorry; that was amazing.” The words tumbled out of him before he could stop himself. Niamh blushed deeper under his praise and continued in step with her master. Fane could see from Hael’s expression that he was keeping his satisfaction on a tight leash. “I say we’re done for the day. I have a feeling Maewyn won’t be feeling too obliged to a rematch before dinner.” Hael said, smiling. Maewyn was practically dead to the world. Fane could have sworn she may have even been snoring softly. Niamh nodded in submission and pulled away from them, walking down to the castle town again. Fane thought her eyes were asking him to follow, but Hael cut in again before he could respond

to Niamh’s unspoken question. “And I believe the boy had some matter to discuss with me?” I should just stop being surprised that mages seem to know my every waking thought. Fane thought to himself bitterly. Outwardly, he nodded and cast an apologetic look to Niamh, who turned and continued down the path. “I’ll see you later, then.” Niamh called behind her, waving as she went. Hael looked at him incredulously. “Come along.”

20 FANE FOLLOWED HIM INTO the house, waiting in the comfortable sitting room while Hael hauled his apprentice up to some hidden bedroom to sleep off her magically induced nap. A tawny reddish- brown bird sat on a fine perch, watching him carefully with blazing eyes. It looked like some sort of hawk or a falcon, though it wasn't any kind that Fane had ever seen before. It barely made a noise, merely twisting its head this way and that, but never looking away from Fane. The bird preened its feathers, revealing a beautiful blazing orange coloring on the underside of its wing. When the Head Mage returned, the fireplace roared to a blaze at his presence. Fane jumped as the room came further to life; the kettle whistling, books flying back to their places on the shelf, and papers fluttering into a neat pile on the table. At Hael’s malicious chuckle, Fane began to understand that the mage enjoyed scaring him. He felt a pang of both pity and admiration for Niamh and any past apprentices that may have gone through similar trials. “So,” Hael began, sinking into one of the armchairs. “I understand that you’re finally ready to ask for my help?” For the second time that day, Fane found himself sputtering again. “How did you know?” Hael raised an eyebrow. At the wave of his hand, a fresh mug of tea found its way into Fane’s waiting hands, who took a drink to steel himself. “You’ve been stumbling around helplessly since you arrived. You’re really not very good at blending in.” Fane stiffened. What could that have meant? If he assumed that Hael knew already that he was the prince, he could give away his secret. But if it was just an innocent comment, he might be acting too suspicious to avoid Hael’s notice. Fane was left with little options.

However, Airem recommended that he tell Hael his identity, and he was the Head Mage. So, despite the man’s abrasive personality otherwise, Fane decided that he was trustworthy. “Since you seem to know that I need help, you should already have an idea of what I want.” Fane said. He purposely kept his words vague, to try and feel out what Hael might have been thinking. He’d seen Friedhelm do it hundreds of times. Hael grinned into his own mug of tea. “Indulge me.” Fane could have cursed him under his breath, but refrained for fear of being magically muted or struck blind or some other ailment Hael was capable of inflicting upon him. “I need you to change my appearance...Somehow.” Hael still didn't look at him. “And why is that?” “Because, as you said, I am not blending in as well as I would have liked.” Fane couldn’t stop the bitter undertone from edging into his voice. This only made Hael grin wider. “That request is extremely vague. I can change your appearance in any number of ways. Are you asking for your hair to be a different color, or perhaps to become a different species entirely?” The master magician swirled his cup once, causing it to fill with liquid again. “How would you fancy being a stag for the rest of your days? Or perhaps a field mouse?” “Please don’t.” Fane breathed, gripping his mug just a bit tighter. Hael chuckled darkly again. Fane ground his teeth in response. “No, I suppose you wouldn’t make a very good field mouse. You would get yourself eaten by a wandering cat much too quickly.” He paused, watching the fire dance in its boundary. He turned fiery eyes to him again. “There’s something else you want to tell me, however.” Fane took a breath. There was no taking back what he was about to say. “Someone is hunting me, but I need to stay alive to find out who.” Hael hummed, still watching Fane carefully. “Who told you this?” “My friend. He...” Fane paused again, swallowing the lump in his throat. “He sent me here for help. He told me I couldn’t return to- where I come from.” Hael nodded slowly, though he said nothing.

Fane didn’t know if it was his desperation, but he continued speaking before he could stop himself. “He told me to find the ‘Phoenix in the mountains’.” “You’ve found him, then.” Hael said. Something in Fane’s chest deflated in relief. If Rune had trusted Hael, then perhaps Fane could lean on that trust. “If your friend sent you to me, then you must need more than a simple disguise.” Hael said, taking a drink of his tea. Fane had sufficiently talked himself into a corner. How stupid was he to expect that he could come to the most powerful mage in the world and he wouldn’t have been able to guess his purpose there? But if Rune told me to find him, then Hael must be the only one who can help. Hael waited, watching him. If the master mage could see Fane agonizing internally, he made no indication of it. Finally, Fane made his choice. “I am... The missing prince.” Hael raised his eyebrows briefly, his cup of tea halfway to his mouth. “Interesting.” He said, setting the cup on the saucer next to him. “Then the captain did his job well.” Fane stilled. “What do you mean?” Hael turned his eyes to him again. “It’s not by coincidence that you find yourself here, Prince Fane.” Hael said. “The captain, I believe he went by ‘Rune’ in Aridia, did he not? I sent him there for the exact purpose of bringing you here.” Just as the sun came over the mountains, realization dawned on Fane. "Rune was sent...by you?" "Yes." "Why? Why would you send someone for me?” Fane asked, feeling as if his friendship with Rune was cast under a shadow. "Because I wanted you alive and untouched by the evil in your land." Hael replied. Fane was speechless. "Wait." Fane thought back to his first conversation with the master mage. "Then you knew about me this whole time? Why did you ask me all those questions when I first arrived? Why didn't you just tell me this when you saw me then?" Hael raised an eyebrow. "The captain was to return with you. I hardly knew to expect you.” He paused, folding his hands together

on his knee. “I suppose he’s chosen to stay behind, for whatever reason, so we will do our best to keep you alive whilst you’re here.” Hael said, though the jesting tone from earlier was gone. “To make sure that your friend’s sacrifice was not in vain, I want to teach you something. Something you're going to need in the days ahead." Fane nodded dumbly, waiting. "You have no magic. You barely have any knowledge of magic, so I wouldn't expect you to know what it feels like. You’ll be able to tell by the heaviness in your spirit. That’s dark magic.” The weight of Hael’s words seemed to bring darkness to the whole room. He continued, “Any time you’re under attack from dark magic, remember to whom you belong.” "Belong?" Fane asked. I don't belong to anyone but myself. He thought. How else could he belong to anyone? Even the question inspired a deep longing even he'd forgotten was there. "You belong to your Father. And you stand under His authority." "My father is dead." Fane said flatly. He had been dead for a long time, and Fane couldn't say he was sad to say it. "The Father of Lights, prince. He is the only One that can never die." Though the words seemed to be a rebuke, his tone was uncharacteristically gentle. There was that name again. "I don't know who that is." Fane said, mystified. "Regardless," Hael continued, "When you're under attack by dark magic of any kind, I want you to tell it that 'you stand under the authority of the Father of Lights. And you are not afraid'. Do you understand? The darkness feeds on your fear. Since you don't have magic, He is your only defense." Fane nodded outwardly even though inwardly nothing made sense. “Good.” Hael said, satisfied. Then, “This is your last chance; are you sure you don’t want to be a field mouse? I hear it’s an excellent life of sleeping in burrows and wandering wherever you wish.” Fane grimaced. “No, thank you.” “Mmhm.” Hael relented and placed a hand suddenly on the crown of the other man’s head. Fane jumped as his scalp tingled, but was pleased to see blond hair appearing in the corners of his vision. It grew to match the length of his braid, falling almost to his shoulders, effectively hiding it. A moment later, it was no longer his golden blond, but more of an earthy light brown color. Mystified,

he ran a hand through his hair. It was the longest it had ever been in his life. Just as Fane thought it was over, Hael roughly pressed his thumbs to the outer corners of Fane’s eyes, creating a far more uncomfortable feeling for him.
