It took everything in him not to pull away, feeling as if Hael might just take his eyes if he felt so inclined. Instead, the world was enveloped in a wave of blue light, then faded back to normal. Hael pulled his hands away as Fane swallowed a sigh of relief. “Those who already know you will not be fooled by the illusion over your eyes, and your hair will fade back to its normal color after a while, but that should suffice for your purposes.” “Thank you.” Fane bowed slightly out of respect. Hael inclined his head and waved him off as if he were an unwelcome pest. “My second apprentice should be making an appearance soon. Perhaps you would walk back with her so you don’t get lost.” Fane noticed with a twinge of bitterness that his immediate thought was not that Maewyn, who was just coming out of a sleeping spell, would not be the one most likely to get lost. "Oh." Hael suddenly turned away from Fane, as if remembering something. "Here." When Hael turned back, he held a sturdy cloak of thick wool in his hands. It was a heathered gray, held by a clasp at the neck that looked like the antlers of a stag. "You're going to need this." Fane hesitated for only a moment before he took the fabric in his hands. It was warm and soft to the touch. "Thank you, sir." "We don't want the prince that I so carefully rescued to die of frostbite, now do we?" Hael said. Fane couldn't tell if he was smiling or not. As if on cue, the sound of bare feet pattering down carpeted stairs floated from down the hall. Maewyn appeared a moment later, rubbing her eyes and yawning. Hael twisted slightly to watch her pad into the sitting room, looking like death. “Ah, I see that Niamh didn’t put you out for as long as she could have.” He chuckled, taking another swig of tea. Fane was suddenly struck with the idea that Niamh could have, indeed, placed Maewyn under a stronger spell than she did. She could have made her sleep for years if she really wanted to. Fane realized with a twinge of fear and admiration. Maewyn rubbed her eyes again, taking a moment to register the

scene around her. Her eyes widened when they fell on Fane, and a slow smile crept over her face. “Oh, Fane. Where did you come from?” She looked at him oddly, tilting her head to one side. “And why is your hair so much longer?” Maewyn gasped suddenly, looking to Hael. “Wait, I wasn’t asleep for that long, was I?” Her hand flew up to her own hair, checking its length. Hael shook his head, rolling his eyes and turning back to the book he’d plucked from the shelf. Maewyn seemed to recover quickly from her bout of sleepiness and bounded to Fane’s side. “Would you like to walk me home, Fane?” She asked, batting her eyelashes at him. Fane merely nodded, smiling politely. Maewyn jumped away, scurrying up the stairs to retrieve her boots and overcoat before flying down a moment later. Fane could only watch as she put both of those items on and was clinging to his arm in mere seconds. She pulled him toward the door. “Thank you again for your help, Master Hael.” Fane said around the corner, before he was dragged into the cold air.

21 AS HARD AS SHE TRIED not to be, Niamh was quite proud of herself for finally besting Maewyn. She was also pleased that Fane had been there to see it, even if she wasn’t sure what that feeling meant. The look of awe on his face was just the pick-me-up she'd been needing after consistently feeling humiliated on the training field. Niamh shook her head. I’m indulging in this too much. Nythaniel’s voice popped into her mind. The outcome of one battle does not determine the fate of the war. Nythaniel had been in plenty of spats in his life to be so wise, and Niamh did her best to take his advice, even if he wasn’t there to give it. On her way home from Hael’s house, she stopped by the tailor’s to purchase some extra needle and thread for her supply at home. Some deep part of her hoped that if she dallied in town long enough, Fane might be finished speaking with Hael and be walking back at some point shortly afterward. This hope kept her shopping. After the tailor’s, she wandered to the nearby dress shop. Bright colors and sweeping fabrics smiled back at her from clean, frost- touched windows. Then she stopped into a bakery briefly, rewarding herself with a soft savory roll which she munched happily as she exited. With every move to each one of her unnecessary stops, her eyes drifted to the way she'd come. To the narrow path leading to her Master's house. An hour passed, yet Niamh continued to make her ambling rounds. The blond man she sought still didn't show himself. Her feet were growing cold in her boots, and her arms grew tired of carrying her small parcels. Maybe I missed him? Maybe he slipped by me when I was in the bakery. She theorized, imagining that was the most likely case.

Stepping into the sunlight again with her bag in hand, Niamh looked to her right to the path one more time. Though no one walked down it, the familiar head of hair she was looking for appeared in front of the bakery she'd come from the hour earlier. Excitedness bubbled up inside of her as she opened her mouth to call out to him. Fane stepped to the side, revealing another familiar face. Maewyn. Maewyn and Fane stood looking into the colorful windows of the bakery together. Neither of them noticed her approach. Niamh opened her mouth again to say an obligatory hello as she approached, but the words died on her tongue as Maewyn’s hand slipped into Fane’s as she excitedly pointed to all the wares staring out at them from the window. Fane made no move to drop her hand, but stared with her. It was such a casual affection, such a natural movement. Niamh was suddenly aware of how perfectly Maewyn's petite frame complemented Fane's height and broad shoulders. How her cheeks grew rosy as she looked up at him, looking as if she was chattering to him about whatever it was they were looking at together. Fane listened dutifully. Perhaps this was why he'd waited at the field; why he had walked back with Maewyn instead of her. Perhaps, Niamh thought to herself before she could stop herself, he was simply being polite with me. Still neither of them noticed Niamh’s presence. Something roiled deep in Niamh’s stomach and she stopped in her tracks. Niamh couldn’t bear to watch them any longer. She turned away and hurried back to the castle. Back to her room in retreat. Perhaps Maewyn had won that day after all. FANE REMOVED HIS HAND from Maewyn’s enthusiastic grasp. She didn’t notice him pull away, still babbling excitedly over the pastries in the window. “Will you buy this one for me? Please?” Her sea-green eyes turned to his, growing practically three sizes larger. He relented, handing her 200 mynt and watching her rush inside the building. Fane sighed, rubbing his nose in annoyance. Something moved out of the corner of his eye, and he looked up to see a glimpse of Niamh’s braid swinging behind her as she walked away from him. Or, at least, he thought it might have been Niamh. There was no

way to be sure with how quickly she disappeared around the nearest corner. Maewyn reappeared with her hands full of a sticky-looking pastry. Berry juice seeped from the inside and flowed down her hand as she munched. “This is the perfect post-nap snack. Thank you, Fane.” He nodded, grateful for her casual courtesy. “Where do you suppose Niamh went off to?” She asked through mouthfuls of food. Before he could answer, she shrugged. “Probably off to one of her haunts. She’s usually only ever in one of three places.” Why did you ask if you were just going to answer for yourself? He thought with irritated amusement. “She’s probably taking a nap somewhere. She’s not been sleeping well, so that’s usually what I’ve seen her do.” “Not been sleeping well?” Fane’s ears perked up at this. He turned to see Maewyn nod. “Yeah, she’s been complaining to herself about staying up too late, and I guess she’s been having bad dreams too.” Maewyn finished off the last of her pastry with a disappointed sucking of her fingers. “Not every night, but enough that I have to hear about it.” Fane considered this. He didn’t spend enough time around her to really notice a difference in her demeanor. Toward him, at least. Then again, I don't know her very well. "We didn’t have anything like this in Corseils." Maewyn said, pulling another from her paper bag. "Corseils doesn’t really do pastries. We have more candies and marzipan and stuff." "Mhmm." Fane muttered, only half listening. "Do you have treats like this where you come from?" The question caught him by surprise. Not that he thought Maewyn was uncaring, by any means, but she wasn't particularly interested in other people's lives, from what he'd gathered. "Uh, yes. We had something similar." Fane said absentmindedly, thinking of the cylindrical shaped pastries of his home, filled with creams of various flavors. He missed them. "Where do you come from, Fane?" Maewyn blinked up at him with innocent eyes. If only she knew how loaded that question was. "Not from here." He replied simply. For anyone else, this might inspire some sort of investigation into the obviously avoidant response. For Maewyn, however, this seemed to satisfy her.

"Ohh, a traveling man, huh?" Her usual flirtatious twinkle returned to her eyes. "Have you ever been to Corseils? Even though it's pretty here, it's nothing like at home. We have oceans as far as your eyes could see. And all the buildings are open-air. Not like here where everything is all tucked together." They continued walking toward the castle again, ducking in to one of the side entrances while Maewyn continued talking. Fane had never been to Corseils; that was his brother's arena as the eldest prince to do all the traveling. But he'd read about it in many of the history books he'd taken to reading the last few years. "We used to have these biiiig parties with lots of fruit and vegetables and fresh fish. We would stay up all night sometimes. And there was lots of wine. So much wine." She said with a laugh. "They don't really eat fish here, do they?" Maewyn scarcely paused for an answer. "I don't really mind all the deer they eat in Eira but it does get kind of old after a while. It all tastes the same." She stuck her tongue out for emphasis. Although the girl beside him didn't interrupt her constant stream of information, it was knowledge that he welcomed from her, for a change. Fane was always interested in knowing more about other places that he had never seen. "Maire and I, we grew up together. Even though we’re cousins, she's more like my older sister. Always telling me what to do." Fane could relate. "Back home, we didn't have to wear so many clothes since it was so hot. All the ladies wore softer colors and lots of white." She sighed wistfully, "I miss wearing my old things." Fane nodded dutifully, even while he scanned the halls looking for an excuse to leave this conversation. Maewyn still occasionally tried to hang on to his arm, though he would shift it out of the way or find some railing to grab while they walked. She was entirely undeterred. "I didn't really get to wear any nice things until I was older, but now I'm attached and I can't go back. Someday I would love to go to Aridia. They have the most money of all the countries, did you know that?" Fane did know that. "They are so wealthy that their gold thread has actual gold in it. Can you imagine what it must be like to actually wear money?" Fane didn't have to imagine. Many of his vests were finely

embroidered with the same thread that she coveted. Color rose to his ears with understanding how privileged he'd been. "Maire and I stopped by there on the way here, but it wasn't nearly long enough. All I got to see was the gardens in the castle. She wouldn't let me go anywhere else." Maewyn puffed her cheeks in annoyance. Fane had no recollection of this happening. It must have been a brief visit, indeed. He maneuvered toward the Library, all the while looking for some unsuspecting soul to distract Maewyn long enough to make his escape. At last, his salvation appeared on the horizon. The giant looming doors were right in front of them, if only he could get Maewyn to stop talking long enough to say goodbye. He vaguely heard her say something about being hungry again. How much can she eat? He thought with dismay. "Uhm, Maewyn, I know the cook sometimes keeps soup on the stove for any of the servants that might want a snack." Fane said, driving a sudden wedge in the middle of her sentence. This was not a lie: The cook did often keep extra food available. And he knew this from many of his nights returning from being out and finding his stomach growling from the exercise. This perked her interest. "You could go see if she's got any left, if you're hungry." "Are you coming too?" "I just have to stop in here for something." He said, gesturing to the Library doors. He didn’t think she’d be much inclined to study, considering her lessons with Hael were only a short time before. He was right. Maewyn shrugged and trotted back down the wide set of stairs they had just come up. Fane ducked into the safety of the Library doors, hearing Maewyn continue to chatter to herself all the way down the stairs. He indulged a sigh of relief.

Maire A TREE LOOMED ABOVE her. Its branches stretched over the vaulted ceiling of the large, cavernous space, blocking any of the stone to be seen. It gave a light of its own, casting the entire space in a bright golden light. Her delicate white hand reached out to its bark, feeling the thrum of ancient magic pulsing within it. The sap dripped over her hand as she brought it to her mouth, drinking its lifeblood and feeling its power thrill through her own veins. It was intoxicating. She drank more. And kept drinking, until the light faded and all went dark. Maire found herself staring at her own reflection in the mirror at her dressing table as she ran a brush through her long hair. Maewyn helped her magically maintain its beauty, so she didn’t even need to brush it at all. Even so, it was a comforting and familiar ritual that she relished in. At the very least, it gave her something to do other than talk to the man currently sitting behind her on the bed. The king sat on the edge of the mattress in a state of undress that only she was allowed to be privy to. His white shirt hung open, exposing the strong lines of his chest. He wore fitted black trousers ending in bare feet. His long black hair was unbound, falling over his broad shoulders. She sat in her fine dressing gown. It fell to the floor and pooled around the legs of the stool she sat on. “Maire.” Airem’s voice was questioning, as if he'd just finished saying something that she'd not responded to. Maire realized after a moment that was exactly the case. “I’m sorry, your Highness, please repeat that.” “I’ve told you before that you don’t have to address me with such formality. We are husband and wife, my dear, and I don’t expect any courtly manners in our own bedroom.” Airem gently chided her.

He rose from the bed and came to stand behind her. Maire made no move to acknowledge his presence. His hand twitched, as if he was refraining from reaching out to touch her shoulder. “I was simply going over today’s events.” He finished, smiling kindly at her through the mirror. “What kind of queenly duties did my wife perform today?” Maire ran through the list, careful not to reveal anything more than what was essential. This was her role, her career, and she would perform it to the perfection that was expected of such a high position. It only took a few moments to relay the information, and when she was finished, she set the silver hairbrush back down on her dressing table. Airem neither looked satisfied nor dissatisfied with her report, merely listening with careful attention. “Were you able to rest today, or take some time to do something enjoyable?” He asked after a long moment, watching her face with a worried expression. “I live to serve my king and country, your Highness, and that is enjoyable enough.” She answered. This only seemed to deepen the lines between his furrowed brows. He gave her what looked like a saddened smile. “I see.” A strained and uncomfortable silence passed between them. Neither of them moved to break it, simply watching each other in the mirror. Airem moved first, stepping directly behind her. “Would you like me to braid your hair for you?” He asked quietly. Carefully. Maire kept her expression neutral. “That’s what a lady’s maid is for. I will call her-” “I would like to be the one to serve you tonight, my queen.” Airem said, his voice low and full of meaning. He did not touch her hair, nor make any indication that he would, until she consented. Against everything that told her otherwise, Maire nodded slightly. “Whatever you wish, your Highness.” Despite the cold, distant words, her husband smiled softly and ran strong, scarred hands over the length of her hair. Reverently, he set to work weaving the thick strands in and around each other, creating a loose but sturdy plait that ran down her back and to the floor. Neither of them spoke as he did this, the silence stretching over several minutes. When he'd finished, Maire rose from the stool. Her dressing

gown trailed behind her, the ruffles brushing Airem’s bare feet as she swept passed him. The king followed her, making his way to the large bed taking up most of the bedroom. It was so vast, it was large enough for four adults to sleep comfortably with room to spare. So different was the casual luxury of the castle than the beds she'd spent most of her childhood seeking out. The thought of the hovels of her youth left a bitter tang in her mind. She pushed the thought away. Maire delicately slipped under the generous covers on the right side of the bed. The bed shifted as Airem took up the other side. They had been married for nearly a month, and the unspoken expectation still hung between them. An expectation that Maire refused to fulfill, and one which Airem had refrained from mentioning after the first two weeks of their union. Any excuses Maire had leaned on had been spent, and she made an effort to avoid sleeping in the same room as him most nights. Tonight, however, she was too exhausted to seek out her separate bower and settled uncomfortably into the bed that she knew she should have been occupying for some time. She faced away from him in the semi-darkness, staring at the fine printed wallpaper, following the swirling lines with her eyes. Airem said nothing, but his breathing didn't slow to the pattern of sleep as she'd hoped. After what seemed like hours, though would have only been a few minutes, his deep voice whispered to her across the expanse between them . “Would you join me for tea in the garden tomorrow?” “If you wish it, your Highness.” An obligatory answer. A queen’s duty to her king. Airem sighed and said nothing else. After several more minutes, his breathing did indeed level and lengthen. Hearing this confirmation that she was alone once again, Maire allowed herself to sleep, knowing full well what would await her in her dreams. The same visions as she'd been seeing since she arrived in Eira. Sometimes it was the image of the mighty golden tree, its sap dripping over her hands as she drank. Other times, there were flashes of a bright palace, overflowing with greenery that was slowly rotting. No one else seemed to notice its decay but her.

22 THE EVENING STARTED much as the last few had: strolling into one of the seedier taverns at the edge of the city and running up a tab. With tankards of foul-smelling ale in hand, the two men would wait. Wait for their prey to show themselves. Members of the Fade would usually be wearing black or sometimes dark gray tones, and they rarely wore any sort of fur or similar warm covering. This is what made them stand out against the rugged woodsmen and travelers from other parts of Eira. From what little information Whitestar had gathered, he’d said that the Fade's choice of attire could be connected to their status within the organization. Fane knew nothing of fanatical cults, as they were unheard of in Aridia, but that sounded like something he thought cult members might do. Once their prey was in sight, Whitestar would make the first move by sidling up to the member's side and leaning over the bar casually offering a mug of ale. Fane couldn't help but notice how Whitestar would actively avoid drinking his own ale, even as he would buy tankard after tankard for the particularly greedy members he would make conversation with. After the first night seeing him do this, Fane followed suit. Better to keep a clear head so one didn't go careening into corners or flying into walls out of drunkenness. They never saw another man so young as the tailor’s son, but his face never left Fane’s mind. After waiting for the better part of an hour, one such opportunity presented itself. A tall, slender man wandered in to the golden haze of the tavern, and took a seat at the long wooden bar at the back of the room. He was hunched over, as if his body couldn’t sustain his stature and was used to ducking under doorways. The woodsman

shot Fane a look under rusted eyebrows and pushed himself up from where he was leaning against the bar. They approached the man together, Whitestar taking the right side and Fane taking the left. "Evening, stranger." Whitestar began, pushing the extra tankard of ale he’d previously ordered toward the man. The Fade member looked up, surprise immediately turning to suspicion. "Evening." He replied, taking a cautious sip of alcohol. Fane made a motion of taking a drink himself, though he closed his lips tightly as the warm liquid touched them. He swallowed for effect. The Fade member barely looked his way. "What brings you here?" Whitestar pretended to drink from his own mug, feigning disinterest. "Kind of a cold night to be out and about." He gave the man a once-over with a critical eye, his usual expression. "And especially without anything to keep one so thin as yourself from freezing to death." Fane nodded in distant agreement. It was truly one of the coldest evenings he'd experienced so far. The doorknobs were nearly frozen over on the outside, and people's breath came in foggy clouds even inside the building. The tavern owners made an effort to lessen the chill with several roaring fires on either side of the open room. Many patrons avoided the window seats and gathered near the fireplaces instead. Those that were not so fortunate as to been granted one of those coveted spots still wore their outer layers of fur and heavy wool. This included Fane and his grumpy companion. "That's none of your concern." The Fade member answered gruffly, despite downing his gifted ale with gusto. Just as soon as he'd finished, Whitestar slid another over to him. "Oh, I think it is." He answered, smiling as pleasantly as his face would allow. "What my companion means to say is that perhaps you’re in need of better clothing?" Fane knew Whitestar's attempts at diplomacy usually didn't go as well as the woodsman seemed to think. The criminal finally seemed to notice Fane's presence and jumped slightly. "Or perhaps you might let us help you?" Fane added carefully. There was a pause. The suspicious man accepted the second mug of ale, albeit begrudgingly, and took another swig. He seemed to consider whether or not he should be forthcoming to these strangers

that were clearly buttering him up. "There's nothing I need from you." The criminal answered finally, but he took a hesitant look over his shoulder. "Maybe it's you that needs something from me." He whispered, angling his body in Fane's direction; being the more amiable of his two options. Out of the corner of his eye, Fane saw Whitestar's eyebrows shoot up in surprise. This was new. Rarely ever were suspected Fade members offering their help. The ale must have worked this time. As if in answer to Fane's thought, the man took another long drink of alcohol. "There's a power, dark and dangerous stuff, that keeps those of us that submit to it warm and healthy as we would ever want." He took another cautious glance around. Another drink. "There's a sickness coming, worse than anything that has ever been, and I joined so that I wouldn't get it. We don't need coats, we don't need food or drink, unless we want it. Our leader even promises that we may never die if we are in it long enough, like our needs fade away." The man downed the last of his ale, and looked disappointed at the bottom of the mug. Whitestar slid another in front of him. Fane was beginning to wonder if the woodsman was ever going to pay his tab. He never actually remembered seeing Whitestar pay any sort of currency to the tavern owner on any of their evenings together. He pushed the distracting thought from his mind as the criminal leaned closer, whispering conspiratorially. Whitestar seemed to lean with him on instinct. Fane made a show of being entranced, interested in whatever the man was clearly holding out on saying. "The sky darkens..." Fane nearly panicked. he'd heard this phrase before, growled into the ground just before Whitestar had knocked the last criminal unconscious. The first time had been one of the first nights he was out with Whitestar, and the woodsman had given the wrong answer. Wrong answers meant that Fane would be spending his evening running at full tilt over icy streets and gaining more bruises along the way. He didn't like when Whitestar gave the wrong answer. Their needs will fade... He scrambled through the few thoughts he had at that moment. The Fade. The criminal looked at him expectantly. Fane's hesitation was

clearly making him more nervous by the second. Either that or the red flush over the man's face meant he was more drunk than when he'd sat down a few moments earlier. The sky darkens... "And all will fade." Fane finally answered, doing his best to pretend that he'd hesitated for dramatic effect. From his spot behind the man, Whitestar looked begrudgingly impressed and perhaps offended that Fane had cracked some code he'd been working on for weeks. Fane couldn't help a smirk of satisfaction. One point for him. The man nodded, a messy and slow movement. A bit of liquid dribbled down his chin and wet his black garment as he threw his head back for another drink. “I got someone else into it. Just last night. Gave the black stuff to his wife and that convinced him.” The criminal said, hiccuping. From the increasingly vacant expression in his eyes, Fane guessed he might have forgotten where this conversation was supposed to be going next. Fane and Whitestar shared a look over the man’s head. “Black stuff”? Fane thought. What does that mean? Whitestar took the liberty of throwing one of his arms, so large it completely enveloped the man's slim shoulders, around the criminal in mock friendliness. "Why don't we find you somewhere to sleep off your alcohol, friend." Fane couldn't help but notice the way he growled the last word. He knew exactly where this would be going. Right out to the alley, out to the cold, so they couldn't be overheard further. Fane stifled a groan. Why the woodsman chose to do business out in the elements, he would never know. As expected, Whitestar led the stumbling man out the back door to the tavern, smiling stiffly the entire way. Fane followed with heavy footsteps. Why do we keep doing this? He wondered, irritated. he'd hoped, in vain apparently, that his diplomacy would allow him to remain inside. As soon as the frigid air hit the three of them, and the back door had slammed closed, Whitestar was shoving the man against the ice-covered wall. As per usual, he began with his questioning and intimidation. "Who leads you?" Because that worked so well last time. Fane thought bitterly. The criminal was clearly not coherent at this point, and seemed to be in a good mood; not at all offended by being shoved against a

wall. He grinned lazily, "I don't know. Who leads you?" The criminal seemed to think this comment was somehow amusing and laughed at his own cleverness. Which made Whitestar even angrier than he already was. Fane suspected that he hadn't helped matters by up- staging him a few moments earlier with his code-cracking. "What is the Fade, and what are their purposes?" Whitestar continued his list of questions, emphasizing the last word with a shake of the man's collar. The criminal's head lolled to the side as his smile widened. "I already told you what the Fade is, don't you remember?" Whitestar was increasingly looking as if he wanted to choke the man where he stood, his arms shaking from the effort of restraining himself. Fane was fully enjoying this. "There are more of us than you could even imagine, woodsman." The man said, grinning and looking up to the clear night sky above them. His breath fogged into the air as he laughed again. "You would be well off if you just joined us and stopped resisting." "You're a fool if you think-" A knife shot out from the darkness beyond the alley, heading directly for Whitestar's head of dark hair. He whipped his head around in that split second to face the death of him straight on. A short sword, clean and elegant, flew from behind the two men, intercepting the knife in the air. They clanged to the stones together. The drunk man pinned against the wall seemed to think this was wildly funny. Whitestar was finally at the end of his patience and knocked the man out cold with a quick jab to his flushed face. The woodsman let him drop to the ground. "Who goes there?" He yelled into the darkness, his hand going for his axes strapped to his thighs. There was a shout from the street, followed by the sound of a large body hitting the stones with a slap. Fane tensed, reaching for his bow. There was complete silence over the street. The only sounds were their breath puffing into the night air and the quiet groan of their leather boots as they prepared for a scuffle. Whitestar turned to face him, scanning the street on the other side of the alley. As he watched, Fane saw a flash of blond hair and a dark cloak behind his companion. Just as he opened his mouth to warn him, the figure stood to their full height, which was nearly a

head taller than his mountain of a companion. "Hey, Ro." Fane had never seen true fear in Whitestar's eyes until then. He jumped slightly as he whirled on his apparent savior. "Kjellfrid." Whitestar looked immediately irritated, even more than he'd been for most of the evening. He took the bridge of his nose between two fingers, looking altogether embarrassed, probably because Fane was witness to this apparent weakness of his. "What are you doing here?" The young woman towered over the woodsman, and looked entirely pleased with herself because of it. Fane couldn’t see anything else of her attire, as she wore a cloak of the deepest gray over the rest of her. On her head, peeking from her hood, was a mask in the shape of a wolf's head, stars and constellations covering the surface. Her rich blond hair fell from it to her waist. She plucked one of the two short swords she carried from the ground, sliding it easily into one of the sheaths on her thighs. Kjellfrid had a pleasantly wide mouth that looked as if she laughed easily, and a playful glint in her forest green eyes. "Is that any way to talk to the woman that just saved your life?" She looked as if she was inspecting her fingernails through her sleek leather gloves with feigned interest, "What is this now? The seventh time I've done so?" Whitestar grumbled. "Don't remind me." Despite the harrowing circumstances, Fane couldn't help but chuckle at the scene. Kjellfrid and Whitestar regarded him as if they only just remembered him standing there. "Who’s your friend?" She asked, nodding her head gracefully in Fane's direction. Whitestar rolled his eyes, "He's not my friend." Fane couldn't disagree with that. "I brought him on to help- er - to join me in hunting down all of these Fade rats scurrying around the streets." Whitestar finished, toeing the unconscious man at his feet with a solid boot. Kjellfrid lifted her cloak to reveal Whitestar's apparent attacker where she dragged him along with one hand. "You haven't been doing a very thorough job of it, I see." She said, humor still edging her voice. "You should be thanking the Father of Lights Himself that I have so graciously decided to help you boys with your hunt." With a scowl, Whitestar shouldered the dead-weight of the man

from the ground, hauling him over his broad back. He began stalking away from Kjellfrid and Fane down to the other end of the alley. "I don't need or want your help." Kjellfrid gave Fane an incredulous look. "I'm assuming he told you the same thing?" Fane nodded, letting an amused huff fly into the night air.

23 DESPITE HER ONE HARD-earned victory against Maewyn, Niamh didn’t get any sleep. By the morning, her eyes were heavy, and every movement was a struggle. She rolled from her covers with a groan. Sunlight streamed in her tall windows, oppressively covering every inch of her room and ruining any chance of sleeping in. The floor was freezing, sending shivers up her spine as she approached the water basin. The water inside was only partially frosted over, and she plunged her hands into it. Anything to wake me up. Splashing the frigid water on her face, she stared at her reflection in the small mirror. The bags under her eyes were clearly apparent. There would be no hiding those today. The auburn waves of her hair were tangled and crusted with sweat. She gathered her clothes for the day ahead, the colors blending together in the mid-darkness of her closet, and headed down the hall to the bathing rooms. The bathing rooms of the castle were luxurious, to say the least. Large pools of steaming water dotted the marble floors, and various soaps and herbs and spices laid out on neat shelves near them for patrons to use. There was a side for women and one for the men, with a sturdy partition between them. After stripping her nightgown, she delicately slipped into one of the nearby pools. Niamh closed her eyes with a sigh. Visions of those dreams returned to her in the darkness behind her eyelids. Slipping on pools of blood as she made her way to the patient’s side. The patients were always different, and she could never see their faces. She didn’t know what they needed, or what had happened to them... but she couldn’t shake the feeling that it was somehow her fault. Rivers of red streamed from the edge of all the beds of the unknown patients, and every step she took only carried her farther

away from where she needed to be. It’s not real. It was just a dream, nothing more. She repeated for what felt like the hundredth time. Niamh rubbed the sleep from her eyes with wet hands. As she opened her eyes, Niamh looked at her hands. They were covered in blood. Niamh started and plunged her hands into the water again in alarm. No red appeared in the water, nothing remained on her hands. Her chest tightened. It’s not real. With a shudder, she quickly lathered with the lavender soap near her head, and rose from the pool. Her long hair dripped into a stream as she made her way to a shower, cooling the steam from her skin. No red appeared beneath her feet either. It wasn’t until she rubbed a lavender oil into her skin that she finally stopped shaking. Niamh was in no mood to socialize, and she dodged through the quieter parts of the castle, dipping in and out of abandoned rooms and empty hallways. At last, she made it to her cottage.. Mercifully, she found that it was quiet, Maewyn nowhere in sight. The fire roared to life at her command, filling the room with its warmth and flickering light. Niamh removed her gloves and set them on the counter. Her nerves settled slightly. She poured herself into the comfort of her occupation. Reading recipes, pulling the respective ingredients from the shelves, mixing and pouring and grinding in her grindstone brought a sense of purpose. Every month, Hael gave her a list of potions, tinctures, and medicines that needed mixing for delivery to the surrounding towns. This was her roadmap as she set to work. As deep winter continued to set in, there would be more and more orders to fill. After she'd made it through several pages of Hael’s list, the sun was high in the sky, casting harsh shadows on the gardens outside. Though sleep never really left her eyes, she was happy to focus on the task at hand to distract her from the memory of her dream replaying in her mind. Niamh lost herself in the task. The last recipe was a medicine for a patient’s heart condition, though some of her handwriting had become smudged over the last hours. Niamh could make out the most important ingredient, though. Foxgloves. Easy enough. Foxgloves would do the trick, allowing for the patient’s heart to settle if just the right amount was used. Any amount larger than a drop would result in a heart attack;

a result of the poisonous nature of the flower. Her hand paused over a bottle of foxglove oil that had already been sitting near her discard pile. Did I already add it? The last few minutes had been a blur. Each recipe seemed to blend in to the next, and her normally sharp memory was failing her, It’s laying out here on the table... but did I add it to another potion already? Though her hand wavered, as if remembering the motions, she shook her head. I would know if I had already added it. She added a drop to the mixture, Pushing away any other second guesses, she tightened the top of the bottle and sealed it for delivery. As she did this, Maewyn popped her head through the door with a bright smile on her face. Niamh groaned inwardly, shoving the recently sealed medicines into a small box to give to the courier. "Yes, Maewyn?" She asked, her back still to the door. The younger mage trotted to her side, carefully watching her as she packed the box, each movement more urgent. Maewyn eyed her face, her nose scrunching. "Are you alright, Niamh?" She asked, noticing her irritation, no doubt. That was a first. "Yes!" Niamh threw her hands up in frustration. "I'm fine." Maewyn's nose scrunched further. "You don't look fine." "I know! I know!" Niamh slammed the bottle, the heart medicine that she'd just made, on the counter. It shattered under her hand, sending liquid spilling across the table and down to the floor. Niamh didn't usually curse, but she felt its fire brimming on her lips as the two women stood staring at the mess. Frustrated tears finally sprung to her eyes. What's wrong with me? Maewyn watched the liquid drip from the edge of the table with her, her eyes wide. Niamh thought, at first, that it was because of her behavior. But then she saw that her eyes were still on the ruined medicine. The bottle of foxglove oil stood tall and untouched, the purple liquid inside still and calm. Maewyn turned to her then, playing with the foxglove oil between her hands, as if weighing it and thinking intently on its contents. "What-" "Niamh, how much of this did you use?" Maewyn asked

uncharacteristically quietly. The air between them was sober. "Just a drop, like the recipe calls for-" Niamh replied frantically. Her hand flew to the paper that was now stained with purple medicine, sitting discarded near the box on the table. Her eyes scanned down the list, landing on the last medicine that she'd made. With a growing horror, she realized that foxglove didn't appear anywhere on it. Her breath caught in her throat. Maewyn reached for it, her own eyes scanning down the page. She saw exactly what Niamh had not. "Niamh..." Her eyes widened further. "This says flax flower. Not foxgloves." Niamh's hands shook violently, letting the paper flutter to the floor. "Did you write this?" Maewyn asked, equally as quietly. "Y-Yes... I did." Her hands came to her face, the tears that she'd been holding in all day spilling over her closed eyes. She took a deep breath. In and out. Taking her hands away from her face, she saw they were covered in deep red blood just like earlier. Niamh gasped, her breaths becoming shorter and shallower. It's not real. It's not real. Maewyn stood awkwardly, apparently not seeing the blood on the healer's hands even as its warmth lingered on her skin. Another glance and it was gone again. They sat like that in silence for what seemed like an eternity. Finally, Niamh looked up at Maewyn through hazy eyes. "Please don't tell Master Hael." She said, her voice weak. Maewyn grinned conspiratorially, all seriousness forgotten. “Tell him what?” Niamh smiled despite herself. "Maewyn." Maewyn turned toward her own work at her desk. “I didn’t see anything.” Some time later, a knock sounded at her- their- door. Niamh was decidedly not in the mood for any visitors, but unfortunately Maewyn answered it. Niamh bit down any hope that a blond head would appear, instead, it was only a red one. "Oh good, you're both here." Hael sounded about as pleased as he normally did, which was not very much at all. "I hope you've finished that order of medicine because you'll be taking it out early."

Finally, a relief. A brief escape from the white-haired nuisance that followed her every step. Niamh inwardly chided herself for that thought, especially after what Maewyn had just done for her not even hours before. It would at least be a welcome distraction from her sleepless nights at home. Niamh and Maewyn briefly met glances, Niamh silently trying to say “Remember what you promised.” Niamh stepped away from her work table. "Yes, Master, I can leave by the morning." "Both of you." Nevermind. Maewyn was immediately delighted, her excitement making her jumpy like water in a hot skillet. "Oh! Thank you, Master! I haven't had the chance to explore yet. Where are we going? Is it somewhere interesting? Somewhere warmer, maybe?" Hael seemed equally as irritated by her sudden burst of energy. "There won't be any exploring. You're taking it to the next town over and coming straight back." The last two words were edged with a particular sternness, and not aimed at Niamh. At least it's a short trip. Niamh had the distinct feeling that the amount of time spent with Maewyn in the wilderness would be directly correlated to the likelihood that some disaster would befall them. Hael seemed to silently agree with this prediction, adding as he turned to leave: "I expect you both home by tomorrow evening. Please stop by my house when you return." The dubious look on his face seemed to add an unspoken "so I can make sure you're both still alive." Thanks for the vote of confidence. Niamh thought grumpily. Maewyn was entirely undeterred. She scurried from the cottage excitedly muttering about packing plenty of warm clothes, leaving master and apprentice staring at each other in silence. Niamh did her best to keep her face neutral and stuffed down any impulse to confess her earlier mistakes with the medicine. She wouldn't be surprised if Hael knew just from looking at her. "You know she's not intentionally trying to ruin your life, Niamh." Hael said flatly after a moment. She shifted uncomfortably. "I know." A tight answer. Curses, why could he always see through her facades? "Do you?" He raised an eyebrow.

No. "Yes." Hael hummed, unconvinced. "I trust that you'll return on time, having accomplished what I asked." He turned to leave again, adding over his shoulder, "With your fellow apprentice." Niamh bowed stiffly, her face willingly blank. "Yes, sir." Her sour mood, predictably, didn't improve for the rest of the day.

24 NIAMH SAT ATOP ALVYSS in an even worse mood than she’d been in yesterday. Maewyn trotted alongside her on her own mount, borrowed from the guard’s stables. From the stiff and uncomfortable way the young Corseilian sat in the saddle, Niamh could tell that she wasn’t accustomed to riding as most Eirans were. This didn't deter her from jabbering on like a talkative raven, however. “So then we were sitting there, and the waves were getting higher, and the boy I was with...Jean, I think his name was? I don’t remember. It’s been so long. He was so handsome, though-“ Niamh stared straight ahead, doing her best to block out the incessant squawking of her companion. Her hand reached instinctively to check the ropes and straps holding the small wooden sleigh to Alvyss’s saddle. Three large boxes of medicine slid along behind them, strapped securely to the sleigh by Niamh’s own hand. She didn't trust Maewyn to secure them as to not fall off at the first rock that bumped underneath it. Each box carried enough medicine to carry the village through a strain of influenza sweeping through the population for the entire deep winter. Though the trip was not long, and healers could be sent there without much trouble, Hael’s firm philosophy was in teaching people how to help themselves before resorting to healers. Between her and Maewyn, it had taken them three days of grinding and mixing, pouring healing magic into each bottle as a binding agent, labeling and painstakingly packing every unit to survive the three hour ride from Ahealarth. Three hours that were increasingly seeming longer. “He had black hair and it was sooo curly. Curlier than yours. I loved running my hand through it, it was like a sheep’s wool or maybe more like wheat? He always used to say that my hair made

him think of starlight, or the foam on the ocean waves. Ugh, so charming. Anyway-“ Niamh allowed herself a curt sigh, and tried to focus on the heavy thuds of the horse’s huge, furry hooves on the packed snow of the road. Or the whistle of the soft winds through the evergreen boughs. Anything to drown Maewyn out. “So the waves are getting higher, and I could tell he was getting nervous. The wind was blowing so hard, everything was flying away. But I had been looking forward to that picnic and he was going to stay. But the sandwiches we made were so good- “ Why is Hael subjecting me to this torment? Niamh lamented silently. As they’d begun their journey three hours earlier, Niamh had made the fatal mistake of smiling politely at the beginning of Maewyn’s story. Apparently, that had been encouragement enough. Niamh barely remembered where this story began and ended, as Maewyn had filled it with enough rabbit-trails to make actual rabbits’ heads spin. Hael is obviously trying to prove a point. The logical side of her knew this. Or he’s trying to punish me for something. That was a very real possibility too. Alvyss huffed beneath her. Though only two hours lay between them and their destination, Niamh realized with a measure of dread that her stomach was empty. The two girls came upon a small mountain. Though “small” was a relative term in comparison to the other ragged and jutting peaks of Eira, it was sizable enough to warrant a tunnel to be drilled through the middle to save travelers the trouble of spending another two hours going over it. Mages past made this opening; Niamh could tell from the clean lines and lack of rubble laying about. She admired their handiwork as she and Maewyn passed through it effortlessly. On the other side was a pleasant clearing, and Niamh could hear the giggling sound of a river nearby. “Let’s rest here a moment.” Niamh announced, purposely cutting through Maeywn’s babbling, and pulled Alvyss to a slow stop. The bottles inside the boxes jingled. He wandered around aimlessly, as if he'd lived in the castle his entire life. She did her best to be as inconspicuous as possible, which was not too hard as Fane was not the most observant person in the

world, she realized. He was also rather predictable. A welcome change from being around Maewyn so often. After a few nights, she felt that she'd seen enough of his patterns to feel confident in following him. She’d never followed anyone in her life. Nythaniel was always on to her if she ever tried anything sneaky when they were younger, so she eventually gave up trying. Niamh chose the longest, darkest cloak she owned, and set out in pursuit close behind her target. Fane exchanged greetings with the guard as he passed. She recognized him. His name was Bannister, and he was one of the youngest guards on staff. Niamh beamed at him as she approached. "Good evening." She said brightly. Bannister nodded and smiled back, his wrinkle-less face brightening at the sight of her. "Evening, Miss Niamh. Where are you heading at this late hour?" "Oh," Niamh hesitated. It hadn't occurred to her to have a cover story this early in the game. "I'm making a house call." She lied, "One of the townspeople needed a healer and I was up late, so I thought I would go." Fortunately, Bannister bought it. The guilt of lying was soon replaced with the sense of excitement that she’d been successful. And that’s why they put him at the back gate. Niamh thought wryly. He waved enthusiastically to her as she walked away. Fane's height and messy head of hair was a beacon against the snowy backdrop, so it was not hard to track him into the city. Niamh ducked around corners, making sure to be far enough away from him that her boots wouldn't echo too loudly on the stone road. Fane didn’t stop, nor waver from his path, and continued straight past the wealthier sections of the city. Past the closed shops and high-end taverns that were open later than some of the others. The only sounds were the flicker of the streetlamps and the occasional whistle of the wind over the buildings. As they walked into the more populated areas, where the shops and taverns were open late into the evening, more people appeared. Most were businessmen that were enjoying their evening after a long day's work, though some of their businesses were more dubious in nature than others. Niamh was relieved to have more consistent cover, though, and she blended into the crowds quite well in her dark blue cloak. She pulled her hood over her head and tucked in her braid. Fane never looked back to check over his shoulder.

27 FANE DONNED HIS COWL, making it harder to follow him, and obscuring his gray eyes. The same eyes that darted around warily every few minutes, though never behind him. Still, Niamh wasn’t accustomed to this shady business and kept dodging for corners and doorways. On one occasion, she nearly shrieked as a snowrat scurried from behind a barrel down the alley. Fane didn’t hear her clap a hand over her mouth. As he delved deeper and deeper into the city, passing by less and less reputable establishments, dread began rising in Niamh’s throat. The crowded streets of the heart of the city gave way to alleys lurking with con men and tavern brawlers. He wasn’t wandering aimlessly this time. He was going down to the docks on purpose. A moment later, just as she almost lost sight of her target, Fane ducked into the warmly lit tavern doors to his right. Niamh cringed inwardly. Ugh, I wish I had illusion magic right now. Never in her life had she been attracted to these kinds of places. But if I don't, I won't know the truth. She waited outside for half a moment before following him inside. The strong, sharp smell of ale struck her nose first, followed by the repulsive odor of sweat and grime. Her mouth twisted in disgust and she brought a protective hand to her nose. Her hood remained on her head, despite the heat of the fireplace and the many bodies inside. Niamh took up a spot near the door, leaning against the wall and keeping an eye out for her target. Burly, rough looking men sat in the corners, at every booth and table, women draped across their laps. Barmaids scurried to and fro, delivering tall tankards of overflowing ale. The floor was sticky with it, and the dim lighting hid the grime covering every surface so well that Niamh might have sworn it was some twisted magic’s

work. Fane sat at the bar, his own cloak now slung over what looked to be some sort of weapon on his back, creating an awkward silhouette. Most of the men there were drunk off of their heels, so no one seemed to notice. Another two men sat with Fane, one of them dressed in heavy furs and sporting a rough looking demeanor judging from the way his large hands handled the person between him and Fane. The middle man was dressed entirely in black, and didn't have a coat or any indication that he ever did. Niamh couldn't hear whatever they said over the din of the tavern. Between groups of rowdy young men swapping hunting stories, and the bustle of all the business going on behind the bar, there was hardly any chance of hearing anything. They talked at the bar while Niamh did her best to keep hidden. Mages, at least in the capital city, didn't tend to mix with lowlifes as these. Niamh wouldn’t be meeting any friendly eyes tonight. She backed herself against the opposite wall, to observe the room. No one looked her way. She relaxed a bit, leaning into the firm wooden wall, resting in the protection of her cape. Several moments passed, possibly nearly an hour by her reckoning, and Niamh's legs were already growing tired of standing. Niamh dared not sit down, for fear of someone sitting next to her. She sighed, letting her eyes close for a moment. "Can I get you anything, miss?" Niamh jumped out of her skin. "Uh..Uhm." She fumbled, self- consciously checking if her hood was still over her face. "No, no thank you, I'm okay." She responded, searching for the source of the question. She found it in the soft brown eyes of the barmaid standing next to her. Judging on her height and the fact that there was very little to fill out the corset she wore under the apron tied at her waist, she looked no older than fifteen, Niamh guessed. Her mousey brown hair was tied back in a half-ponytail, and she had a refreshingly unremarkable face. Niamh spent so much time around the beautiful courtiers and nobles of the palace that she was immediately at ease being around a normal person again. The barmaid’s dress, though clean and in good-repair, judging from the patches dotting it, was old and threadbare, a shawl covering her shoulders. She held a tray aloft in her hands. The girl forced a smile, her eyes devoid of any mirth. “That’s

quite alright, miss. Please don’t hesitate to ask if you change your mind.” As she turned to leave, something tugged at the deep places of Niamh’s heart. Before she realized what she was doing, her hand gently reached for the girl’s arm. The girl instinctively jerked at her touch, to which Niamh allowed her hand to drop respectfully. “I’m so sorry to intrude, but...” Niamh started. The girl turned her confused eyes to her. “What’s your name?” Niamh had no idea why such a question was even coming from her mouth, but something continued tugging at her spirit. You aren’t ever coming back to this place. Don’t get involved. She thought to herself. The girl didn’t answer for a long moment, the raucous noises of the tavern hall drowned the silence between them. Niamh’s awkwardness nearly overtook her, and she opened her mouth to apologize and move to another spot. Just as she was about to, the girl averted her eyes to her worn flat slippers. “Elise.” She answered at last. “And I beg your pardon, miss, but I must be returning to my-“ “How long have you been here, Elise?” Niamh asked, that tug inside of her unrelenting. She hesitated, lowering her tray under her arm. “My uncle runs this place, and I don’t know where my parents are. So... For as long as I can remember.” As the tray was lowered, the shawl slipped from her shoulder, revealing the bruise that ran from shoulder to elbow, purple and yellow and brown mingling in a stormy pattern. Elise noticed Niamh’s assessing eye and covered it again self-consciously. “N-Now I really must be going ba-“ “Would you like me to heal that for you?” Niamh asked quietly, casting a cautious glance at the man standing behind the bar counter. The young woman looked fully at her then, weighing the possibility of a choice in her mind. Her eyes narrowed in suspicion. “What’s your price? What do you want?” Niamh extended a hand with her gloved palm exposed, the healing magic already pooling in it. “There’s no cost. Simply a favor from me to you.” Elise visibly weighed her options, setting down the tray on a nearby table. She extended a tentative arm to Niamh, eyeing her with distrust.

Delicately rolling the sleeve from Elise’s wounded shoulder, Niamh laid a gentle hand on the expansive bruise. Elise sighed with relief as the skin faded back into a healthy pink tone, Niamh’s fine tendrils of magic repairing and soothing. It bumped against something else, something familiar that sang in harmony with her magic. Niamh gave the girl a knowing smile. “If you had the proper training, you could do this yourself.” She whispered, reveling at the shocked realization that washed over Elise’s face. She looked as if she was restraining herself from asking every question that had probably been burning inside of her for years. “I-I don’t think-“ She glanced back at the hard-faced man running the bar at the back of the room. “I don’t think I can..Find training, I mean.” Niamh nodded understandingly, rolling the sleeve back over her now-healed shoulder. “My door is always open for you, if you wish to learn such things. I'm an apprentice." Niamh heard the pride creeping into her voice, and did her best to shove it down. Pride was not befitting a healer, for sure. She picked up the discarded tray and handed it back to Elise. “My name is Niamh Sagesinger. Please come and find me at the castle if you change your mind.” The barmaid dipped clumsily. “Thank you, miss-“ A sheepish smile. “Niamh.” And with that, she scurried away to continue serving patrons, casting a thankful glance as she went. Niamh turned her attention back to the bar she was supposed to be watching. The taller man that Fane had been meeting with was now standing, near the doorway where another man stood conversing tensely with him. The taller man’s face remained obscured, though the new arrival was dressed completely in a tight- fitting black tunic, wicked knives hanging from his belt. A strange emblem was crudely sewn into one arm of his tunic- an anatomical heart shape, though it looked to be made of crystal. It was broken in half, one side higher than the other, with a spattering of crystal shards in between. Niamh stared at it for a long moment. He was greasier, smaller, and looked at Fane’s companion with a growing fear washing over his face. As Fane rose from the booth, the greasy-looking man startled and bolted out of the front

door. Fane and his hooded companion followed suit, close behind on his heels. Niamh leapt to a run, barely stopping the heavy door as it flew back to hit her in the face, diving into the icy air of the streets again. Her boots pounded against the stone, her hood flying from her braided hair, causing it to come loose and slap against her back. Ice formed on her eyelashes as she pushed her way through the mist, freezing to her skin under her shirt beneath her coat. I’m not meant for running. She thought miserably. Fane’s hood also flew from his head, and it was an effort to keep him in her sight. He'd grown stronger, gained more stamina, in the weeks since she met him in the forest. Now she began to understand why. He kept up with his taller, stronger companion with ease as they sprinted through the labyrinth of alleys and back doors. Niamh lost sight of them quickly. Stopping for only a moment to catch her breath, Niamh sent a tendril of raw magic out ahead of her, to keep track of them even if her eyes couldn’t. After what seemed like an eternity of burning lungs and straining muscles, Niamh skidded to a halt at the entrance to one of the many back alleys of the docks. She was met with the sight of Fane- the librarian's assistant- poised with a taut bowstring, an arrow aimed to the head of the man that his companion was currently interrogating against a wall. The taller man growled something in a low voice too quiet for Niamh to hear, grasping the criminal's collar in a fist. A bearded chin emerged from his hood. Fane's bowstring groaned at the strain, his silvery gray eyes locked on his target, not seeing the young healer watching him from a short distance away. The sound of a rock hard fist finding a face echoed through the alley. Niamh winced at the second blow. Tempted as she was to rush in; to stop the violence, as was her nature, she dared not move from where her feet were firmly planted on the icy cobblestones. At the third blow, the criminal crumpled to the ground. Niamh heard a faint curse. Fane lowered his weapon, keeping a hand on the feathers of an arrow, making a comment on "going too far again." She wished the wind wasn't so loud, as it carried away any other words being said. Against her best judgment, Niamh stepped from the shadows.

"So this is where you've been running off to all these nights." Both men whirled to face her. Fane stretching the bowstring in alarm, the taller man reaching for a weapon at his belt. Fane's eyes widened in surprise, nearly dropping the bow from his slackened hands as he stood from the defensive crouch he'd been in. "Niamh. What..?" He glanced between her and the unconscious man behind him, shame crawling up his face. "What are you doing here?" "I could ask you the same question." She shot back, her eyes flaring. Why couldn’t he have told me the truth? The other man straightened. He was tall, his broad muscled chest straining against his black shirt, his belt laden with multiple knives with handles of antler, two axes slung across his back. Though the forest green hood he wore obscured his eyes, his beard was a deep rusty brown and neatly cropped to his angular, strong jaw. "Niamh?" A deep voice rumbled in surprise, her name smooth as silk over his tongue. "Niamh Sagesinger?" She started as a large hand threw back his hood, revealing smoldering brown eyes as deep as tilled earth. Strands of his long rusty brown hair had slipped from the knot he kept it in, falling in front of those eyes that she hadn't seen in seven years. "ROHYR?" As Fane watched, recognition washed over Niamh's face. Going against every assumption that Fane had built, his usually belligerent companion laughed suddenly and rushed toward Niamh. Before she could react, he scooped her into a warm embrace, lifting her small boots from the ground. She squealed with delight as he spun her once. An emotion he couldn't name rose in his stomach. He quickly swallowed it. Fane had never seen her laugh so freely. And who was Whitestar- Rohyr, apparently- to Niamh that she was welcoming of his touch? He shoved the arrow he never fired back into its quiver, slinging the bow roughly back over his shoulder with a low grumble.

She embraced him tightly, her head resting so casually on his broad chest. As they pulled apart, Whitestar scruffed her braided head with an affectionate hand. "You're so much taller than last I saw you." She marveled, having to tilt her head to meet his eyes. Whitestar towered over her by at least a full head. He grinned. He can smile? "I could say the same for you, Little Sparrow." Oh, we have pet names too? Fane suppressed a bitter comment, instead readjusting his cloak to cover his arms again against the equally bitter cold. The prince strode toward them, straightening as he walked. Neither of them acknowledged him standing there. "How's Nythaniel doing these days?" Whitestar asked, folding his arms over his chest. Whoever that is. Fane thought with irritation. "Oh, he's off on the king's business." Her finger curled around the neckline of her cloak as she swung it back on "He's been gone for months now." Whitestar's face darkened at that, an expression that Fane was far more familiar with, but he didn't comment further. "Well..." Mirth appeared in his eyes again, smiling down at Niamh. "I never expected you to subject yourself to these slums, Little Sparrow." He’s a completely different person around her. Fane mused with irritation. "You and me both." He muttered, swallowing the rebuke rising in his tone. "Ah...Well.." Niamh fingered a strand of her loose hair, tucking it behind an ear. "I wanted to make sure Fane wasn't getting himself hurt somewhere." She tossed an apologetic look toward him from under long lashes, which melted his rising temper in an instant. Of course. As if remembering herself, her eyes widened. "Oh, and by the way, Fane. This is Rohyr. But... I suppose you knew that already." She paused, realizing that introductions were useless at this point. "He and I - Ah... Our families were good friends when we were growing up." I guess that explains the pet name. "It's late for you to be out here, Niamh." Whitestar noted, concern in his voice. Fane was shocked. He's concerned about someone? Who have I been spending all this time with? He scratched his beard, looking between her and the criminal they had all but forgotten still in a heap on the cobblestones.

Niamh gave the two men an incredulous look. Fane stared at the abandoned criminal with Rohyr. "The least we could do for the man is to take him somewhere warm." Fane said, casting an admonishing glare at his companion. The woodsman merely shrugged. Fane stepped between them to Niamh’s side, resisting the urge to shove Whitestar away, offering his arm gracefully. "Let us at least escort you home to make up for dragging you all the way out here." He gave her his most charming smile, and felt a sliver of satisfaction at the way her hand slid through his arm. He resisted looking at Whitestar's expression, and instead turned with her back toward where she’d come. The clatter of a body being tossed into the nearby tavern's back door sounded through the alley and Whitestar stepped behind them in the seconds that followed. "He's warm now." He said simply, sheathing the remainder of his weapons with a smirk.

Maire THE EDGES OF HER VISION were dark. They always were. And perhaps they always had been. The man that had vowed to be her husband stood nearby, though she felt no warmth from his body and she gave no warmth from her heart. "Yes, commissioner, that will be all." His voice answered some question she didn't hear. She looked over at him, met those golden sunset eyes with her own, and saw no love behind them. If she couldn’t get love, approval would do. Her aunt would have agreed, in that same slithering graceful tone that she often heard in her dreams. "I'm glad you liked that suggestion." She heard her own voice say, though it felt like someone else was speaking. Airem nodded. He reached for her hand, though she moved it behind her skirts. Maire couldn't think to reply past the pounding in her head, nor the weakness that suddenly pervaded her every sense. Darkness encroached, greeting her like an old friend. Her vision narrowed even further. Before she could stop herself, Maire fell to the floor. A vague shattering of a nearby vase echoed near her head before the world was thrown into darkness. A tree appeared, looming above her head as she lay sprawled across its gnarled roots. The red of her gown spread downward, dripping on to an intricately gilded marble floor. The room was filled with light, all of the golden branches reaching outward into the palace beyond. A palace that was open-aired, bright, and joyful. It didn't even occur to her as odd that she knew that it was, indeed, a palace. Nor was it odd to her that the tree appeared to be made of gold.

It was as if she'd been here her whole life. A royal family entered. The king and queen were arm in arm, while their youngest son ran to where she sat among the roots. The same light of the tree shone in their golden hair. The young boy looked up at her as if she had hung the stars. He was saying something, though she could not hear the world. Everything sounded muffled and far away. Her own mouth moved to reply, but it was not her voice. The young prince laughed and scampered around the tree. He returned two or three times before Maire realized that this was a regular game that she - or he, the young man that had replied to the boy earlier - often played. When her eyes fell on the blond king and queen again, the queen was nowhere to be found. The king stood alone, his expression darkening with every second that passed. The young boy grew too, passing years in mere seconds. Vines and thick leaves climbed the glass panels of the whole room, choking the light from outside. The only light that remained was the tree, and even that was slowly fading. The gnarled roots she sat on moved outward, strangling the edges of the room, even as they continued to fade and the gold color became black and ashen. Through the openings between the vines that were left, Maire saw fire. The city surrounding the great palace was burning. When she turned her head back toward the center of the room, the once bright, once young boy was now an adult. His sword was at her throat even as tears streamed down his bloodied face. Maire's eyes opened to see her husband's hand in her own. He was turned away from her, his black hair obscuring the strong jaw behind it. He seemed to be speaking to the small group of healers that had gathered near her bedside. She took her cold, pale hand from his warm, strong one. He turned toward her then, with a flicker of hope behind the concern on his face. They stared silently at one another for a moment. She thought he almost reached a hand to feel her forehead, but refrained. "I don't need you here." She said flatly through the weakness in her voice. "Very well." Airem's small smile cracked. "Take care of her, please." He said to the healers before striding from the room. Of course he would leave. A small twinge of longing stirred in her

chest before she shoved it down. He always will. One of the healers approached her nervously. “Get out." Maire rasped. The young healer flustered. "But, your Majesty-" "If you stay in here a moment longer, I will not be the one needing a healer." Maire could hardly stop the threats coming out of her mouth. No one can know. You show no weakness. The healer nodded silently, backing out of the room with her companions. "Y-yes, majesty." With that, the door closed, and Maire was left alone in her private room. She pulled the covers over her head and was enveloped in darkness once more. Though no more dreams came to her that night.

28 A LOUD, PERSISTENT knock sounded at his door. Fane’s eyes cracked open, exposing his sleepy mind to the harsh sunlight determined to find its way in. He grumbled. Who could be bothering me at this hour? He rolled from the bed, grunting as he hit the cold floor. Though he was still learning the sun’s positions and how to read them, from where it stood in the sky, it looked to be about 6 in the morning. After he and Whitestar delivered Niamh safely to the castle the night before, he’d gone right back out on Whitestar’s orders. They hadn’t caught anyone else, and Fane didn’t return to the castle until several hours later. If he could have had the presence of mind to calculate, he would have only had two hours of sleep by the time the unwelcome sound of knocking came to his door. His hand missed the door handle when he reached for it. Another ear-splitting knock. “I’m coming.” Fane muttered, his voice husky from sleep. He finally successfully swayed to his feet and opened the door with a bit more roughness than he intended. There was Maewyn, fully dressed and bouncing on the balls of her feet. “Fane! Good morning!” Her bright voice seemed to send stars across his eyes, booming into the small space. He groaned and held his forehead, not quite fully aware of what was happening. “Maewyn.” He croaked, closing his eyes against the relentless sunlight thrashing his pupils. “What do you want?” He only wished he could close his ears. “Well! I was thinking that I needed to take a trip around town today and I thought you would come with me! So here I am to retrieve you!” She laughed, usually a cheery sound now only shrill and grating against his nerves. He squinted at her. “Apparently I have no choice in this

matter?” Maewyn’s answering smile looked a bit too eager, crazed even. “No! Not at all.” She pushed her way passed him, and was soon banging through his drawers and rummaging around in his clothes. “Ooo, this one is nice! You picked this out yourself?” She proudly displayed a dark blue vest, delicately embroidered at the hem with silver leaves. There were a few snags in the thread, as if it had been done by an amateur seamstress training in her craft. Fane could only watch as she tossed it at him, along with a gray linen shirt and black breeches. “Get dressed, sleepy head!” Maewyn scurried outside, closing his door behind him with a bang. He dressed quickly, knowing that any second wasted was one that she could barge in again. Only a moment later, he joined her in the hallway outside. He tugged the vest over his shirt and shoved his hunting knife in its sheath with a grumble. If Maewyn noticed his displeasure, she didn’t comment. Her voice only seemed to gain volume as they continued up the stairs to what Fane assumed was leading to the front doors. Instead, she led him up three more flights, passing the foyer and continuing into the finer rooms of the castle. The stone hallways of the servants’ quarters gave way to elegant carpets and walls of gold-laid ice. Down a wide hallway flanked with tall windows, she stopped in front of an elegantly carved wooden door. “Who are we-?” He started, cut off by another one of her excited knocks on this new door. A groan sounded from inside. She knocked again, this time louder and more relentless. “You said we could go to town today!” She nearly yelled through the door, making Fane wince. No response. “Okay then! I’m coming in! I warned you!” She pushed her way into the darkened room. Dark red curtains blocked out much of the sunlight streaming in the tall, curved windows. A fireplace smoldered with the dying embers of last night’s fire on one wall, and across from it was a four poster bed hung with a canopy matching the curtains. The room was a modest size, with enough space for the bed, a dresser, and a small closet. There were some comfortable looking sitting chairs in front of the fireplace, and short shelves nearby. The room was kept neat, and it was unassuming for the most

part. The only thing indicating who it belonged to was a tall staff of curving wood leaning against the bedpost. Fane’s gut clenched in embarrassment. Niamh’s room. The owner of this modest living space was indeed curled up in a mound of blankets. Her auburn waves were spread out across the pillows, emerging like vines from under the covers. The mound rose and fell softly, to which Maewyn responded by leaping on top of it. Niamh grunted in annoyance. “Maewyn...” She groaned, her voice thick with sleep. “Time to get up! You said we could take a trip around town today!” Even though Maewyn acted every bit Niamh's junior by four years as she was, as she poked and prodded various places over Niamh’s blanket hoard. “Go away...” Niamh moaned in a whiney voice. This brought the corners of his mouth up in amusement, even as he was backing his way toward the door. Gentlemen never entered a lady’s room without her permission. Maewyn watched him go with a mischievous twinkle in her eye. “Aw, Fane, where are you going? Don’t you want to help Niamh pick out her outfit?” Maewyn did nothing to check her volume, even as the curtains swallowed much of the echo. “Fane?” Niamh’s voice sounded panicked from under the covers. Maewyn looked between them, her fox-like smile returning. Fane took this opportunity to turn on his heels and stand right outside in the hall. It didn’t matter what Maewyn was going to tease him with. After sounds of bare feet shuffling along a carpet and some hushed protests, Maewyn promptly burst from the room with a giggle. Fane could hardly guess what went on in there. Only a couple minutes later, Niamh emerged. She wore a dress similar to Fane’s vest. It was also dark blue, with a pair of white embroidered fawns meeting noses at the point at the top of the bodice. Fane guessed that Maewyn picked it for her. Niamh’s long hair was brushed, but hung around her like a curtain to her thighs. Fane had never seen her hair down before. “Blue must be your favorite color, Niamh, because you have way more of it in there than any normal person does.” Maewyn remarked with a playful roll of her eyes. “I think your perception of what normal people’s closets may look like is a bit skewed, Maewyn, considering who you’re related

to.” Niamh muttered, something akin to grumpiness in her sleepy voice. Fane’s grin returned, absolutely relishing in this glimpse of an unguarded Niamh. She shoved a handful of hair pins into Maewyn’s hand without a word, and set to braiding her hair into four plaits, curling them in a tightly woven crown and pinning it securely. The whole process took several minutes, as Fane watched her in amazement. It was like a new kind of magic. He could now see her eyes, still half-open from sleepiness, and gazing straight ahead at nothing in particular. She seemed to have even forgotten his presence. She didn’t say another word to either of them as Maewyn prattled on, greeting every guard they came across as loudly as possible. The pair walked in silence behind their attendant, all the way down into the center of the city. As they reached the shops that Maewyn was so intent on visiting at the early hour, Fane could see why she wanted to get a head start. The bakeries in the center square wafted rich smells of every kind of baked good imaginable. Fresh meat was being hung in the butcher’s windows, new books being displayed in book shop windows, and the kirk bells pealed their first chime of the day joyfully. His spirits lightened. How different it was to spend time in the city in the daylight again, not to worry about members of the Fade hiding around corners. A sidelong glance at Niamh’s face showed him that she was not enjoying this excursion as much as he was, and he imagined that it was because Maewyn’s carrying-on was now directed mostly to her. Fane spied a young dressmaker, a tall young man with a mess of black curls, repairing a sign outside of his shop. Without appearing too obvious, he steered their little group toward the young man. “Maewyn.” He addressed the young mage, interrupting some speech about how Niamh kept her bottles too organized. Fane gestured with a sweeping hand toward the unsuspecting young man perched on the ladder that looked at Maewyn appreciatively. “Perhaps our dressmaker friend here has some new creations that you might like to browse?” Maewyn eyed the boy up and down like a cat inspecting a mouse. “What kind of dresses do you make?” “Would...? “The young man started hesitatingly, cutting an unsure glance at Fane who smirked at him knowingly. “I can show

you...” His sentence trailed off as Maewyn eagerly made for his store front. He clamored down from the ladder and led her inside, leaving Fane alone with Niamh in the street. The early morning sun was just starting to flood into the square, glinting cheerfully off of the store windows and the fresh snow piled in the corners of alleys and stairwells. Niamh’s shoulders seemed to relax and she yawned. They let the silence wash over them for a moment. Birds chirped sweetly in the rafters. Finally, when he could bear the awkward silence no longer, Fane took the liberty of taking Niamh’s hand and pulling her toward one of the bakeries across the square. If she didn’t like this gesture, she made no move to protest. A bell jingled above the door as they stepped inside. Warm, buttery smells of pastries and breads floated around them.
