The shelves in the glass case were filled to the brim with lebkuchen, loaves of dusty brown bread, cakes, sweet rolls, bowls of candied nuts of various kinds, streusel, and even little bears and eagles made from colorful marzipan. This seemed to bring a smile to Niamh’s face, and she peered into the case with an eager anticipation. “Pick whatever you like.” He told her, bringing his earnings from his pocket. Delivering criminals with Rohyr was turning out to be lucrative for more than just his muscles, he'd decided, and Fane was struck with a rush of pleasure to see Niamh turn to him in surprise. “Are you sure?” She asked, tentatively. He merely nodded, beaming at the excited way she ran her finger along each line of the case. “You can pick something for me too. I haven’t gotten a chance to try many Eiran pastries.” He said, his hands in his pockets. She nodded wistfully, speaking with the baker in a quiet tone. He handed over two items wrapped in paper a moment later, and Fane paid him. They walked out with them in hand, and Niamh led him to sit on the stairs overlooking the dress shop. Maewyn could be seen chattering to the young man through the window, his face looking increasingly weary as he realized that there was no escape for him now. Niamh handed him a warm, spiced bread. It smelled of nutmeg and cinnamon, topped with a sweet glaze that smelled of maple sap. Fane took a bite of the heavenly pastry, letting its warmth and

freshness sink into his stomach. He could feel her watching him to gauge his reaction. He nodded pleasantly. An awkward moment of silence fell between them again. “How’s your arm doing?” Niamh asked, her voice more guarded than before. Fane grimaced. He’d almost forgotten about that night. “It’s-” He cleared his throat, “It’s fine.” Niamh paused. “You were wounded when you were out with Rohyr. There was no training accident.” “No.” Fane looked at her then, “You’re right. I’m sorry I lied.” Niamh watched him with a firm set to her mouth. Her pastry remained uneaten in her hand. “Don’t lie to me again.” She said. All the other things he was keeping secret weighed just behind his tongue. Some part of him wished he could confide in her, tell her everything about who he was and where he came from. But there was no knowing how she would react. Or how much danger she might be in if she knew. Instead, Fane merely nodded. “How long have you been doing this? How did you meet Rohyr?” Niamh asked, the suspicion in her voice replaced with curiosity. “It was that night I got lost at the docks.” Fane said. The corner of his mouth twitched up, “The first time. He helped me find my way back to the castle, and he-” Niamh couldn’t know all the reasons Fane chose to follow Whitestar. He bit his tongue. “He needed help bringing criminals in to the guards.” Niamh was thoughtful for a moment. “I’ve never thought Rohyr to be the vigilante type.” She said, studying the paper in her hands. As Fane was about to ask what she meant, Niamh continued. “Just...Don’t do anything reckless while you’re out with him. I don’t want you to get hurt.” She turned sincere eyes to him. Anything he might have said died on his tongue. “I won’t.” Fane reassured her. Liar. Satisfied, her eyes turned to the birds that were flitting among the high windows of the kirk. The corners of her mouth twitched up like the tail feathers of the little yellow creatures, and Fane caught another glimpse of that far-away serenity that he sometimes saw in her eyes. “Do you like birds?” It was the only question that came to mind. Fane was trying desperately to get Niamh on to more pleasant, less

intrusive topics. She turned to him in surprise for the second time that hour. “Well... Yes. I suppose. They are just so small and fragile, but they fly anywhere they wish and see things we can only dream about.” Niamh answered, her voice wistful. “Do you want to fly anywhere you wish?” He asked, though he didn’t know why. Having grown up in court, he was trained to be constantly aware of every word that passed his lips, constantly training his body to make only the movements necessary. So as to not give away anything, not to create any sort of disturbance. Maintain the illusion of a perfectly controlled prince. Not with her, though. Something about Niamh set him at a strange ease. Even if she was a mage. Niamh hesitated, thinking over his question carefully. “I don’t think so.” Her hands clutched the roll, crinkling the paper. “But...I have never been outside of Eira.” Her eyes turned toward the distant mountains, the morning sun sparkling on the snow capped peaks. That wistful longing came over her face again, captivating him. “And I’ve always wanted to see open fields. And the ocean.” She added, “I’ve never seen a green field, actually. My family; and later my brother and I, we raised horses when I was younger and-“She stopped suddenly, catching a glimpse of Fane watching her. Blush creeped up her cheeks. “I’m sorry if this is boring you.” She said quietly. Fane shook his head, “No, please, go on.” Niamh obliged. “Um, yes, we raised horses. We would run them down in the valley, but they deserve to feel the grass.” She looked up at him, “I’ve always wondered what it would be like to ride a horse at full speed through a field. I can only imagine what that feels like...” She trailed off again, taking another dainty bite of her pastry. Fane felt a tug at his heart, like he wanted nothing more than to give that to her at the earliest possible opportunity. To allow her to mount his own stallion from the royal stables and ride alongside her as they raced through green grass under a clear sky. She turned shy eyes to him again. “That sounds silly, doesn’t it? You’re from Aridia, aren’t you?” Fane’s throat tightened. “Yes.” “Then you must have seen fields like that? Do...do people often

ride...through them?” Her eyes dropped to her pastry again. “I know it sounds silly.” She repeated, her mouth twitching to a smile. “No. No, not at all.” Fane said. “I hope that-” Their quiet moment was inevitably interrupted by Maewyn bounding over to them, a new parcel under her arm. “Niamh! Wait until you see this new dress that I just bought.” She turned a suggestive eye to Fane. “I’m sure you’ll appreciate it even more, Fane.” Fane felt Niamh stiffen next to him. He gave Maewyn his practiced smile, forced and polite, but no false enthusiasm to be found. “I’m sure it’s a lovely choice.” He said mildly. Niamh remained stiffly seated on the steps. “Since I have this new dress, I definitely need new shoes to match!” Maewyn bounced excitedly, already prancing in the direction of the cobbler. Fane exhaled and rose from the step. He offered his hand, and Niamh took it, rising to stand beside him.

29 AS THE SQUARE FILLED with more and more people, bustling in and out of shops, Fane and Niamh dutifully followed Maewyn to all the places she stopped along the way. They said little else to each other, Niamh painfully aware of Maewyn’s presence. Maewyn’s blatant flirting with Fane was starting to get to her. Though, try as she might not to think of it, she had to admit that Fane and Maewyn seemed to get along well. Her vivaciousness was a nice fit for his easy manner. He accepted everything she said with cocked smiles and amusement in his eyes. It made Niamh’s throat clench every time. After a couple hours, the sun was getting higher in the sky. They were nearing the entrance to the city, the large wooden gate looming at the end of the wide walkway. The same gate that Niamh had brought Fane through when he’d first arrived. She shook her head. I must be tired if all of this is getting to me. She thought, sneaking a glance at Fane’s profile. His pointed nose and high forehead looked aristocratic against the sun, its light giving his hair a golden sheen. I barely know him. I don’t even know where he comes from. Niamh, you’re being ridiculous. She knew she shouldn’t care so much. But the way he looked at her as they talked about her dreams of riding a horse through an open field...She cringed. What a silly thing to talk about. Maewyn really shouldn’t have awoken her so soon, she obviously couldn’t keep a guard on her mouth so early in the morning. As Fane held the door open for them into the (hopefully) final stop, the bell above the door jingled. They entered into a dimly lit apothecary, its shelves lined with pre-prepared tinctures and medicines. Dust floated in the light from the windows, giving it a homey and pleasant feeling. The owner was bent over the counter on one elbow, chatting

with customers. The shop was fairly busy for so early, as it was only reaching about 9am by that point. Maewyn knew exactly what she was looking for, and trotted up to the correct shelf to retrieve several bottles of varying ingredients that Niamh couldn't make out from the distance. She and Fane stood awkwardly near the door. The two customers at the counter, men laden with dust and slush from the roads, carrying heavy packs on their backs, talked cheerfully with the owner. No one bothered to keep their voices hushed, as she was sure that the whole town would get wind of the travelers’ news by the end of the day. “Where do you fellows come from? “ The owner asked, running a hand over his beard. Maewyn strolled up to him without a care for whatever else he may have been doing and plopped her handful of items on the counter. “We’re on the road from Corseils, delivering supplies.” One of them said, taking a swig from his flask. “Just passed through the northern half of Aridia.” Out of the corner of her eye, Fane stood rigid. Niamh perked her ears to listen closer. Maewyn rummaged around in her bag for her purse. “Strange stuff going on down there.” The other commented, shifting on his feet. Maewyn brought forth the money to pay the owner. He took it with a smile and packaged her medicines for her. The first traveler cleared his throat. “Apparently their prince has gone missing.” FANE’S GUT ROILED, and it took all of his willpower to remain standing upright. His heart was leaping forward like a deer, over and over again, and he barely heard anything else being said. “Some people think that he’s dead. Or that there never was a prince in the first place, and the king just got tired of pretending that there was.” Maewyn nodded thoughtfully, something rare for her, and thanked the owner. Fane could feel Niamh’s eyes on him, no doubt noticing how much of a statue he’d become. “Fane?” Niamh’s voice barely registered for him. It felt as if every eye was on him. The sun glinted harshly, bringing an exposing light to everything it touched. Sweat beaded on his brow.

A touch to his shoulder. “Fane?” She asked again, clearly now. He cleared his throat and sloughed her hand away. “I’m fine.” Regret immediately flashed in her eyes and in his gut. “A missing prince, huh?” Maewyn mused, glancing at the tall castle spires. They glittered in the sun like stained glass. “I haven't met a prince before. Well, except for Airem. He was a prince once, right? Corseils doesn’t have any princes to offer.” Her eyes sparkled with anticipation. Fane did his best not to hyperventilate. “What do you think a prince of Aridia even looks like?” Maewyn continued, heaving a few of her parcels onto Niamh’s arms without any sort of permission. “I bet he’s the happiest person in the whole world. Surrounded by wealth and leisure, not having to work or buy his own groceries for that matter.” She cast an annoyed glance at her pile of items, as if she wasn’t the one that dragged them all out of bed to retrieve them. “And I’ve seen his palace! It’s the biggest, most opulent thing I’ve ever seen. I got lost in their gardens when we stopped by there on the way here. It wouldn’t surprise me if he was there in the gardens with me and I never met him.” Fane did not respond. Niamh did, though, as she shifted Maewyn’s packages into a manageable stack. “That doesn’t sound like it would make anyone happy.” She said, not focusing on anything but the brown paper in her hands as she switched the larger ones to the bottom. “Just because someone is rich doesn’t mean that they aren’t lonely.” She added. Maewyn seemed to mull over that answer for half of a second before resuming her bouncing step. “Well. Even if he’s not happy, I’m sure he’s handsome. Every prince has to be handsome. It’s part of the job description.” Fane nearly choked. His presence of mind slowly returned, along with the anxious thoughts he tried so desperately not to think for so long now. If the whole kingdom knows that I'm gone, then who else might know that I'm here? Maewyn and Niamh continued leading him through the square, oblivious to the mental anguish he'd fallen into. It was stupid of me to think that I could hide forever. Is Airem going to expose me? No, he wouldn't do that.

He vaguely heard Maewyn chattering away about something else in the background. He felt Niamh's eyes on him, watching his every move with concern. I’ve neglected looking for whoever it was that tried to kill me. Maybe they have given up and are satisfied with the rumor that I'm already dead? It was a weak hope, he knew, but one he indulged without another choice. What if they figure out that I'm the prince? It's not that hard to figure out if they really think about it. Do they think about it at all? What would Niamh do if she knew? His stomach kept churning, and Maewyn kept talking, but Niamh's eyes still never left him. Fane felt the sweat drip down his back, despite the chill in the air. She must know, if she keeps looking at me like that. His chest was tight, but Fane managed to plaster a false smile on his face and stopped in his tracks. "I'm going to leave you two to it." He said, strangling any squeak in his voice. "Are you sure you're going to be alright by yourself, Fane?" Niamh asked carefully. Her hand started to reach for him before she dropped it again to her side. Fane's stomach twisted. “I'll see you later." Niamh nodded, albeit slowly and looking like she didn't want to let him go, Maewyn waved goodbye as he turned on his heels and walked out of the city. He knew Niamh's eyes followed his back until they had walked out of sight. "WHITESTAR." Fane stumbled into the clearing that he so often frequented at night. It appeared completely different in the stark daylight. I know he's here. "Whitestar!" A low groan came from one of the thicker trees spread over the edge of the clearing. If Fane didn't know any better, he would have thought it was an animal. Following the sound, he came upon the redheaded woodsman. His hair was sticking out from a deep hollow in the tree, though that was the only indication that there was anyone there. "What."

"I knew it. You do sleep here." A rustle of dried leaves and another irritated groan later, Whitestar glared at him from under a thick fur cloak. "I don't sleep here every night, you idiot. I would freeze to death." "What do you want? Why are you waking me up at this ungodly hour?" Whitestar continued. "It's already nearly noon." Whitestar rolled his eyes and looked as if he was about to decidedly ignore the interruption and go back to sleep. "I need to talk to you." “I don't need to talk to you." Fane made an irritated noise at the back of his throat. The pair were at a stand-still for several long moments. "I'll buy you breakfast." This seemed to get the man's attention. Not like he doesn't have enough money to buy it himself. Fane thought with some injustice. His small monetary sacrifice did the job, however, and Whitestar emerged from the hollow in a tower of dirt, melted slush, and dried leaves. He shook out his furs as a wolf shakes water from its haunches before stretching noisily. "Don't you have a house somewhere? A lean-to? Something?" "Shut up." Fane knew he wouldn't be getting anywhere conversationally until Whitestar had a chance to wake up and eat, so he decided not to push his luck any further.

30 WHY ON EARTH DID I ask him for help? Fane wondered to himself, with no shortage of bitterness. Whitestar, or Rohyr, as Fane knew now, sat across from him completely silent. This particular tavern was much different during the daylight hours, the dark wood looking friendlier and cozy rather than foreboding and heady with the sun streaming in. The patronage was completely changed as well, consisting of happy families out to breakfast together and cheery elders chatting over non-alcoholic drinks. Fane's eyes were still sandy from sleepiness, despite the earlier adrenaline rush that morning. Whitestar didn't look much more awake, and his red mop of hair was even more unruly than usual. The woodsman glared at him from across the table. "What's this about?" Whitestar grumbled, running a hand over his face. Fane swallowed hard and glanced around nervously, as if everyone in the room would already know his identity. Whitestar watched his eyes dart, seemingly following his paranoid gaze. "You’re far too jumpy this early in the day." He commented with an amused expression. Fane glowered at him. "At least wait until we have our food. Then I'll tell you." Whitestar watched him carefully, if irritated. "Strangely withholding today, too." Fane sighed, exasperated. He's going to make this way harder than it needs to be, I just know it. A young barmaid with dark hair brought their food. She smiled shyly at Whitestar as she set their plates on the table. He either didn’t notice or care, and merely grunted in acknowledgement. Their plates were piled high with all kinds of food: eggs, bread, different hot and cold meats, cheeses, and all manner of fruits

tumbling over one another. Whitestar started eating as soon as the food was set in front of him. He acts like he's not eaten in days. Fane thought. Fane carefully laid his napkin over his lap, and cut into a smaller piece of meat with methodical precision. The weight of Whitestar's eyes fell on him. "You're not doing yourself any favors eating like that." Fane froze with his knife mid-cut. "What makes you say that?" He said hastily, with far more paranoia than he'd intended. Whitestar didn't miss this. "Oh ho, touchy today, too." Whitestar took a huge bite of everything on his plate stuffed onto his fork. "What's wrong with you?" Fane didn't answer immediately, taking a moment to survey the room for the hundredth time. There was no one that looked like anyone of the Fade, nor did any of the patrons seem to be interested in their conversation. No one could see the tightening noose of anxiety around Fane's neck. Finally, the world-weary prince sighed. "Apparently, word of my-" What should he have called it? His abandonment of his post? Word of his murder, perhaps? Fane met Whitestar's eyes, which he was surprised to see were actually interested in what he was about to say. "-disappearance has gotten around." He finished, setting down his silverware. Whitestar said nothing. "I heard some merchants today talking about how I-" Fane paused again, taking another nervous look around. He lowered his voice further, "How the prince of Aridia has gone missing." "And?" Whitestar said through a mouth-full of food, with an incredulous raise of his thick eyebrows. "And that's a problem." "People were bound to notice at some point." Fane scowled. "That is the problem. I still haven't figured out who it was that tried to kill me, and why that stag wouldn't let me go back home where it was safe." "Stag?" Whitestar looked at him like he was insane. Perhaps he was. "Never mind." Fane waved it away with an irritated hand. "And who says where you came from was any more safe than here?" Whitestar continued, talking through a mouthful of what

appeared to be potatoes. "People have been trying to kill you either way." "So you're saying...?" "How do you know that the person who tried to kill you wasn't from Aridia to begin with? You’re assuming they were some foreign force sent from elsewhere." Whitestar said. The thought had never occurred to Fane until that moment. "I guess-" He began, suddenly feeling as if the floor had opened under his feet. "I guess I don't know that." "And how exactly do you think sneaking around and hiding in a foreign country is going to solve your problems, prince?" "Don't say that too loudly." Fane resented the way Whitestar used his title; always with a tone of sarcasm and contempt. Whitestar gestured to him and slapped a hand on the table, making the liquid in their glasses shiver. "This is what I'm talking about. You're sneaking around, lying about your identity, and hiding. But what have you really accomplished here? You’re nothing more than a coward." Fane glared at him, his mouth in a thin line. Before he could retort, Whitestar continued. "If you were really a prince, wouldn't you care about your own people? They don’t benefit anything from their leader running away and hiding." The woodsman stabbed the table knife into the soft wood absentmindedly, "I would think a prince would take responsibility for the lives under him, rather than laying around on couches all day or running away without a fight." Whitestar's accusation sparked a white-hot heat in Fane's chest. "You don't know anything about me." He growled, leaning forward. Tension hung in the air, muffling the cheery din of the tavern. Whitestar, never one to back down when he was ahead, lowered his voice even more. "And," he snarled, "how many people have died because you only care about yourself?" That was the last straw for Fane. He shot up from his seat without a word, the scrape of wood against wood the only sound in his ringing ears. Whitestar followed suit, grabbing Fane's collar. The simmering heat in Whitestar's eyes told Fane that all the woodsman had on his mind was the desire to break something in his face. Fane didn't care anymore. "Do it." He whispered, "Knock me out and get this over with. That’s how you solve your problems, isn’t it?"

Whitestar breathed for a moment, probably thinking that sounded very inviting indeed. His brown eyes met Fane's gray ones as if they were two predators meeting over the same kill. "That would be too easy." Whitestar finally said, the growl under his tone sounding more animal than human. “Nothing will knock that selfishness out of your head.” Just as he was about to reply, Fane realized suddenly that the whole room had lost all its din. Their tension created quite a commotion in the quiet tavern, and both men forgot momentarily that that sort of behavior was only appropriate for the evening crowd. Alarmed patrons stared at them silently, and Fane saw the bartender start toward them with a sigh. Fane and Rohyr glowered between the bartender and each other, both of them deciding simultaneously that brawling was not worth getting kicked out over. Whitestar released him, and they sat down again without another word. The two men glared at each other over their plates of cold food. Patrons returned to their business, and soon the room was filled with the sounds of the morning again. The bartender went back behind the bar, shooting a watchful glance toward the prince and woodsman every so often. Whitestar finished his meal as if nothing happened, and Fane tentatively did the same. Families came and went, tables were cleaned, waitresses ran to and fro, and still the two men didn't speak. Though the time couldn't have been more than fifteen minutes, to Fane it felt like an hour. Finally, as Fane felt the rage melt from his body, he elected to go first. "Someone did die." He said quietly, not meeting Whitestar's eyes. Fane refused to let the woodsman see the moisture forming in the corner of his eye and quickly turned away. "So you're right." Whitestar nodded nearly imperceptively. Fane met his eyes again. "People have died because of me." There it was. The first time he'd said it aloud. His guards. Rune. They died protecting him. And Fane often wondered if he was worth it. The terrible truth that he'd been avoiding was now staring him in the face. Just as Whitestar did now. As Fane looked back, there was no longer any animosity in the man's face. Though his expression was blank, his eyes softened.

"Me too." Rohyr said, not unkindly. Fane nodded. He had nothing else to say. "You said something about a stag?" Rohyr asked, leaning back in his chair. "Yes..?" Fane started again, watching Rohyr carefully. "What does that have to do with anything?" Rohyr said nothing. Fane sighed. "A stag appeared to me in the forest right before-" Right before Rune had taken an arrow that should have been for him. "Right before my friend died. I turned back when I heard my men fighting in the forest." Rohyr waited. "As Ru- my friend was dying, he told me that I couldn't go back.." Fane's heart twisted in his chest at remembering all of these specific details of that day. Details he would have rather forgotten, but kept him up every night since. It was somehow relieving to finally tell someone the whole story out loud, even if that someone was Rohyr. "The only thing I knew about him was that he was from Eira, so I headed toward the mountains as long as I could." Fane looked up from his tankard to see Rohyr staring at him incredulously, one bushy eyebrow raised. "He was your friend and you didn't know anything else about the man?" "That's not the point." Fane said defensively. "I have to question what you consider to be 'friends'." Rohyr said, smirking into his own tankard, which the same mousey waitress had just returned to refill. "Are you listening?" Fane said, irritability brimming in his voice again. Rohyr merely grinned, and waved for him to continue. "Anyway." Fane did his best to get his temper under control again. "The same stag appeared to me again in the forest when I was on my way here. It must have done something to me because the next thing I know, I was waking up in some old man's house in the middle of the woods." "I know of him." Rohyr said. Of course he does. Fane thought with an inward roll of his eyes. "That's when Niamh arrived, and-" "And you followed her home." Rohyr interrupted, his tone clearly implying that Fane had nefarious purposes in doing so. "And I escorted her the rest of the way to the castle." Fane said with emphasis, "Hael allowed me to stay here until I could go home.

Who knows when that will be, though." Rohyr rubbed his beard with one calloused hand, pausing thoughtfully. Fane glanced down at the axes strapped to Rohyr’s thighs, as they always had been. He noticed, for the first time, that the blades glowed green where they poked out of the leather sheaths. “Why do your axes look like that?” Fane asked suddenly, distracted. Rohyr didn’t answer for a moment. He looked as if he was debating answering at all. After a long tug of his drink, Rohyr leaned on his elbows on the table. “Magic.” He answered. Fane sucked in a breath. Was every Eiran a mage?! “Since when do you have-” Fane started to ask, before Rohyr promptly cut him off. "Has it ever occurred to you that the stag was trying to protect you?" Rohyr said, clearly trying to avoid the magic topic. Fane didn’t mind. “Perhaps you were meant to be here. And I would suggest you find out why, so your friend didn’t die for nothing.” Rohyr crossed his arms, already finished with his second mug of whatever they were drinking. Fane still didn't know. "In the meantime, you can help me figure out who is behind the Fade. If you do a good job keeping your head down, and refrain from announcing your presence to every Fade leader we come across-" Fane knew he was referring to the incident with Malik a few nights back. "-Then maybe you might have a chance at staying incognito, and keep yourself alive long enough to go home." Rohyr said, scratching his beard again. If he knew he was being uncharacteristically helpful, he didn't show it, and Fane wasn't about to complain. It felt good to allow someone else into the problems banging around in his head. As annoyed as Fane was at Rohyr's rough nature and tendency to be as rude as he could get away with, Fane found a strange comfort in knowing that Rohyr was not going to treat him as everyone else had his whole life. Like he was fragile, or unattainably higher and nobler than he really was. "Then you can go home and get out of my hair." Rohyr finished, back to his surly tone. There he is. Fane thought, sighing inwardly. Fane would never have admitted it to the woodsman, but he was

glad he'd asked him for his help. If Fane was honest with himself, he wasn't sure he wanted to go home anymore. For the first time in his life, he'd found people that saw him. Not only for who he truly was, but people who just saw him at all. Life at the Aridian palace, in his plush bed in his huge bedroom, with its expansive library and lush gardens, was far lonelier and more isolated than any of his nights in his tiny bed in the servants' quarters. he'd found a sense of purpose, and wasn't sure if he wanted to give that up anymore. "Well." Rohyr rose unceremoniously from the table, stretching as he did so. "I'm heading back to bed. You go back to doing whatever it is that you do during the day and I'll see you tonight." Fane was left alone with his thoughts, and the hefty bill, as the woodsman strode out of the tavern into the bright sunlight outside.

31 IT WAS HAPPENING AGAIN. This dream was not new. It haunted her for years, and just when Niamh thought she was rid of it, it would appear again. It started out the same every time. It had been a sunny, unusually warm day in Wolfrau. The snow on the ground was wetter than usual. Niamh always started the dream looking down on her younger self. She and Nythaniel were just finishing their morning chores in the horse barn. She could still hear the clink of the metal on the straps of the saddles they just oiled, and the way Nythaniel sang to himself as he lifted it onto its hook above her head. Though she'd seen the dream many times, it was always a surprise to her that this was a scene from before their parents died. We had to sell all the horses afterward. Her older self thought. She was seven or eight at the time. That means Nythaniel would have been about twelve? She could never remember in the fog of dreams. Predictably, a feminine voice drifted over the snow to where they stood near the barn door. Niamh looked out to see a woman running toward them. Niamh assumed after a while that this must have been their mother. Her face was always obscured. Everyone, even then, had always told her how much she resembled her mother, but Niamh could never conjure her face, as hard as she tried. This was always where the dream became fuzzy and unfocused, coming to her in sounds and pictures, scattered and out of order. Nythaniel's face as he watched their mother's approach. Niamh knew he caught on much sooner than she did that there was something wrong. "Niamh, I need you." The woman had said, panting. Niamh could clearly hear panic in her voice, as much as she tried to hide it.

Suddenly, she found herself standing in a fine bedroom in the Mead Hall at the center of the village. Nythaniel was no longer next to her, and there was a woman in a large bed in front of her. Niamh's view had switched to her own eyes, and movement was slow and difficult in the dream from there on to the end. Her mother whispered to the woman in soothing tones. Niamh caught the presence of several of the hall's servants standing on the edges of her vision, all looking helpless. Her mother motioned for her to come closer, which she did with great trepidation. Older Niamh knew just what was about to happen, and she already felt the anxiety clawing its way up her chest. She knew who the woman was, even if younger Niamh did not. The lady of Wolfrau, the Laird's wife. Laboring with what would have been her fifth child. The lady's red hair was spread across the pillow and soaked with the sweat of hours of a difficult childbirth. Niamh's mother was one of the only trained midwives available in the village, and she'd been the only one there that day. Niamh could never hear what her mother was saying to her. As instructions were lost in the distorted reality, Niamh always only heard one sound and one sound only. The lady's struggled breath. The way her cries slowly muted, and no one but her seemed to notice. "Keep her alive for just a few more minutes." "I'll be right back." Her mother dashed from the room, and Niamh sent as much healing magic as her little body could muster into the lady's. Older Niamh, trapped inside her child self, knew she shouldn’t have done that without the threads she would get much later in her life. Channeling raw magic, especially as untrained as she was, and so small, could have been fatal if her mother had been gone too long. Her small hands on the woman's round torso looked completely ineffective. Niamh always wondered why her mother had left her alone. Then there was the worst part. Niamh looked down, and where there used to be white sheets, there was now blood. Rivers of red dripped to the floor, covering everything it touched. No one moved.

Why is no one helping? Her child hands moved from the lady's body for only a few seconds, that was all. The lady's breath vanished. But the blood continued. Niamh's child hands were covered in it before long. She never heard her mother return in the dream. The only thing that she ever heard was her own voice screaming for her. Even as she woke up.

32 FANE REELED AS HE MADE his way through the castle. The Fade’s assortment of weaponry was getting more and more varied by the day. This time, one of them had caught him across the chest with a wickedly jagged short dagger. Fortunately, the wound was shallow and un-poisoned this time, but it still hurt to even breathe as he stumbled his way through the gardens. Part of him prayed that Niamh wouldn't be there, and he might happen upon Hael, someone that might heal him without asking questions. Considering the late hour, almost one in the morning by his guess, the chances were good that he wouldn't catch her there. Though she knew that he was out all night fighting criminals, Fane preferred that Niamh be spared the darker details of the Fade. If he could borrow some of Niamh’s medical supplies, he might be able to get himself healing enough on his own, non-magical power. Floating lights guided his way between the ice animals, bringing the familiar cottage into view. His heart dropped to see that there was indeed a light on inside, and he braced himself for Niamh’s searching, too-curious eyes as he knocked on the door. A bright voice called to him from inside, far more energetic than the one he was expecting. “Come in!” The door opened to the warm room, the fireplace blazing full blast against the wall. Maewyn’s white head bobbed as she drifted back and forth between stations on the long table, mixing multiple ingredients for multiple potions, he guessed. Maewyn flicked her sea-green eyes to him. “Oh! Fane! My, this is a surprise.” She wiped her hands on her work apron and grinned at him. Fane was relieved to see that Niamh was not waiting for him with her questions tonight. He

wasn’t sure how he could explain away such a large gash; she would probably know he was lying anyway. Fane did his best to bow politely as fire ripped across his chest when he moved. “Maewyn.” Maewyn caught sight of the slash across the front of his tunic. Her eyes widened. “What did you do to yourself?” She exclaimed, dropping her task and moving toward him. Why do they always assume I’m the culprit? He thought exasperatedly. “I need this mended. If you’re willing.” He said, gesturing to his chest and he knew that Maewyn knew he didn’t mean his shirt. The young woman hesitated, a rare sight, and inspected the wound carefully. “I’m not as good at healing as Niamh is.” She admitted. Fane nodded. “I would prefer that Niamh didn’t know anyway.” He immediately regretted that last part, as Maewyn cast him an incredulous look. With a wave of her hand, she shooed him toward the all-too- familiar sitting chairs and moved the other directly in front of him. Definitely a more abrasive approach than Niamh. Maewyn stared at him. “What?” He asked, uncomfortable at her sudden seriousness. “Take off your shirt.” She said. He grimaced. “Why?” “I can’t very well fix you up if you’ve got bloody strips of fabric in the way.” She replied. He supposed she was right. Fane obliged and gingerly rolled the shirt from his back, careful not to bend too far over to agitate the wound. He threw it behind him to the floor, making sure not to bloody the girls’ furniture. As he sat, Maewyn set to work cleaning the wound for him. She hesitated, as if running through the steps in her mind, before finally settled crouching in front of him. He was stronger now than he was the last time he came to the cottage. All those nights running around the slums and training with Rohyr were paying off, and he was pleased to see definition toning his chest and abdomen. Gone was the prince that laid about, hiding from servant girls. He was replaced by a man that hunted criminals and won. A man that he could be proud of. Once Maewyn had cleaned the wound, she gave him a sheepish look. “Like I said, I’m not as good at this as Niamh is. Master Hael

helped me make the thread for healing magic, like, a week ago.” This did nothing to set Fane’s mind at ease. He was beginning to wonder if asking Maewyn was a mistake he would never recover from. Mages, even healers, still hadn’t proved to him that magic could be trusted. Rubbing her hands like one starting a fire, Maewyn summoned a glow of blue-green light to her palms. Though it reminded him of the way it looked when Niamh did it, the light was not as bright or as steady as hers usually was. Maewyn knew this too, and carefully laid her hands on his chest as if she wasn’t sure if she would be successful. Her magic smelled like a salty breeze blowing from the shore, mixed with the mild scent of peaches. Fane smiled, which was quickly replaced by an involuntary laugh as Maewyn’s fierce magic fizzed across his chest and tickled him. She giggled, too, probably encouraged enough to keep her magic from flickering. She leaned into him, allowed her magic to flow deeper and more confidently, healing as she went. Fane watched her as her face came closer to his. He could feel her breath on his chin, her hands sliding outward to cover more of the wound that was slowly shrinking. He instinctively leaned back. His awkwardness was worsened as she rose from her own chair, leaning into his body as the warmth of her magic spread across his chest. If Maewyn noticed that she was appearing immodest, she didn’t show it. She focused intently on the wound, as if taking her eyes off of it would result in failure. “Maewyn-“ Fane started, sliding further into the chair uncomfortably in an effort to escape. Maewyn was jolted out of her concentration at once. “What? I’m almost done.” The door to the cottage suddenly opened. Both Fane and Maewyn whipped their heads to see Niamh step through the door, her eyes bleary. Those eyes widened as Niamh took in Fane’s half- nakedness, and Maewyn’s hands spread across his chest. There was no time to explain away what it looked like. He watched as her eyes took in their prostrate position, flicking between Maewyn’s face near his own. A flush crept up Fane’s ears. The implication was clear on her face. Niamh’s eyes went from alarm, to grief, to embarrassment in a moment’s flicker of emotion. His stomach dropped through the floor.

“Oh.” Niamh stammered, averting her eyes. The red of rose petals crept across her nose and up to her ears. “Oh, I’m sorry. Y- You’re obviously...busy.” She seemed to be frozen in place, staring at the two of them. Fane shot from his chair, wincing at more than just the physical pain. “Niamh-“ Maewyn was promptly sloughed to the floor. Fane quickly stepped around the chair, toward the young healer now slowly backing her way toward the door. He was extremely aware of the cold breeze washing over his bare chest. Niamh didn't meet Fane’s eyes. “I-I just needed-...some sleeping potion...but I can get it tomorrow...” She continued backing away from him. He reached a hand toward her, trying to catch one of hers. Niamh jerked away, her eyes not leaving the floor. “Fane just needed a little help, Niamh.” Niamh’s eyes turned toward Maewyn, who was leaning anxiously over the back of the couch, her brows knitted. “Help?” Niamh looked up at Fane accusingly, as she hugged herself. Before Fane could say anything else, Niamh turned on her heel away from him, nearly running out of the door to the cottage and vanished into the darkness. It was all Fane could do to pinch his nose, closing his eyes. “That was not how I imagined this ending.” He muttered to himself, Maewyn’s presence forgotten. Regret was Fane's dearest friend. EVERYTHING NIAMH HAD suspected had been true. Though she'd suspected that Fane and Maewyn had some secret meetings or...or secret feelings...Niamh never expected that they would be meeting in her cottage in the dead of night. In fact, it wasn’t what she expected. It was worse. Her thoughts and feelings swirled in her head, mingling together until she couldn’t tell them apart, as she continued swiftly back to her room. She had only wanted to find the simple lavender and chamomile mixture she kept a stock of in her work drawers, but she regretted ever going down there so late now. Maewyn and Fane?

Niamh could hardly think of the words that she wanted to say, that she'd been trying to say for weeks now. Everything that she thought she shared between her and the handsome golden haired stranger was a lie; the fantasies of a silly girl desperate for attention. Niamh cursed herself silently for the attachment that she had convinced herself was there, for pretending that he saw her as anything more than the castle healer available to him when he got himself into trouble. His chest was so much harder than last she had seen it, honed with muscle that glimmered with sweat in the firelight. How could I have been so foolish? She thought miserably, finally reaching her room once more. With a sharp inhale, Niamh threw her clothes to the floor and slipped into her nightgown. There was never anything there. She told herself firmly, staring at the dark ceiling above her head as she lay in her bed. I had simply imagined it, and Fane should not be held responsible for my own... She rolled over, blinking away the tears stinging her eyes. For my own wishful thinking. Despite her best efforts to push Maewyn, and Fane especially, from her mind, the image of them leaning into each other in the light of the fire still floated across her vision. Closing her eyes, she saw nothing but the firm wall of Fane’s chest, Maewyn’s hands laid gently over it, and a deep, selfish part of her wished that they were her own.

33 A KNOCK AT THE DOOR woke Niamh from her restless dozing. After the incident in the cottage, she’d barely been able to sleep until several hours later. She rolled over, wishing the warm covers would send her back to her, for once, dreamless sleep. Another knock, this time more frantic. "Miss Niamh, you're needed urgently." The woman on the other side sounded panicked and out of breath. Niamh rose from her bed and quickly crossed to open the door. A midwife stood there, one of the girls she’d trained with Hael only a few months prior. "What's going on?" Niamh was immediately awake, stepping into her slippers and donning a thin robe. "It’s your friend.” The midwife panted, her hand to her chest. Niamh’s blood turned cold. “What about my friend? Who is it?” She said, grabbing the midwife’s shaking arm. “Ailish. She-she went into labor. It's too early, by a month, at least." The midwife said, her eyes wide. “She’s in the stables. We couldn’t move her further than that. She tried to come find you.” Without another word, Niamh grabbed her apothecary bag from near the door and followed the midwife down far too many stairs. Even before they reached the stables, Ailish’s thin and distressed cries could be heard echoing across the courtyard. Niamh was already running through the procedures in her head, checking off all of the stages of delivery that may have come before if she was already screaming. As they burst into the stables, running to one of the closer stalls, she had her confirmation. Ailish would have already been in labor for most of the evening at this point, and the two other midwives gathered around her tried in vain to soothe her pains. Niamh wished her husband could be there with them, but he would have to hear about it later. Niamh immediately rolled up her sleeves and stepped into a

position where she could see all that she needed to. As she thought, Ailish was dilated enough at that hour to give birth properly. It's clear she's having the proper amount of contractions. Niamh saw, with dismay, that all three of the midwives present were only newly trained, and were all slightly younger than her. No one of significant experience, other than herself for as much as it was worth, was to be seen. "How long have you been working with her?" She asked one of the other women near her. "Nearly four hours now." The midwife answered. Niamh nodded. That was nothing unusual. She had seen births take up to nearly twelve hours when she assisted the healers of Wolfrau. Ailish's face was twisted with pain and sweat soaked the hay around her. Niamh rubbed her ankles soothingly. "Ailish, I need you to focus and breathe with me." Niamh laid a hand on her friend’s rounded stomach. Just as she had hoped, Ailish opened her panicked eyes and met Niamh's calm blue ones. Ailish visibly relaxed. “Niamh. You came.” "Yes. I’m here.” Niamh said, “Breathe in." She commanded softly, breathing in herself as a demonstration. Ailish followed suit. "And out." Again, Ailish obeyed. The two of them continued breathing together, even as Niamh could see her friend was clearly in excruciating pain. "Keep breathing, and I will help you from there. Your job is to breathe, Ailish. Can you do that for me?" Ailish nodded sharply, her shoulders tense. She turned to the midwives. "I need someone to bring me fresh hot water, and crush the sage that I have brought in that bag." Niamh sprung into action, acting completely on instinct and her healer's intuition. Start with the basics, then go from there. Her mother’s voice popped into her mind, repeating the instructions that she often told herself. She took a moment amidst the stress of the situation to wash her hands and take a deep breath. It was always better to start with taking a breath of one's own before asking the mothers to do it themselves. Another thing she had learned over her years in Wolfrau. Once the midwives had provided the hot water, Niamh stirred the crushed sage into it. The swirling herbs helped calm her own mind, and she set to work running through the birthing procedures. As she worked, Niamh selected the most experienced of the three

new midwives to help her in holding the wetted cloths to the right locations. The other two were tasked with providing supplies and speaking soothing words to the mother. After the second hour of this, Niamh felt dread stirring in the back of her mind. Much to Niamh’s distress, Ailish was seemingly less and less responsive as the minutes dragged on. Her breathing slowed. Something is wrong... The baby is nowhere near being delivered... Niamh could sense that even the midwives were beginning to fade. The younger girls were even seemingly relieved that she was no longer screaming in pain and instead seemed to be relaxed. No one but Niamh was concerned. While Niamh was distracted studying the faces around her, she felt something hot gush over her hands. A look down revealed exactly what she dreaded seeing most. Where there should have been the head and shoulders of a baby, there was instead a growing stain of bright red over the sheets, the Ailish's legs, over Niamh's hands, and dripping to the floor. No. No, not again. Please not again. Just as in every one of her dreams, her hands were covered in blood. It ran down her arm, staining the sleeves of her nightgown. Everything seemed suddenly far away, as if she had been pulled from the scene. Is this another dream? As much as she tried, she couldn't look away from her hands. It's not real... Niamh knew she was breathing, though she couldn't hear the sound. She felt herself standing on solid wood, but her feet suddenly felt as if they were not her own. It was as if she was standing outside of herself, watching the scene unfold around her. "Miss Niamh." Her breath came in short gasps. It's not real. A pool of a woman's blood continued to grow around her. Or is it Nythaniel's blood? Who is dying? "Miss Niamh!" Everyone in the room was panicking. Niamh could only stand and watch, paralyzed. The only sound she heard was the drip of blood to the fabric of her nightgown as it flowed down her hands. "What do we do?" The younger midwife grasped Niamh's wrist, nearly crying. "We..." Niamh started, still staring between her bloodied hands

and Ailish, dying on the bed. "We need..." Ailish’s face looked more like the Lady of Wolfrau. Her eyes closed, her chest rising in shallow waves. Sweat pouring down her pale face. "What?! We need what?" "We need Master Hael." His was the only name she could bring to mind at that moment. "Go get Master Hael." At the sudden clear direction, the young midwife ran from the stables. Clarity was beginning to make its way back to Niamh, and she counted the seconds as they ticked by. Mentally following the girl to Hael's house, Niamh did her best to staunch the bleeding with the tools she had. She dared not look down again, nor pay any attention to her hands as they worked. Everyone waited with baited breath. Ailish was losing life by the second. Niamh listened to the drip of her sweat falling to the wood floor to stay focused. They didn't need to wait long. There was a flash of orange light from outside, accompanied by a sudden wave of heat. Hael stepped into the room, hurrying immediately to take Niamh's position. He didn't acknowledge her beyond a quick nod before he set to work. Hael held more healing magic in his hands at once than Niamh could muster in a week, and he needed no thread to channel his power. His hands glowed with a warm yellow light, pulsing with his heartbeat. He laid a healing hand on Ailish’s abdomen, causing her to settle into a truly restful state. His magic went to work as all of them watched, soothing pain, stopping the bleeding, and bringing her body into alignment. The other young healers looked on in awe, and Niamh could only do the same. Hael had at least fifty more years of experience on her, and it was apparent in his efficiency and bedside manner. "Niamh." Hael's cold, focused voice interrupted her thoughts. "I want you to use your magic to turn the baby while I'm doing this. On my word, you will coax him into delivery while I heal the ruptures. Do you understand?" "Yes, sir." Niamh, glad to have something to focus on, went up to stand at Ailish's side. If Hael was angry with her, he was doing an excellent job of hiding it. He only spoke to the mother in soothing, calm instructions. There was nothing but concentrating, concerned tenderness in his eyes. Niamh did as she was told, streaming her magic into her friend’s

womb to internally turn the baby inside in the right direction. It didn't protest, even cooperating with her as she gently wrapped it in soft magic. Thanks to the connection that her healing magic gave her, Niamh could feel that the baby was as eager to come into the world as she was to deliver it. This gave her a sense of calm even in the midst of the chaos. She smiled. You're almost there. She closed her eyes, letting her magic sweep her away into the task. The room, with all its anxious eyes watching her work, disappeared and fell into a haze. Her magic blended and intertwined with her Master's like waves that run over each other and mingle as they crash against a rocky shore. Master and apprentice's magic worked together, in and around the other, healing as they went. "Niamh." With a gentle but firm push, Niamh tugged the baby's tiny body into the correct position just as Hael sent one last surge of magic in and around the process taking place. Only minutes later, a healthy boy emerged wailing into Hael's waiting hands. Niamh was snapped back to reality by the sound of crying, seeing Hael hand the boy gingerly to the midwives to be washed off. They did exactly that and moments later, handed him to his mother to nestle against her chest. Ailish was showing good color again, all her pain forgotten. Hael still didn't say a word to Niamh, even as he smiled and congratulated the new mother. Only after he determined that all was well, that Ailish was out of danger, and the midwives were put to work cleaning the mess, did Hael turn to take his leave. It had been less than an hour since the time that Niamh was summoned from her room, but it felt like an eternity. Hael passed by without looking at her. Maybe, in the midst of all the confusion, Niamh might’ve been spared the lecture she deserved and be able to go back to bed. "My office. Now." She thought wrong.

34 THEY WALKED THE LONG hallways back to Hael's office in strained silence. If Niamh couldn't tell that Hael was angry back in the stables, she definitely could now. Wrath seemed to billow off of him like clouds of steam. All futile hope she had that he would go easy on her for this mistake was gone as soon as his heavy door shut with a click. "What was that, Niamh?" Hael threw his bloodied cloak over the back of his chair and turned on her. He met her eyes with a furious heat. "What was that?" Shame flooded her. "I don't know." "You needed my help with a complicated birth? That's something that should have been easy for you. You're telling me that situation was unmanageable for you?" Hael's normally brown eyes seemed on fire, burning through her. "Your hesitance. Your uncertainty. Your failure to perform your responsibility as my heir apparent, as a healer, almost cost that woman her life. And her child." Hael’s voice cracked strangely at the last word. He held his hands behind his back, as if restraining from throwing things. His bird ruffled its feathers at being disturbed. She winced. "Would you care to inform me what made you hesitate? This isn't like you, Niamh." "Th-there was blood." As soon as the words fell from her mouth, she regretted them. Hael would have laughed if he wasn't so incredibly furious with her. "Blood. You saw blood." She nodded feebly. She couldn't even gather the words to explain. "It was on my hands." Hael ran a tired hand down his face, seemingly defeated. He sighed. "There was blood on your hands."

Tears welled in Niamh's eyes. Why can't I tell him? "I haven't been...sleeping...very well." She knew it sounded ridiculous. Juvenile. Stop making excuses. Hael stared at her. "You're telling me that a mother almost died because you were tired." "Yes." She cursed inwardly. "No. I-" Niamh's exhale shook. "I haven't been able to sleep for- a while- and every time-" She looked at her hands, blood still crusted under her fingernails. The sleeves of her robe were stained with it. And every time I open my eyes, all I see is blood. She wanted to tell him everything. About the nightmares, about Maire’s vague threats. She even wanted to tell him about Maewyn..And Fane. All that she wanted to say died on the edge of her tongue. "With all that's been going on; with this mysterious illness going around that I'm trying to solve, I can't have you, my best healer, suddenly dropping all of your duties." Hael was pacing now,. "So, I will ask you again: What seems to be the problem that is so pressing that it's ruining your ability to do your job?" Hael waited, watching her and seething. "I feel like I've been halluc-" Niamh stopped, her mouth paralyzed. "Yes?" Hael was losing what sliver of patience he had left. "I..I can't-" Why can't I just say something? Her eyes filled with frustrated tears. You're already on thin ice. You're failing at the one thing that he entrusted to you. Am I going insane? Her mental barrage on herself only continued unhindered. "I-I.." What did she need? How could he help? Even saying that out loud sent Niamh down another spiral of shame. She was a healer, the heir to the Head Magician, she should know if there was something wrong with her. But deep down, Niamh knew, there was nothing to heal. She was a disappointment, and she knew it. Hael sighed again, closing his eyes and sitting in the chair behind his desk in defeat. He pinched the bridge of his nose. "Niamh. Do you understand why I chose you to be my apprentice? Most magicians take on apprentices constantly, but you were my first one in many years." Niamh dared not take her own seat. She didn't deserve to. Hael continued without waiting for a reply. "Because you have such talent. Focus, control. You also have intense empathy and

compassion. That is what makes you a good healer. If you don't have all of those things, how can I trust you to do your job?" "I'm sorry, Master. I'm trying." Oh, how she despised that whining edge to her voice. Hael’s bird focused on her, as if seeing right through her. She could hardly look at it. Niamh squelched the indignance rising inside. Hael was right, as he always was. "Niamh." Hael watched her intently, all ferocity replaced by heavy weariness. Almost as heavy as her own. "If you can't perform the duties that I have trained you to do. If there are any more careless mistakes, I-" He paused, as if he couldn't bring himself to finish the sentence. Niamh held her breath. "If you falter again, I am going to have to reevaluate your eligibility as my apprentice." Niamh swallowed every ounce of protest. There was nothing she could say. Did the queen say something to him? But Hael knows that I’m not usually like this. Shame bit at her heart like a dark wolf, and she bowed her head under it. Niamh could barely speak for the lump in her throat, opting to nod to hide the tears welling in her eyes. Hael waved her out without another word. Niamh turned and left, pausing as she closed the door to lean against its hard wood for comfort. I have to be better. She brought a shaky hand to her forehead, wiping her eyes to keep the tears from dripping freely. Why do I keep making mistakes? The ringing in her ears and numbness in her heart did not let up as she pushed off from the door back to her waiting bed. Out of sight from the rest of the world, Niamh let her emotions wash over her. Her pillows were soon soaked from her tears.

35 FANE HAD BEEN AVOIDING both Niamh and Maewyn since the incident in the cottage. He’d taken to staying out later with Rohyr and checking around every corner for the both of them. Niamh, he wasn’t worried too much about, since she was likely to avoid him just as much. But Maewyn was another story. One evening, after he’d finished his work in the Library, Fane was taking his usual shortcut through the main hall of the castle. He began his usual tactic of skulking against the wall, around columns, and dodging servants, when he heard familiar voices on the verge of argument. "It's no use giving me that look, Niamh. You don't want to go, I know." Hael's voice said. Fane couldn't decide if he sounded amused or not. "Why can't Maewyn go? I've got so much to do." Niamh's tone was bordering on a whine. Fane smirked. That was new. "The queen has specifically requested that you do. And I don't trust Maewyn to bring back accurate information, frankly. And she has work to do with her embroidery." There was a tense silence. With a sigh, Niamh relented. "When do I leave?" "As soon as possible." "And I'm only heading up north? What do you want me to bring back?" "Information. I need to know the situation, the symptoms people have, how many people are sick, things like that." "I'm going alone?" "Do you want to?" Niamh was silent again. Fane could almost picture her face as she thought about her answer. "Well.. No. Not really." "I have just the person. Fane!" Fane jumped at the sound of his name. Hael suddenly turned toward him where he waited behind

the corner. "If you'll stop skulking around corners and eavesdropping on others’ conversations, you might be of some use." Fane emerged rather sheepishly, joining the two of them. Niamh flicked icy eyes in his direction for only a moment before watching her boots with an unusual interest. "You'll escort my apprentice to the northern towns, I'll let the Keeper know that you'll not be in the Library." "What?!" Niamh protested, looking at Hael as if he’d just announced some great betrayal. Fane cringed inwardly. "Master, I can assure you-" "I'll expect you both back before the Festival, if you please." Hael was apparently settled on the matter. He turned and walked down the hallway. "Be sure to dress warmly, Fane. We don't want Niamh to have to carry your frozen body all the way back by herself." He said over his shoulder. Fane could have sworn he laughed to himself. There truly was no reprieve. The master mage was gone before Niamh could protest further. The pair stood alone in painfully awkward silence. Niamh still refused to look at him, the tips of her ears turning red as the seconds ticked on like hours. Tightness guarded her every move, and she kept her hands closely clasped to her middle. "Niamh-" Fane started. "Meet me at first light in the courtyard." She said, her voice as hard and sharp as the icicles hanging outside the window. Niamh turned on her heel and marched away without another word. The next morning, Niamh swung up on to her huge draft horse, Alvyss, as he stood awaiting their arrival outside the stables in the courtyard. She was dressed in sturdy riding clothes, warm leggings under her layered skirts of dark blue. Fane matched her movements and mounted his own horse, dressed in basically all the clothing he owned. He had a feeling this trip would be cold, and not just because of the weather. Without a word, the pair rode toward the castle town and beyond its gates. The wilderness of Eira spread before them. Fane glanced to Niamh, who stared straight ahead. Her face was as cold as the wind whipping their hair. This was going to be a long trip. THEY ARE SENDING ME out into the wilderness with him, of all

people. Niamh clenched her hands tightly in her soft leather gloves. She resented everything about the situation: Hael sent her out to investigate this sickness, and with the one person she didn't want to see the most. While Maewyn gets to stay at home, in the warm castle. She felt like a cast-off, like Hael was trying to keep her from underfoot. A nuisance. I know it's because of my blunder with that birth. She thought critically to herself. Hael knew that a trip out of the castle walls was more of a punishment for Niamh than it would have been for Maeywn. And that's why he sent me. She thought with bitterness. Niamh slid her eyes to the man riding next to her, his features hidden by the scarf of his cloak. Only his gray eyes peered from the dark gray cocoon. This was the first time she had seen him since the incident in her cottage a few nights previous. Albeit with much less clothing. A fact that had filled her with dread as soon as Fane had joined their conversation the day before. This wasn’t like her; this judgmental, punishing avoidance of someone she called her friend. Is he my friend? Does he see me as his friend? Something about the idea of being just his friend tied her stomach in knots. Niamh shook that thought away. Fane would have to work for every word that he would get from her. She was determined to make this trip as difficult as possible to keep him from getting too comfortable in her presence again. AFTER THE FOURTH HOUR of riding, as the sun dipped beneath the mountain passes, the pair stopped for the evening. The wind whipped colder by the minute, snow blowing into Fane’s eyes and freezing his limbs. He honestly had no idea how the people of Eira continued to subject themselves to this harsh and unforgiving environment. him, startling Fane. He jumped at the sight of a dark red beard and a head of long hair appearing next to him. many of the older generation. Chuckles circled around. "Most of you know how tonight's going to go, yes?" He clasped his hands together and nodded along with everyone's noises of affirmation. He came back briefly to fill a kettle with water, leaning around her at the water basin to draw it from the hand pump. She handed him a sturdy mug in his free hand. "You can pour yourself a cup of tea and then pour the rest of that water in here so I can finish cleaning." "Yes, taskmaster." Niamh rolled her eyes, even as Rohyr did as she asked. Her heart sank with a sense of nostalgia. This was exactly how mornings with Nythaniel often went. How she missed that casual banter they had. It was nothing but manners and social graces at the palace. Moments later, Rohyr stood over her, carefully pouring the scalding water into her water basin while she removed her hands. His other hand held a steaming mug of the strongest tea she had in her cabinet. The aroma filled the whole room. "Why did you come by this morning, Rohyr?" She asked. He finished pouring and set the kettle aside on a knitted pad. "I wanted a moment alone with you without him here." "Then you have it." She said. Niamh coated her hands in magic like a pair of gloves and wetted a rag in the soapy water. She set to work wiping off all the surfaces in the small kitchen. "What do you have to say? Rohyr sighed, cutting right to the chase. "You're worried about Nythaniel. More than usual. And I can tell you're not sleeping well because of it." You don't know the half of it. She thought. Out loud, she said, "I'm not sleeping well for a lot of reasons." "You know I'm not the person to lie to make you feel better."

Rohyr watched her work from where he leaned on the counter. "So you might have reason to worry. He hasn't ever been away this long without saying anything, has he?" "Like you would know." Niamh nearly clapped a hand over her mouth. Rohyr raised his eyebrows, catching the resentment that she let slip, even if she wished he didn't. "I-I mean..." Niamh started, flushing. "I mean that you have been away for so long and you haven't-" "No, no." Rohyr held up a hand, his face betraying his apparent enjoyment of this scene, "I want to hear exactly what you wanted to say the first time." Niamh paused, still flushed. I really must have more of a hangover than I thought. Rohyr waited, sipping on his still-too-hot tea in the silence. "Well..." Niamh scrubbed the counter harder, trying to transfer her annoyance to her hands instead of her mouth. "It's just that-" He still waited. Infuriatingly patient when she was trying to be mad at him. "You wouldn't know. Because you haven't been around. I haven't seen you in several years and then you have the nerve to show up and be concerned for me and Nythaniel? When did you start caring, Rohyr? Why did you decide to show yourself out of the blue when I have already decided that I don't need..you.." There it was. Niamh had given up needing him or anyone else a long time ago. The only sound between them was the wussh of her rag against the wooden countertops. She avoided his eyes. "Do you want the real answer?" He asked in a measured, even voice. He was seemingly unfazed by her raw feelings. "I came back because someone needed to deal with the Fade. No one else was going to, and the rats were only growing in numbers, so I came back to do what I could." So he didn't come back for me, after all. Niamh tried not to let that truth sting too deeply. "But," He continued, "Nythaniel did ask me to keep an eye on you whenever he would leave town." He set his empty mug on the counter and watched her carefully. Niamh's hand wasn't even moving anymore. She met his eyes. "I'm sorry I haven't been doing a good job of that, Little Sparrow."

The sudden admittance of guilt from someone such as Rohyr sent Niamh's stomach into nervous butterflies. "I-I mean, I've done a good job taking care of myself." Rohyr chuckled through his nose and reached over to scrub her hair affectionately. "Yes, you have." Niamh returned to cleaning. “Why are you doing this?” Niamh paused thoughtfully, wringing her cloth. “This vigilante work. This isn’t usually like you, Rohyr.” "People were disappearing from the outer villages." Rohyr's eyes darkened as he looked out the window to their left. “The young men would be gone without a trace, their families left with some mysterious illness. Even their healers couldn’t solve it." He looked at her, though there was no judgment in his eyes. “No one was coming to save them.” “We...” Niamh said, her cloth forgotten in the water. “We didn’t even hear of this.” “You didn’t hear of it because all of their soldiers were the young men going missing,” Rohyr said, “And no one else in the villages were well enough to send word. So that’s why I came back to the city- to get to the bottom of it all.” “Why aren’t you getting the guards involved?” Niamh asked, “Wouldn't they be willing to help?” “It’s hard to convince them of criminal activity when there’s no evidence.” Rohyr grumbled, “And that’s why they’re happy just to take them off of my hands, but they’re not willing to get their own hands dirty. They say there’s no proof of conspiracy.” He scoffed, “And besides, they have their own families to worry about. I’m sure there’s plenty of them that know something is amiss, but they are unwilling to get involved for the sake of their families.” He paused, watching her carefully. “That’s why I’m perfect for the job.” “You still have your father, Rohyr.” Niamh said. She stood, dumping the dirty water into the sink. Rohyr didn’t reply, merely staring out the window again. “It took me a while to make the connection. When I first arrived, there were hardly any loose threads to connect at all. Then, one night, I saw one of them coming out of a house, out the back door. He had some symbol on his arm, like a broken glass heart-” “A heart?” Niamh interjected. That’s a strange choice for a symbol. “And you think they’re behind these people disappearing?”

“The Fade... They’re some kind of...criminal organization. Like a syndicate. It doesn't matter how many of them I haul in to the guards, two take their place." "And that's why you needed Fane's help?" "I didn't need it." Rohyr growled, "But, yes, that's why I keep him around." Niamh wrung out her cloth thoughtfully. "Did he tell you about the Dark Tree?" Niamh spent the next few minutes filling Rohyr in on all the details from her and Fane's travels. Everything from the villagers dying in the towns, to the Tree itself. Though she left out the part when Fane carried her all the way home after she had apparently passed out. Rohyr didn't need to know that tidbit. "I think that maybe the sickness and the Tree are connected." Niamh said at last. She had finished her cleaning and was now sitting at the table while Rohyr remained leaning against the counter. "The closer we got to it, the more people were dead. So proximity to the Tree is directly tied to the rate of mortality." She paused, troubled. “I don’t think it can be cured with normal medicine.” Rohyr hadn't said a word during her whole monologue save for the occasional nod or grunt of acknowledgement. "Maybe the Fade are connected too?" She finished. "Who knows." He said thoughtfully. Knowing Rohyr as well as she did, however, Niamh knew that Rohyr knew more than he let on. They sat in comfortable silence for another several moments. "Are you coming back with us?" Niamh asked. Rohyr nodded distractedly. She waited. Rohyr nodded again, plucking his furs from the other chair and shrugging them on. "Someone's got to keep that skulking character away from you while we're on the road." Rohyr smirked good- naturedly. Niamh shook her head. "At least I have you around to do that for me." She smirked back.
